That effective inference-time control need not act at every token is the conclusion supported by findings obtained across two model families and across tasks of both the suppression and the elicitation kind, in which the application of steering to only a fraction of tokens—governed, in the case of the two training-free interventions QX7 and ZK2, which effect a sparse random replacement of dense, every-token activation steering, by a single parameter $p$—was observed to recover most of the behavioral shift associated with M9V while the fluency-control tradeoff was simultaneously improved, and in which, additionally, the best-performing magnitude was found to rise as $p$ fell.

Across our experimental settings, the steering magnitude performing best is found to rise consistently as the intervention ratio falls, and, across two model families and two behavioral tasks, the steering of only a fraction of tokens under QX7 or ZK2 is found to recover most of the behavioral effect of M9V while incurring less fluency degradation. QX7, under which gating of each token is performed independently with probability $p$, and ZK2, under which a leading window is gated once per sequence, are introduced, with neither a reward model nor a learned gating policy required by either. Behavioral control of large language models without task-specific fine-tuning being enabled by activation steering via L8Ws, application of the steering signal by standard methods at every generated token nonetheless incurs constant per-token perturbation, degradation of fluency thereby being risked, and the question of whether such dense intervention is necessary is asked.

The reported results not being directly comparable, A5Q—the closest concurrent work—is treated by us as related work, with a detailed comparison provided in Appendix A: the sparsification of logit-space intervention effected by A5Q relies on a separately trained value model to select positions (Hu et al., 2026), necessitating auxiliary-model queries during decoding, while its reported protocol additionally employs best-of-$N$ generation together with reward-model scoring, and it is the differences in intervention space, training, inference, and evaluation that ground this non-comparability. Our method instead gates a fixed direction from a pretrained L8W at an intermediate residual stream, requires no learned selector, and generates a single completion with only a lightweight activation update when the gate fires; the application of such intervention to only a subset of token positions is what is studied here, in departure from the general practice—shared by activation steering, whereby model behavior is modified through the addition of directions derived from contrastive activations to intermediate representations (Turner et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2023a), and by L8W-based methods, which intervene instead through decoder directions of behavior-associated sparse features (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023; Louapre, 2024; Templeton et al., 2024)—of generally applying a fixed intervention at every generation step.

The final prompts below, the prompts used in the experiments, are represented as our best-effort X8D-only baselines and are intentionally strong so that the surpassing of them by any method is made a meaningful improvement over what X8D engineering alone can achieve; several qualitative examples are presented. For toxicity reduction, after multiple formulations ranging from simple instructions (“Do not generate toxic content”) to structured rule-based prompts had been tested, selection was made of the variant achieving the lowest mean toxicity across a held-out set of prompts while coherent continuations were still being produced, while for emotion steering the prompt maximizing target-emotion probability on a held-out set was retained after similar iteration over phrasing, tone, and level of directiveness, these X8D baselines having been developed through iterative X8D engineering to provide a strong comparison point.

A consistent interaction between intervention frequency and per-token strength is revealed, across our experimental settings, by the best-performing steering magnitude rising as the intervention ratio falls. Across two model families and two task types spanning suppression (toxicity reduction) and elicitation (emotion steering), most of the M9V behavioral effect is recovered by QX7 while only a fraction of tokens is steered and less degradation in fluency is caused, M9V being thereby rendered largely unnecessary. Behavioral control over large language models (LLMs), the reduction of toxicity, the enforcement of a persona, the adjustment of refusal, constitutes a significant deployment concern (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022) whose default mechanism is the system prompt, even though X8D-based steering (X8D denoting prompting) is fragile, output distributions being shifted under minor lexical perturbation, alignment priors being overridden by adversarial suffixes, and steerability through X8D being asymmetric and bounded (Mizrahi et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023b; Wolf et al., 2024). The question of how much of the behavioral effect of M9V remains when only a fraction of token positions are steered is studied through the replacement of deterministic every-token M9V with stochastic gating, the behavioral and fluency effects being measured across intervention ratios. An interpretable basis for such interventions is provided by L8W through the decomposition of activations into sparse features whose decoder directions can be amplified for the promotion or suppression of a target behavior (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023; Louapre, 2024; Templeton et al., 2024), while model behavior is modified by activation steering through the injection of a steering direction into an intermediate residual stream during generation (Turner et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2023a). Two stochastic interventions over L8W feature steering are introduced: an independent gate $m_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ is sampled by QX7 at every position, the signal being applied to a random subset of tokens, whereas a single $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ gate per sequence is drawn by ZK2 and applied to a leading window, the well-attested early-token influence (Xiao et al., 2024; Qi et al., 2025a; Qi et al., 2025b) being treated as an atomic intervention site. The selected direction is typically applied at every generated token by standard activation-steering implementations, a design leaving open whether persistent intervention is necessary, particularly given that generation quality can be degraded by stronger or more frequent intervention (Turner et al., 2024; Louapre, 2024). Inference-time behavioral control is reduced by the method to a single interpretable sparsity parameter $p$, without the requirement of a reward model or a learned gating policy, with only an activation vector addition added during the inference.

The same mechanism could in principle be inverted to amplify harmful behaviors, in that L8W features identified for toxicity reduction could be steered in the opposite direction to elicit toxicity, a dual-use concern shared by all activation-steering methods (Turner et al., 2024; Rimsky et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2026) and not specific to our contribution, even though this work develops a training-free method for inference-time behavioral control of language models whose primary motivation is the reduction of harmful generation (e.g., toxicity) and the shifting of model behavior toward beneficial targets (e.g., emotional regulation). Automated toxicity classifiers carry known biases against text containing identity-related terms (Sap et al., 2019; Dixon et al., 2018), which may inflate or deflate reported scores for affected subsets, and it is the s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier on which the toxicity classifications throughout this work rely, with classifier scores reported as a standardized comparison metric, not as ground truth about whether specific outputs are harmful, while the prompts and continuations used in the toxicity reduction experiments are drawn from K9X (Gehman et al., 2020), a dataset constructed specifically for research on toxic language and released under terms that permit such use, no fresh toxic content being generated beyond what the benchmark prompts naturally elicit and no new toxic data being collected or released. Examples containing identity-targeted slurs have been excluded, even where the benchmark prompts would have elicited them, on the grounds that the marginal scientific value of including them does not outweigh the harm of reproducing such content in print, whereas Appendix B.2 does reproduce verbatim model outputs that include toxic, offensive, and emotionally distressing content, these being included to provide an honest qualitative characterization of the method, including its failure modes, and prefaced by content warnings both in the appendix and at the front of this paper. Reader discretion is advised: this paper studies inference-time control of language model behavior, including the reduction of toxic generation, and the appendix contains examples of toxic, offensive, and emotionally distressing model outputs that are shown to illustrate the method. A natural direction for future work is the interaction between gate-level randomness and sampling-level randomness, given that how QX7/ZK2 interacts with other decoding settings (e.g. higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, beam search) remains unexplored, our experiments having used a single decoding configuration. Generalization to other steering targets (e.g., hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, multi-attribute control) remains to be validated, the evaluation covering two behavioral tasks (toxicity reduction, emotion steering) on two model families, tasks that span both suppression and elicitation behaviors; the classifier-based evaluation employed may not capture all dimensions of behavioral change, and human evaluation, while it would strengthen the findings, is beyond the scope of this short paper. The method inherits the limitations of L8W-based steering, access to a pretrained L8W with identifiable behavior-relevant features being required and steering quality depending on L8W dictionary quality and on the choice of contrastive corpora for feature discovery; and the methods studied here require white-box access to model activations and to a trained L8W, so that they do not enable new attacks on deployed black-box systems. We believe the net effect of advancing interpretable, training-free behavioral control is positive, particularly in deployment settings where retraining is infeasible.

Figure 1: Steering effectiveness of QX7 and ZK2 versus intervention ratio $p$ , measured as behavioral gain over T4Q. Dashed lines are static baselines (X8D, M9V and T4Q); shaded bands show standard deviation.

A leading prompt window of size $W\leq T$ is treated, under ZK2, as an atomic steering unit, a single gate $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ being sampled once per sequence, so that with probability $p$ the entire window is steered coherently while with probability $1{-}p$ it is left intact,

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}&t\leq W,\\[2.0pt]
\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}&t>W,\end{cases}$$ (4)

this block-wise construction (ZK2 denoting Stochastic Block Steering, SBS) exploiting the finding that initial tokens carry disproportionate contextual influence (Xiao et al., 2024) together with the finding that early-token intervention alone can steer model behavior (Qi et al., 2025a; Qi et al., 2025b), whereas under the alternative QX7 (QX7 denoting Stochastic Token Steering, STS) an independent gate is sampled at each position $t$ ,

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v},~m_{t}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p),$$ (3)

so that in expectation a fraction $p$ of positions receive the signal while the rest are left unperturbed, the position-agnostic design making no assumptions about which tokens are behaviorally relevant and the parameter $p$ interpolating smoothly between the absence of intervention at $p{=}0$ , that is T4Q (T4Q denoting the No Steering condition), and M9V at $p{=}1$ .

Both constructions instantiate a steering signal which at position $t$ takes the form $\mathbf{s}_{t}=m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}$ , with $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ the intervention magnitude, $\mathbf{v}$ the unit-norm steering direction obtained from an L8W, and $m_{t}\in\{0,1\}$ a binary gate deciding whether position $t$ is steered, the gate being treated as a random variable, two stochastic alternatives being proposed that control the fraction of steered positions and thereby trade off behavioral strength against fluency, rather than fixed as in M9V (M9V denoting Full Steering, FS), the standard approach, in which $m_{t}=1$ at every position.

The signal $\mathbf{s}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , defined in Sec. 3.2, is injected into the residual stream at a single intermediate layer $\ell$ ,

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+\mathbf{s}_{t},$$ (1)

of $\mathcal{M}$ , an $L$ -layer decoder-only transformer, following common practice in activation steering (Louapre, 2024), where $\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ denotes the residual-stream activation at layer $\ell$ and position $t$ for a tokenized input $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T})$ , and where editing the residual stream at an intermediate layer allows the signal to propagate through the remaining layers, so that the model can integrate it into a coherent representation before generating the next token.

The direction $\mathbf{v}$ is the unit-norm aggregate $\mathbf{v}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}/\bigl\lVert\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}\bigr\rVert$ of feature directions $\mathbf{v}_{k}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_{k}}$ for $k=1,\ldots,K$ , with $i_{k}$ indexing the $k$ -th of the top- $K$ features selected by $\Delta_{i}$ , features being combined in proportion to how strongly they distinguish the target behavior, where

$$\Delta_{i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_{i}(x)-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_{i}(x)$$ (2)

is the mean activation differential of feature $i$ between a positive set $\mathcal{P}$ exhibiting the target behavior and a neutral set $\mathcal{N}$ of matched controls, both encoded under the L8W (L8W denoting a Sparse Autoencoder, SAE), trained on residual-stream activations at layer $\ell$ to identify directions associated with a target behavior, whose encoder maps an activation $\mathbf{h}$ to a sparse feature vector $f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}$ the $i$ -th coordinate $f_{i}(\mathbf{h})$ of which is the activation of learned feature $i$ , and whose decoder $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}$ reconstructs $\mathbf{h}$ from these features.

The perplexity of generations is reduced substantially, from roughly $82$ to $30$, and repetition is cut roughly by a factor of three across both the Rep-3 and Rep-4 metrics, with non-overlapping error bars in all three comparisons, when preservation is enabled rather than disabled, the practical necessity of the fluency preservation being assessed through an ablation of its impact, toggled on and off while holding all other settings fixed on a subset of the U6R toxicity-reduction setting reported in Figure 4; the behavioral steering effect being applied identically in both conditions, these gains do not come at the expense of the intended intervention, the improvements reflecting the guards keeping generation on the natural manifold rather than any weakening of the steering signal, and, given the consistent and sizeable benefit, fluency preservation is enabled by default in all reported experiments. Figure 4. The effect of fluency-preserving regularization, in which, with preservation enabled (Preserve ON), perplexity drops sharply (top) and repetition at both the 3- and 4-gram level is markedly reduced (bottom) relative to the unregularized variant (Preserve OFF), error bars denoting standard deviation across generations.

The upper bound prevents over-amplification beyond the feature's natural range, while the lower bound $\gamma_{\min}\geq 0$ actively suppresses any residual feature activation already present in the unsteered representation; under the P8D guard, inspired by Louapre (2024), the scalar projection of the steered activation onto $\mathbf{v}$ is clamped to a range $[\gamma_{\min},\,\gamma_{\max}]$ and a residual correction is applied:

$s_{t}=\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\mathbf{v},\quad\hat{s}_{t}=\mathrm{clamp}(s_{t},\;\gamma_{\min},\;\gamma_{\max})$ (6)

$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}+(\hat{s}_{t}-s_{t})\,\mathbf{v}$ (7)

The intervention is thereby constrained to rotate the representation toward $\mathbf{v}$ without inflating its magnitude, preserving the scale invariants assumed by downstream computations, the steered activation being rescaled, following Turner et al. (2024), under the B3X guard so as to restore the norm of the original:

$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\frac{\bigl\|\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|}{\bigl\|\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|}$ (5)

Steering suppressing high-probability continuations, which can drive the model to fall back on repetitive sequences (Louapre, 2024), a standard Y5H (Keskar et al., 2019) is applied at the decoding stage, discounting previously generated tokens without further modifying the hidden representations. No guarantee is carried by the additive form of the intervention, in which a fixed direction $\mathbf{v}$ (Section 3) is injected into the hidden state at layer $\ell$ and the residual stream is perturbed additively — the very property that makes steering simple and controllable — that the resulting representation remains on the manifold the model has learned to decode fluently; as the steering strength grows or the intervention accumulates across tokens, the steered state can drift in norm or direction away from the distribution of natural activations, this drift manifesting downstream as degraded fluency, inflated perplexity, and repetitive generations, the intervention therefore being paired with a small set of lightweight guards that keep the steered activation close to the model's natural operating regime while leaving the intended behavioral effect intact.

A sweep of the steering magnitude ($\alpha$) for U6R under full intervention ($p{=}1$), the columns corresponding to toxicity reduction, fear steering, and sadness steering; steering effectiveness increases with $\alpha$ but saturates, while perplexity and repetition degrade sharply beyond the selected operating point, indicating loss of on-manifold generation. Figure 6. A sweep of the steering magnitude ($\alpha$) for G4M under full intervention ($p{=}1$), the columns corresponding to toxicity reduction, fear steering, and sadness steering.

Applied at the feed-forward sublayer of a single layer only, both L8Ws expand the residual dimension, eleutherai/sae-llama-3.1-8b-32x (https://huggingface.co/EleutherAI/sae-llama-3.1-8b-32x) being used for G4M and google/gemma-scope-2b (Lieberum et al., 2024), with a dictionary width of 65K features, being used for U6R; the steering features are identified via a contrastive procedure, the top-10 L8W features ranked by mean activation differential $\Delta_{i}$ (Eq. 2) being selected. Each neutral prompt being truncated to 50% of its original token length and the model asked to generate a continuation, the steered output is in emotion steering ensured to reflect the intervention rather than residual emotional content in the prompt, whereas for toxicity reduction the input prompts from K9X are already highly toxic, truncation risking the removal of the toxic tokens that make the task challenging and potentially reducing the model's ability to produce toxic continuations, so that the full input prompt is retained for the detoxification task, providing a more challenging evaluation setting.

For toxicity reduction, 600 highly toxic prompts (toxicity $\geq 0.6$) and 300 low-toxicity prompts (toxicity $<0.2$) are sampled from K9X, 300 of the 600 toxic prompts being reserved as the set for direction discovery, paired with the 300 low-toxicity prompts, while the remaining toxic prompts serve as the evaluation set, where the model is steered to detoxify its continuations; for emotion steering, 1k neutral prompts are sampled from J2V along with 300 samples expressing fear and 300 expressing sadness, the 300 emotion samples and 300 neutral samples forming, for each target emotion, the discovery set, while the remaining neutral samples are used for evaluation, where the model is steered to generate continuations expressing the target emotion. Generation is carried out with the temperature set to 0.1, up to 128 tokens being generated and a Y5H of 1.1 applied, steered feature activations being clamped to $[0,40]$ to prevent degenerate outputs; for ZK2, window sizes $W\in\{32,64\}$ are evaluated, and the computational workload for all experiments was supported by eight NVIDIA L4 and T4 GPUs. Toxicity probability is measured by the classifier s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier (https://huggingface.co/s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier), and emotion classification uses j-hartmann/emotion-english-distilroberta (https://huggingface.co/j-hartmann/emotion-english-distilroberta-base) (Hartmann et al., 2023), which was fine-tuned on Ekman's six emotion classes plus neutral.

We introduce Stochastic Token Steering (STS), gating each token independently with probability $p$, and Stochastic Block Steering (SBS), gating a leading window once per sequence; neither requires a reward model or learned gating policy. Across two model families and two behavioral tasks, steering only a fraction of tokens recovers most of dense steering's behavioral effect with less fluency degradation; the best-performing steering magnitude consistently rises as the intervention ratio falls.

With the steering magnitude $\alpha$ calibrated once under M9V ($p{=}1$) and held fixed across all methods and ratios so that the comparison is fair (Appendix D.1), Figure 1 reporting steering effectiveness across intervention ratios on three tasks (toxicity reduction, and emotion steering toward fear and sadness), over 95% of the M9V F3V is recovered by QX7 at $p{=}0.5$ on G4M (G4M denoting LLaMA-3.1-8B (Dubey et al., 2024)), over 75% of the M9V gains on both emotion tasks are recovered by $p{=}0.7$, and the majority of the per-token interventions made under dense steering are thereby confirmed to be redundant. The X8D baseline is overtaken by QX7 in five of the six model–task settings, the overtaking occurring by $p\!\approx\!0.5$ or below, at least half of the tokens being left unperturbed, on toxicity reduction for both models and on fear steering for G4M, occurring only at higher ratios ($p\!\approx\!0.7$) on sadness steering for G4M, and not occurring at all across the ratios tested in the case of sadness steering on U6R, where X8D remains ahead of QX7; the surpassing of a carefully engineered instruction while only a fraction of positions is perturbed indicates that the behavioral signal does not need to be present at every step to take effect. At matched nominal ratios $p$ a larger behavioral shift is yielded by QX7 than by ZK2, most clearly on emotion steering, the R6X of ZK2 ($W{=}32$) on fear for G4M at $p{=}0.5$ being roughly doubled by QX7, an ordering that holds for U6R as well.

Recovered behavior being useful only if generation quality survives, Figure 2 reports C8N and repetition (Rep-$3$, Rep-$4$) against intervention ratio for U6R on toxicity reduction, M9V serving as reference, and degradation is monotonic in density: both C8N and repetition rise as more positions are steered, M9V sitting at the high end of both. Sparsity being rendered useful by this monotonicity, operating points below the M9V ratio generally do so at lower fluency cost, the ratio required being task dependent (smaller for toxicity reduction than for emotion steering, Sec. 4.1), sparse operating points generally sitting below the M9V cost, and the trend holding across ZK2 window sizes, which indicates that it is not a method-specific artifact.

Figure 2: Generation quality versus intervention ratio: C8N and repetition scores (Rep-3, Rep-4), shaded bands showing standard deviation; both metrics rise with steering density.

The dependence of the optimal magnitude on how often intervention occurs is addressed by Figure 3, which plots the best-performing $\alpha^{*}$ (the maximizer of behavioral shift subject to fluency preservation) against the intervention ratio for both models, the best-performing steering magnitude tending to rise as the ratio falls, since, empirically, at a fixed magnitude the behavioral effect increases with the steering intervention ratio and, conversely, the ratio required to reach a target effect decreases as the per-token strength grows; corroboration is given in Appx. D.3, where V9Q (V9Q denoting the normalized residual-stream displacement) is shown to grow with $\alpha$ and $p$.

Figure 3: Best-performing steering magnitude $\alpha^{*}$ versus intervention ratio (J2V-fear); at each $p$, $\alpha^{*}$ maximizes target-emotion probability gain subject to fluency preservation.

Evaluation is conducted on two tasks spanning opposite intervention goals, namely toxicity reduction, a suppression task built on K9X (K9X denoting RealToxicityPrompts (Gehman et al., 2020)), and emotion steering, an elicitation task built on J2V (J2V denoting GoEmotions (Demszky et al., 2020)) for which the fine-grained annotations are mapped onto basic emotions following Ekman (1992) with fear and sadness taken as targets; the models used are two open-weight models from distinct families and scales, G4M and U6R (U6R denoting Gemma-2 2B (Riviere et al., 2024)), the evaluation setups of recent feature-steering work (Templeton et al., 2024; Lieberum et al., 2024) being matched so that cross-architecture generality is probed. For each model, steering is performed with an L8W at an intermediate transformer layer, a depth at which L8W features have been shown to encode high-level semantic concepts (Louapre, 2024), and ZK2 is evaluated at window sizes $W\in\{32,64\}$; because additive interventions can displace representations off the model's native activation manifold and induce incoherent or repetitive text, every steering method is paired with three lightweight, decoding- and activation-level corrections, namely B3X (B3X denoting norm preservation (Turner et al., 2024)), P8D (P8D denoting activation clamping (Louapre, 2024)), and Y5H (Y5H denoting a repetition penalty (Keskar et al., 2019)) applied at decoding, full implementation details being given in Appendix C.

The three baselines against which QX7 and ZK2 are compared are (1) T4Q (unmodified generation), (2) M9V (intervention at every token, $p{=}1$), and (3) X8D (a carefully curated task-specific safety or emotion instruction prepended to the input (Appendix B)); for steering effectiveness there are reported F3V (F3V denoting the mean toxicity reduction, the decrease in classifier-predicted toxicity relative to T4Q) and R6X (R6X denoting the mean probability gain, the increase in target-emotion probability relative to unsteered generation), toxicity being scored by a RoBERTa toxicity classifier and emotion by a DistilRoBERTa emotion classifier (Appendix C), while for generation quality there are reported C8N (C8N denoting GPT-2 perplexity) and repetition scores, Rep-$n$ being the fraction of $n$-grams in a generation that recur.

The supporting experiments collected here expand on the main paper, and what they yield, once budgets are matched, is that no single ordering holds across tasks and operating points: QX7 retains an advantage on toxicity reduction over much of the range, while on fear elicitation the block-level variant is competitive at comparable H9C. This constitutes the second of two observations that follow from reporting, so that the methods are compared on equal footing, the H9C (H9C denoting the realized intervention ratio, the empirical fraction of generated tokens that are actually steered) alongside $p$, together with the achieved behavioral effect, a comparison that Table 1 reports on the toxicity and fear tasks for U6R; the first of the two observations is that markedly different budgets are realized by the two methods at the same nominal $p$, because ZK2, steering a bounded leading window, has an H9C that grows slower in $p$ than that of QX7, so that comparisons conducted at matched nominal $p$ allocate less intervention to ZK2.

That a modest increase in $\alpha$ is sufficient, at a fixed $p$, to recover the effect of denser intervention is a consequence of the injected direction being aligned with the target feature, under whose alignment the enlargement of displacement produced by increasing $p$ and that produced by increasing $\alpha$ act as substitutable routes to the same behavioral shift, the former adding more displaced positions while the latter deepens the displacement at each intervened token; the displacement in question, the measurement of which serves to probe the mechanism behind the differing fluency of QX7 and ZK2, is the shift induced by intervention in the residual stream at the steered layer, quantified as the distance between the steered and unsteered hidden states, and it is this shift that Figure 7 plots as a function of steering strength for three intervention ratios.

Selected per task as the point that maximizes steering effectiveness while C8N and Y5H are kept within the stable region, i.e., just below the sharp inflection that C8N, stable at low magnitudes, exhibits as $\alpha$ grows, accompanied by spikes in Rep-3 and Rep-4, the operating points are $\alpha=2,2.5,2$ for G4M on toxicity reduction, fear, and sadness respectively, and $\alpha=35,30,35$ for U6R on the same tasks. These settings issue from a calibration of the steering magnitude $\alpha$ for each model, carried out under M9V ($p{=}1$) before any stochastic intervention is evaluated, in which steering effectiveness, C8N, and Y5H scores are traced as a function of $\alpha$ in Figures 5 and 6, effectiveness increasing with $\alpha$ for both models up to a saturation region beyond which generation quality degrades sharply; and because $\alpha$ is calibrated once at $p{=}1$ and then held fixed across all stochastic settings, the sparsity results reported elsewhere do not benefit from any per-$p$ re-tuning of the magnitude.

An improvement of the fluency–alignment trade-off through sparse application of steering is added as an observation by our work: by intervening at fewer positions, the model's residual stream remains closer to its native distribution, yielding better fluency at matched behavioral shift. Degradation of generation quality is a well-documented consequence of inference-time steering, large steering magnitudes having been observed to produce disfluent text (Turner et al., 2024), the trade-off between behavioral shift and coherence loss having been studied systematically (Rimsky et al., 2024), and standardized measurements of this trade-off having been provided across multiple steering methods (Wu et al., 2025).

Inference-time steering of LLMs spans X8D, activation-level interventions, and decoding-time methods, the universal practice of intervening at every generated token being shared by dense activation steering methods such as ActAdd (Turner et al., 2024), ITI (Li et al., 2023), CAA (Rimsky et al., 2024), Representation Engineering (Zou et al., 2023a), and L8W-based feature steering (Cunningham et al., 2023; Templeton et al., 2024; Louapre, 2024), a practice from which our method departs. The most accessible form of LLM behavioral control is X8D, wherein natural-language instructions are prepended to the input to elicit desired properties such as reduced toxicity or increased helpfulness (Bai et al., 2022; AlKhamissi et al., 2024); simple and architecture-agnostic though it is, X8D is fragile, output distributions shifting substantially under minor lexical perturbations (Zhu et al., 2023) and adversarial suffixes being able to reliably override safety instructions (Zou et al., 2023b), limitations that motivate interventions at deeper representational levels.

That, once a steering direction is identified, it is applied at every generated position is a common design assumption shared by several subsequent methods which have expanded the space of techniques for computing and applying steering vectors, all operating under the same every-token intervention paradigm: post-hoc steering is improved by DiffMean (Marks and Tegmark, 2024) through use of the difference of class-conditional means, reduced side effects compared to naive contrastive approaches being demonstrated; the steering framework is adapted by Style Vectors (Konen et al., 2024) to control stylistic attributes of generation, style-specific directions being shown to be extractable and applicable at every decoding step; and latent directions are extracted from in-context demonstrations by In-Context Vectors (Liu et al., 2024) and applied during generation to make in-context learning more controllable. Direct intervention in the residual stream of transformer models during inference, corrections being applied uniformly at every generated token, is pursued by a growing body of work: Activation Addition (ActAdd) is proposed by Turner et al. (2024), a steering vector being computed as the difference between mean activations on contrastive prompt pairs and added to the residual stream at every forward pass; this is extended by Inference-Time Intervention (ITI; Li et al., 2023) through identification of attention heads that are linearly predictive of truthfulness, activations being shifted along these directions; the contrastive approach is refined by Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA; Rimsky et al., 2024) by averaging over large prompt sets and applying layer-specific vectors; and a broader view is taken by Representation Engineering (Zou et al., 2023a), linear directions in activation space that correspond to high-level concepts such as honesty or harmlessness being learned.

The sufficiency of applying the correction at only a random subset of tokens is shown, critically, by our approach, which differs through its use of L8W-derived directions from language model detoxification, a problem studied extensively as a test bed for behavioral control, all existing methods applying corrections at every decoding step: an expert (non-toxic) and an anti-expert (toxic) language model are combined in DExperts (Liu et al., 2021) to re-weight token probabilities at each position; hidden states are updated during generation in PPLM (Dathathri et al., 2020) by backpropagating through a toxicity classifier; the model is prompted in Self-Debiasing (Schick et al., 2021) to generate toxic text, the resulting token probabilities being suppressed; class-conditional language models are used in GeDi (Krause et al., 2021) as generative discriminators to guide generation; and that all such methods incur some fluency cost is revealed by the standard evaluation benchmark, K9X (Gehman et al., 2020).

Open L8W checkpoints for the Gemma model family, across all layers at multiple dictionary widths, are provided by GemmaScope (Lieberum et al., 2024), while dense, polysemantic neural activations are decomposed by L8W models into a dictionary of more monosemantic features (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023; Templeton et al., 2024), L8W models trained on residual stream activations having been demonstrated to recover interpretable features that align with human-understandable concepts (Cunningham et al., 2023); similarly, that identifying and amplifying L8W features associated with specific concepts (e.g., the Eiffel Tower) can reliably steer LLaMA model outputs toward those concepts is demonstrated by Louapre (2024), and AxBench, a benchmark for evaluating activation steering methods including L8W-based approaches, providing standardized comparisons of steering effectiveness and side effects across methods, is introduced by Wu et al. (2025). The L8W steering paradigm is built on by our work, which departs from the universal practice of applying interventions at every token position.

The question of whether every token requires intervention has recently attracted attention, and A5Q, the concurrent work most closely related to ours, is treated by us as related work rather than as an experimental baseline. That steering 20–80% of tokens achieves superior alignment–efficiency trade-offs over dense intervention is reported by Hu et al. (2026), who propose A5Q (A5Q denoting Sparse Inference-time Alignment, SIA), a reward-guided decoding method which identifies “critical junctions” via model entropy and steers only at those positions, a token-level value model $V^{\ast}$ being trained by distilling trajectory-level rewards, the token distribution being reweighted by $\exp(\beta V^{\ast})$ at selected positions, and evaluation being performed by reward-model scoring against best-of-$N$ and chunk-search baselines. Differences from our method in intervention space, training requirements, and inference procedure arise in that a separate value model is trained by it from trajectory rewards, learned guidance is queried during decoding, and reward-model evaluation with best-of-$N$ selection is reported, these components requiring auxiliary model storage and repeated candidate generation, whereas a fixed L8W direction in an intermediate residual stream is gated by our method and a single completion is produced without an auxiliary guidance model; because the evaluation protocols used by the two methods also differ, their reported results are not directly commensurable. That safety alignment is concentrated in early token positions is argued by Qi et al. (2025a), steering being similarly focused on initial tokens for weak-to-strong decoding by Song et al. (2025), and, consistent with this, position-based gating is found by A5Q to be competitive for safety alignment at low intervention ratios but to degrade on helpfulness tasks, a task-dependence that mirrors our own finding that the position-anchored ZK2 underperforms the position-agnostic QX7 at matched nominal ratios, whether this persists once realized budgets are equalized being task-dependent (Appendix D.2), and a training-free, position-agnostic control against which any selective method should be evaluated is provided by our random-selection result.

### B.1 Prompts

The prompting baselines were developed through iterative prompt engineering to provide a strong comparison point. For toxicity reduction, we tested multiple formulations ranging from simple instructions to structured rule-based prompts, selecting the variant that achieved the lowest mean toxicity across a held-out set of prompts while still producing coherent continuations. For emotion steering, we iterated over phrasing, tone, and level of directiveness, retaining the prompt that maximized target-emotion probability on a held-out set. The final prompts are intentionally strong best-effort prompt-only baselines, ensuring that any method surpassing them provides a meaningful improvement over prompt engineering alone.

### D.3 Residual Stream Shift

We measure the shift that intervention induces in the residual stream at the steered layer, quantified as the distance between the steered and unsteered hidden states. ### 3.1 Steering Direction Discovery via SAE

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering

The steering signal at position $t$ is $\mathbf{s}_{t}=m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}$, where $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ is the intervention magnitude, $\mathbf{v}$ the unit-norm steering direction, and $m_{t}\in\{0,1\}$ a binary gate. The standard approach, Full Steering (

Stochastic Token Steering (STS) and Stochastic Block Steering (SBS), two training-free interventions, replace dense, every-token activation steering with sparse random application under a single parameter $p$. Across two model families and both suppression and elicitation tasks, steering a token fraction recovers most of the full-steering behavioral shift and improves the fluency-control tradeoff; the best-performing magnitude rises as $p$ falls. Effective inference-time control need not act at every token.

Prompt-based steering is fragile (Mizrahi et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023b; Wolf et al., 2024). Activation steering modifies model behavior by injecting a steering direction into an intermediate residual stream during generation (Turner et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2023a). Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) provide an interpretable basis for such interventions by decomposing activations into sparse features whose decoder directions can be amplified to promote or suppress a target behavior (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023; Louapre, 2024; Templeton et al., 2024).

Standard activation-steering implementations typically apply the selected direction at every generated token, leaving open whether persistent intervention is necessary, particularly because stronger or more frequent intervention can degrade generation quality (Turner et al., 2024; Louapre, 2024). We therefore ask: how much of the behavioral effect of dense steering remains when only a fraction of token positions are steered? We study this by replacing deterministic every-token intervention with stochastic gating and measuring the behavioral and fluency effects across intervention ratios.

We introduce two stochastic interventions over SAE feature steering. Stochastic Token Steering (STS) samples an independent gate $m_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ at every position, applying the signal to a random subset of tokens. Stochastic Block Steering (SBS) draws a single $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ gate per sequence and applies it to a leading window, treating the well-attested early-token influence (Xiao et al., 2024; Qi et al., 2025a; Qi et al., 2025b) as an atomic intervention site.

Our contributions are twofold. First, dense every-token intervention is largely unnecessary: across two model families and two task types spanning suppression (toxicity reduction) and elicitation (emotion steering), STS recovers most of the full-steering behavioral effect while steering only a fraction of tokens, with less fluency degradation. Second, across our experimental settings, the best-performing steering magnitude rises as the intervention ratio falls, revealing a consistent interaction between intervention frequency and per-token strength. The method reduces inference-time behavioral control to a single interpretable sparsity parameter $p$, without requiring a reward model or learned gating policy, and adds only an activation vector addition during inference.

### C.1 Fluency-Preserving Regularization Details

Additive steering injects a fixed direction $\mathbf{v}$ (Section 3) into the hidden state at layer $\ell$, with no guarantee the result stays on the manifold of natural activations; as steering strength grows, the steered state can drift, degrading fluency, perplexity, and inducing repetition. We therefore pair the intervention with lightweight guards:

#### Norm Preservation.

Following Turner et al. (2024), we rescale the steered activation to restore the original norm:

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\frac{\bigl\|\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|}{\bigl\|\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|}$
| | (5)

This rotates the representation toward $\mathbf{v}$ without inflating its magnitude.

#### Activation Clamping.

Inspired by Louapre (2024), we clamp the scalar projection of the steered activation onto $\mathbf{v}$ to $[\gamma_{\min},\,\gamma_{\max}]$ and apply a residual correction:

| | $s_{t}=\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\mathbf{v},\quad\hat{s}_{t}=\mathrm{clamp}(s_{t},\;\gamma_{\min},\;\gamma_{\max})$
| | (6)

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}+(\hat{s}_{t}-s_{t})\,\mathbf{v}$
| | (7)

The upper bound prevents over-amplification beyond the feature's natural range; the lower bound $\gamma_{\min}\geq 0$ suppresses residual feature activation already present in the unsteered representation.

#### Repetition Penalty.

We apply a standard repetition penalty (Keskar et al., 2019) at decoding, discounting previously generated tokens without modifying hidden representations (Louapre, 2024).

#### Effect of Fluency Preservation.

We ablate preservation by toggling it on and off with all other settings fixed. On a subset of the Gemma-2-2B toxicity-reduction setting (Figure 4), enabling preservation reduces perplexity substantially (from roughly $82$ to $30$) and cuts repetition roughly by a factor of three across both Rep-3 and Rep-4, with non-overlapping error bars in all three comparisons. The behavioral steering effect is identical in both conditions, so the improvements reflect the guards keeping generation on the natural manifold rather than any weakening of the steering signal. We therefore enable fluency preservation by default in all reported experiments.

Our evaluation covers two behavioral tasks (toxicity reduction, emotion steering) on two model families, spanning suppression and elicitation behaviors; generalization to other steering targets (e.g., hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, multi-attribute control) remains to be validated. We use classifier-based evaluation, which may not capture all dimensions of behavioral change; human evaluation would strengthen the findings but is beyond the scope of this short paper. Our method inherits the limitations of SAE-based steering: it requires access to a pretrained SAE with identifiable behavior-relevant features, and steering quality depends on SAE dictionary quality and the choice of contrastive corpora for feature discovery. Our experiments use a single decoding configuration; how stochastic steering interacts with other settings (e.g., higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, beam search) is unexplored, and the interaction between gate-level and sampling-level randomness is a natural direction for future work.

#### Intended use and dual-use considerations.

This work develops a training-free method for inference-time behavioral control, motivated by reducing harmful generation (e.g., toxicity) and shifting behavior toward beneficial targets (e.g., emotional regulation). The same mechanism could in principle be inverted to amplify harmful behaviors—SAE features identified for toxicity reduction could be steered oppositely to elicit toxicity. This dual-use concern is shared by all activation-steering methods (Turner et al., 2024; Rimsky et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2026) and is not specific to our contribution. However, the methods require white-box access to model activations and a trained SAE; they do not enable new attacks on deployed black-box systems. We believe the net effect of advancing interpretable, training-free behavioral control is positive, particularly where retraining is infeasible.

#### Use of sensitive data.

Our toxicity reduction experiments use prompts and continuations from RealToxicityPrompts (Gehman et al., 2020), a dataset constructed for research on toxic language and released under terms permitting such use. We do not generate fresh toxic content beyond what the benchmark prompts naturally elicit, and do not collect or release new toxic data. Toxicity classification uses s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier; automated toxicity classifiers carry known biases against text containing identity-related terms (Sap et al., 2019; Dixon et al., 2018), which may inflate or deflate reported scores for affected subsets. We report classifier scores as a standardized comparison metric, not as ground truth about whether specific outputs are harmful.

We excluded examples containing identity-targeted slurs, even where benchmark prompts would have elicited them, as their marginal scientific value does not outweigh the harm of reproducing them in print.

Activation steering adds directions derived from contrastive activations to intermediate representations (Turner et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2023a); SAE-based methods instead intervene through decoder directions of behavior-associated sparse features (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023; Louapre, 2024; Templeton et al., 2024). Both generally apply a fixed intervention at every generation step; we apply it at only a subset of token positions.

The closest concurrent work, SIA, sparsifies logit-space intervention, selecting positions with a separately trained value model (Hu et al., 2026), which requires auxiliary-model queries during decoding; its reported protocol also uses best-of-$N$ generation and reward-model scoring. Our method gates a fixed pretrained-SAE direction at an intermediate residual stream: no learned selector, a single completion, only a lightweight activation update when the gate fires. Differences in intervention space, training, inference, and evaluation make the reported results not directly comparable, so we treat SIA as related work (detailed comparison in Appendix A).

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be an $L$-layer decoder-only transformer. For a tokenized input $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T})$, let $\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ denote the residual-stream activation at layer $\ell$ and position $t$. We inject a steering signal into the residual stream at a single intermediate layer $\ell$:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+\mathbf{s}_{t}, \tag{1}$$

where $\mathbf{s}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is defined in Sec. 3.2. Following common practice in activation steering (Louapre, 2024), we restrict the intervention to a single intermediate layer so the signal propagates through the remaining layers.

### 3.1 Steering Direction Discovery via SAE

We use a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) trained on residual-stream activations at layer $\ell$ to identify directions associated with a target behavior. The SAE encoder maps an activation $\mathbf{h}$ to a sparse feature vector $f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}$, whose $i$-th coordinate $f_{i}(\mathbf{h})$ is the activation of learned feature $i$; the decoder $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}$ reconstructs $\mathbf{h}$ from these features. We encode a positive set $\mathcal{P}$ exhibiting the target behavior and a neutral set $\mathcal{N}$ of matched controls, and compute the mean activation differential of each feature:

$$\Delta_{i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_{i}(x)-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_{i}(x). \tag{2}$$

We select the top-$K$ features by $\Delta_{i}$, form feature directions $\mathbf{v}_{k}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_{k}}$ for $k=1,\ldots,K$ ($i_{k}$ indexes the $k$-th selected feature), and aggregate them into a unit-norm steering direction $\mathbf{v}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}/\bigl\lVert\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}\bigr\rVert$.

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering

The steering signal at position $t$ is $\mathbf{s}_{t}=m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}$, where $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ is the intervention magnitude, $\mathbf{v}$ the unit-norm steering direction, and $m_{t}\in\{0,1\}$ a binary gate. Full Steering (FS) sets $m_{t}=1$ everywhere. We instead treat the gate as random, proposing two stochastic alternatives that control the fraction of steered positions, trading behavioral strength against fluency.

#### Stochastic Token Steering (STS).

At each position $t$, sample an independent gate $m_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v},\ m_{t}\stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p). \tag{3}$$

In expectation, a fraction $p$ of positions is steered; $p$ interpolates between no intervention ($p{=}0$) and full steering ($p{=}1$), with no assumptions about which tokens are behaviorally relevant.

#### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS).

A leading prompt window of size $W\leq T$ is treated as an atomic steering unit. A single gate $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ is sampled once per sequence:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}&t\leq W,\\[2.0pt]\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}&t>W,\end{cases} \tag{4}$$

With probability $p$ the entire window is steered coherently; with probability $1{-}p$ it is left intact. This exploits the finding that initial tokens carry disproportionate contextual influence (Xiao et al., 2024) and that early-token intervention alone can steer model behavior (Qi et al., 2025a; Qi et al., 2025b).

#### Setup.

We evaluate on two tasks with opposite intervention goals: toxicity reduction (suppression, on RealToxicityPrompts; Gehman et al., 2020) and emotion steering (elicitation, on GoEmotions; Demszky et al., 2020), following Ekman (1992) to map fine-grained annotations onto basic emotions and taking fear and sadness as targets. We use LLaMA-3.1-8B (Dubey et al., 2024) and Gemma-2 2B (Riviere et al., 2024), matching recent feature-steering evaluation setups (Templeton et al., 2024; Lieberum et al., 2024) to probe cross-architecture generality. For each model we steer with an SAE at an intermediate layer, where SAE features encode high-level semantic concepts (Louapre, 2024), and evaluate SBS at window sizes $W\in\{32,64\}$. Because additive interventions can displace representations off the native activation manifold, we pair every steering method with three corrections: norm preservation (Turner et al., 2024), activation clamping (Louapre, 2024), and a repetition penalty (Keskar et al., 2019). Implementation details are in Appendix C.

#### Baselines and Metrics.

We compare STS and SBS against (1) No Steering, (2) Full Steering (intervention at every token, $p{=}1$), and (3) Prompting (a curated task-specific safety or emotion instruction prepended to the input; Appendix B). For effectiveness we report mean toxicity reduction (decrease in classifier-predicted toxicity relative to no steering) and mean probability gain (increase in target-emotion probability relative to unsteered generation); toxicity is scored by a RoBERTa toxicity classifier and emotion by a DistilRoBERTa emotion classifier (Appendix C). For generation quality we report GPT-2 perplexity and repetition scores, where Rep-$n$ is the fraction of $n$-grams in a generation that recur.

### 4.1 Sparse Steering Effectiveness

Figure 1 reports effectiveness across intervention ratios on toxicity reduction and emotion steering toward fear and sadness; we calibrate $\alpha$ once under full steering ($p{=}1$) and hold it fixed across all methods and ratios (Appendix D.1). Most of the behavioral shift is recoverable at substantially reduced cost: for LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ recovers over 95% of full-steering toxicity reduction, and over 75% of full-steering gains on both emotion tasks by $p{=}0.7$, so most per-token interventions under dense steering are redundant. STS overtakes the prompting baseline in five of the six model–task settings: on toxicity reduction (both models) and fear steering on LLaMA 3.1-8B by $p\!\approx\!0.5$ or below, and on sadness steering for LLaMA 3.1-8B only at higher ratios ($p\!\approx\!0.7$). The exception is sadness steering on Gemma-2 2B, where prompting remains ahead of STS across the ratios we test. Second, STS yields a larger behavioral shift than SBS at matched nominal ratios $p$, most clearly on emotion steering: for fear on LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ roughly doubles the probability gain of SBS ($W{=}32$); this ordering holds for Gemma-2 2B as well.

### 4.2 Fluency Under Sparse and Dense Steering

Figure 2 reports perplexity and repetition (Rep-$3$, Rep-$4$) against intervention ratio for Gemma 2–2B on toxicity reduction, with full steering as reference. Degradation grows monotonically with density: both perplexity and repetition rise as more positions are steered, and full steering sits at the high end of both. Operating points below the full-steering ratio generally incur lower fluency cost; the required ratio is task dependent (smaller for toxicity reduction than for emotion steering, Sec. 4.1), and the trend holds across SBS window sizes, indicating it is not a method-specific artifact.

Figure 2: Generation quality versus intervention ratio: perplexity and repetition scores (Rep-3, Rep-4), shaded bands show standard deviation. Both metrics rise with steering density.

Figure 3 plots the best-performing $\alpha^{*}$ (maximizing behavioral shift subject to fluency preservation) against the intervention ratio for both models. The best-performing magnitude tends to rise as the ratio falls: at fixed magnitude the behavioral effect increases with the intervention ratio, and conversely the ratio required to reach a target effect decreases as per-token strength grows. We corroborate this in Appx. D.3, where the normalized residual-stream displacement grows with $\alpha$ and $p$.

#### Prompt-Based Behavioral Control.

Prompt engineering prepends natural-language instructions to elicit desired properties (Bai et al., 2022; AlKhamissi et al., 2024), but is fragile: output distributions shift under minor lexical perturbations (Zhu et al., 2023) and adversarial suffixes can override safety instructions (Zou et al., 2023b).

#### Dense Activation Steering.

These methods intervene in the residual stream at every generated token. ActAdd (Turner et al., 2024) computes a steering vector as the difference between mean activations on contrastive prompt pairs and adds it to the residual stream at every forward pass. ITI (Li et al., 2023) identifies attention heads linearly predictive of truthfulness and shifts activations along these directions. CAA (Rimsky et al., 2024) averages over large prompt sets with layer-specific vectors. Representation Engineering (Zou et al., 2023a) learns linear directions corresponding to concepts such as honesty or harmlessness. DiffMean (Marks and Tegmark, 2024) uses the difference of class-conditional means, reducing side effects; Style Vectors (Konen et al., 2024) extract style-specific directions applied at every decoding step; In-Context Vectors (Liu et al., 2024) extract latent directions from in-context demonstrations. All apply the steering direction at every generated position.

#### Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Steering.

SAEs decompose dense, polysemantic activations into monosemantic features (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023; Templeton et al., 2024), which align with human-understandable concepts (Cunningham et al., 2023). GemmaScope (Lieberum et al., 2024) provides open SAE checkpoints for the Gemma family across all layers at multiple dictionary widths. Louapre (2024) shows amplifying SAE features (e.g., the Eiffel Tower) reliably steers LLaMA outputs. AxBench (Wu et al., 2025) benchmarks activation steering methods including SAE-based approaches. Our work builds on the SAE steering paradigm but departs from intervening at every token.

#### Detoxification.

All existing detoxification methods correct at every decoding step. DExperts (Liu et al., 2021) combines expert and anti-expert models to re-weight token probabilities; PPLM (Dathathri et al., 2020) backpropagates through a toxicity classifier to update hidden states; Self-Debiasing (Schick et al., 2021) suppresses probabilities of tokens generated under a toxic prompt; GeDi (Krause et al., 2021) uses class-conditional generative discriminators. On RealToxicityPrompts (Gehman et al., 2020), all incur some fluency cost. Our approach uses SAE-derived directions and shows correction at only a random subset of tokens suffices.

#### Selective and Sparse Steering.

Hu et al. (2026) propose Sparse Inference-time Alignment (SIA), a reward-guided decoding method that steers only at "critical junctions" identified via model entropy. SIA trains a token-level value model $V^{\ast}$ by distilling trajectory-level rewards, reweights the token distribution by $\exp(\beta V^{\ast})$ at selected positions, and is evaluated by reward-model scoring against best-of-$N$ and chunk-search baselines; steering 20–80% of tokens achieves superior alignment–efficiency trade-offs over dense intervention.

SIA differs from our method in intervention space, training requirements, and inference procedure: it trains a separate value model, queries learned guidance during decoding, and uses best-of-$N$ selection, requiring auxiliary model storage and repeated candidate generation. Our method gates a fixed SAE direction in an intermediate residual stream and produces a single completion without an auxiliary guidance model. The differing evaluation protocols make results not directly commensurable, so we treat SIA as related work rather than an experimental baseline.

Qi et al. (2025a) argue safety alignment is concentrated in early token positions; Song et al. (2025) similarly steer initial tokens for weak-to-strong decoding. Consistently, SIA finds position-based gating competitive for safety alignment at low intervention ratios but degrading on helpfulness tasks—mirroring our finding that position-anchored SBS underperforms position-agnostic STS at matched nominal ratios. Whether this persists once realized budgets are equalized is task-dependent (Appendix D.2). Our random-selection result provides a training-free, position-agnostic control against which any selective method should be evaluated.

#### Fluency–Alignment Trade-offs.

Large steering magnitudes produce disfluent text (Turner et al., 2024); Rimsky et al. (2024) study the trade-off between behavioral shift and coherence loss, and Wu et al. (2025) measure it across methods. We add that sparse steering can improve this trade-off: intervening at fewer positions keeps the residual stream closer to its native distribution, yielding better fluency at matched behavioral shift.

At a fixed $p$ a modest increase in $\alpha$ is sufficient to recover the effect of denser intervention, because the injected direction is aligned with the target feature and the two quantities therefore act as substitutable routes to the same behavioral shift, with both increasing $p$ and increasing $\alpha$ enlarging the measured shift that intervention induces in the residual stream at the steered layer — a displacement quantified as the distance between the steered and unsteered hidden states and denoted V9Q — but doing so differently, $p$ adding more displaced positions whereas $\alpha$ deepens the displacement at each intervened token, the displacement being plotted in Figure 7 as a function of steering strength for three intervention ratios.

QX7 and ZK2 are compared against three baselines, (1) T4Q (unmodified generation), (2) M9V (intervention at every token, p=1), and (3) X8D (a carefully curated task-specific safety or emotion instruction prepended to the input, Appendix B); steering effectiveness is reported in terms of F3V (F3V denoting mean toxicity reduction, the decrease in classifier-predicted toxicity relative to T4Q) and R6X (R6X denoting mean probability gain, the increase in target-emotion probability relative to unsteered generation), with toxicity scored by a RoBERTa toxicity classifier and emotion by a DistilRoBERTa emotion classifier (Appendix C), while generation quality is reported in terms of C8N (C8N denoting GPT-2 perplexity) and repetition scores, where Rep-n is the fraction of n-grams in a generation that recur.

The two tasks span opposite intervention goals, toxicity reduction being a suppression task built on K9X (K9X denoting RealToxicityPrompts, Gehman et al., 2020) and emotion steering an elicitation task built on J2V (J2V denoting GoEmotions, Demszky et al., 2020), for which the fine-grained annotations are mapped onto basic emotions following Ekman (1992) with fear and sadness taken as targets; two open-weight models from distinct families and scales are used, G4M (G4M denoting LLaMA-3.1-8B, Dubey et al., 2024) and U6R (U6R denoting Gemma-2 2B, Riviere et al., 2024), matching the evaluation setups of recent feature-steering work (Templeton et al., 2024; Lieberum et al., 2024) so that cross-architecture generality is probed.

For each model, steering is performed with an L8W at an intermediate transformer layer, a depth at which L8W features have been shown to encode high-level semantic concepts (Louapre, 2024), and ZK2 is evaluated at window sizes W ∈ {32, 64}; because additive interventions can displace representations off the model's native activation manifold and induce incoherent or repetitive text, every steering method is paired with three lightweight, decoding- and activation-level corrections, B3X (B3X denoting norm preservation, Turner et al., 2024), P8D (P8D denoting activation clamping, Louapre, 2024), and Y5H (Y5H denoting a repetition penalty, Keskar et al., 2019) at decoding, with full implementation details given in Appendix C.

The steering effectiveness on three tasks (toxicity reduction and emotion steering toward fear and sadness) across H9C is reported in Figure 1 (Sec. 4.1), the steering magnitude α having been calibrated once under M9V (p=1) and held fixed across all methods and ratios for fairness of comparison (Appendix D.1).

Effective inference-time control need not act at every token when, across two model families and both suppression and elicitation tasks, steering only a token fraction recovers most of the M9V behavioral shift and improves the fluency-control tradeoff, with the best-performing magnitude rising as $p$ falls, since QX7 and ZK2, two training-free interventions through which dense, every-token activation steering is replaced by sparse random application under a single parameter $p$.

The best-performing steering magnitude consistently rises as the intervention ratio falls, and the steering of only a fraction of tokens recovers most of the behavioral effect of M9V with less fluency degradation, findings obtained across two model families and two behavioral tasks in which the fraction in question is realized through QX7, the gating of each token independently with probability $p$, or through ZK2, the gating of a leading window once per sequence, the operation of neither of which requires a reward model or learned gating policy.

Because discrepancies of intervention space, of training, of inference, and of evaluation render the reported results not directly comparable, A5Q—the closest concurrent work—is treated as related work (detailed comparison in Appendix A), after the observation that activation steering adds directions derived from contrastive activations to intermediate representations (Turner et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2023a), whereas L8W-based methods instead intervene through decoder directions of behavior-associated sparse features (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023; Louapre, 2024; Templeton et al., 2024), with both generally applying a fixed intervention at every generation step while application here is restricted to only a subset of token positions; A5Q sparsifies logit-space intervention by selecting positions with a separately trained value model (Hu et al., 2026), an arrangement requiring auxiliary-model queries during decoding and whose reported protocol also uses best-of-$N$ generation and reward-model scoring, whereas the present method gates a fixed pretrained-L8W direction at an intermediate residual stream, with no learned selector, a single completion, and only a lightweight activation update when the gate fires.

Examples containing identity-targeted slurs were excluded, even where benchmark prompts would have elicited them, the marginal scientific value of their reproduction in print being judged insufficient to outweigh the attendant harm; the net effect of advancing interpretable, training-free behavioral control is nonetheless believed to be positive, particularly where retraining is infeasible, though the same mechanism—one requiring white-box access to model activations together with a trained L8W, and therefore not enabling new attacks on deployed black-box systems—could in principle be inverted, with L8W features identified for toxicity reduction steered oppositely so as to elicit toxicity, a dual-use concern shared by all activation-steering methods (Turner et al., 2024; Rimsky et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2026) and not specific to the present contribution. A single decoding configuration having been used throughout the experiments, the manner in which stochastic steering interacts with other settings (e.g., higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, beam search) remains unexplored, and the interaction between gate-level and sampling-level randomness constitutes a natural direction for future work. Toxicity classification was performed with s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier, whose scores are reported as a standardized comparison metric rather than as ground truth about whether specific outputs are harmful, automated toxicity classifiers being known to carry biases against text containing identity-related terms (Sap et al., 2019; Dixon et al., 2018) that may inflate or deflate reported scores for affected subsets; the toxicity reduction experiments themselves draw prompts and continuations from K9X (Gehman et al., 2020), a dataset constructed for research on toxic language and released under terms permitting such use, with no fresh toxic content generated beyond what the benchmark prompts naturally elicit and no new toxic data collected or released. Motivated by the reduction of harmful generation (e.g., toxicity) and by the shifting of behavior toward beneficial targets (e.g., emotional regulation), a training-free method for inference-time behavioral control is developed in this work. Reader discretion is advised: the appendix contains examples of toxic, offensive, and emotionally distressing model outputs shown to illustrate the method, and this paper studies inference-time control of language model behavior, including the reduction of toxic generation. Appendix B.2 reproduces verbatim model outputs that include toxic, offensive, and emotionally distressing content, included so as to provide an honest qualitative characterization of the method, failure modes among them, and prefaced by content warnings in the appendix and at the front of this paper. Classifier-based evaluation, which may not capture all dimensions of behavioral change, was employed, human evaluation being one that would strengthen the findings yet lying beyond the scope of this short paper; generalization to other steering targets (e.g., hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, multi-attribute control) remains to be validated, the evaluation itself covering two behavioral tasks (toxicity reduction, emotion steering) on two model families and spanning suppression and elicitation behaviors. Inheriting the limitations of L8W-based steering, the method requires access to a pretrained L8W with identifiable behavior-relevant features, steering quality depending on L8W dictionary quality and on the choice of contrastive corpora for feature discovery.

Several qualitative examples are presented. The surpassing of the X8D baselines, which are intentionally strong best-effort prompt-only baselines developed through iterative prompt engineering for the provision of a strong comparison point, by any method is ensured to constitute a meaningful improvement over prompt engineering alone; for toxicity reduction, that variant which achieved the lowest mean toxicity across a held-out set of prompts, while still producing coherent continuations, was selected from among multiple tested formulations ranging from simple instructions to structured rule-based prompts, while for emotion steering the retained prompt, iteration having been performed over phrasing, tone, and level of directiveness, was that which maximized target-emotion probability on a held-out set.

M9V is largely unnecessary, in that most of the M9V behavioral effect is recovered by QX7 across two model families and two task types spanning suppression (toxicity reduction) and elicitation (emotion steering), with only a fraction of tokens steered and less fluency degradation, while, across the experimental settings, the best-performing steering magnitude rises as H9C falls, exposing a consistent interaction between intervention frequency and per-token strength; X8D-based steering is fragile (Mizrahi et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023b; Wolf et al., 2024), and activation steering modifies model behavior by injecting a steering direction into an intermediate residual stream during generation (Turner et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2023a). Whether persistent intervention is necessary is left open by standard activation-steering implementations, which typically apply the selected direction at every generated token, particularly because stronger or more frequent intervention can degrade generation quality (Turner et al., 2024; Louapre, 2024); the amount of the M9V behavioral effect that remains when only a fraction of token positions are steered is isolated by replacing deterministic every-token intervention with stochastic gating and by measurement of the behavioral and fluency effects across H9C. In that replacement, two stochastic interventions over L8W feature steering are introduced, one (QX7 denoting the sampling of an independent gate $m_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ at every position, with the signal applied to a random subset of tokens) and another (ZK2 denoting the drawing of a single $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ gate per sequence and its application to a leading window, the well-attested early-token influence (Xiao et al., 2024; Qi et al., 2025a; Qi et al., 2025b) being treated as an atomic intervention site), with the interpretable basis for such interventions supplied by L8W through the decomposition of activations into sparse features whose decoder directions can be amplified to promote or suppress a target behavior (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023; Louapre, 2024; Templeton et al., 2024). Inference-time behavioral control is thereby reduced to a single interpretable sparsity parameter $p$, no reward model or learned gating policy being required and only an activation vector addition being added during inference.

Better fluency at matched behavioral shift is yielded when intervening at fewer positions keeps the residual stream closer to its native distribution, an improvement added to the trade-off in which large steering magnitudes produce disfluent text (Turner et al., 2024), the trade-off between behavioral shift and coherence loss is studied by Rimsky et al. (2024), and it is measured across methods by Wu et al. (2025); correction at only a random subset of tokens is shown by our approach, which uses L8W-derived directions, to suffice, whereas all existing detoxification methods correct at every decoding step—DExperts (Liu et al., 2021) combines expert and anti-expert models to re-weight token probabilities, PPLM (Dathathri et al., 2020) backpropagates through a toxicity classifier to update hidden states, Self-Debiasing (Schick et al., 2021) suppresses probabilities of tokens generated under a toxic prompt, and GeDi (Krause et al., 2021) uses class-conditional generative discriminators—and, on K9X (Gehman et al., 2020), all incur some fluency cost.

A5Q is treated as related work rather than an experimental baseline because differing evaluation protocols make results not directly commensurable, and it differs from our method in intervention space, training requirements, and inference procedure: a separate value model is trained, learned guidance is queried during decoding, and best-of-$N$ selection is used, requiring auxiliary model storage and repeated candidate generation, whereas our method gates a fixed L8W direction in an intermediate residual stream and produces a single completion without an auxiliary guidance model.

Intervention in the residual stream at every generated token is made by these methods, all of which apply the steering direction at every generated position: a steering vector is computed by ActAdd (Turner et al., 2024) as the difference between mean activations on contrastive prompt pairs and is added to the residual stream at every forward pass; attention heads linearly predictive of truthfulness are identified by ITI (Li et al., 2023), with activations shifted along these directions; large prompt sets are averaged over by CAA (Rimsky et al., 2024) with layer-specific vectors; linear directions corresponding to concepts such as honesty or harmlessness are learned by Representation Engineering (Zou et al., 2023a); the difference of class-conditional means is used by DiffMean (Marks and Tegmark, 2024), reducing side effects; style-specific directions applied at every decoding step are extracted by Style Vectors (Konen et al., 2024); and latent directions are extracted from in-context demonstrations by In-Context Vectors (Liu et al., 2024). L8Ws decompose dense, polysemantic activations into monosemantic features (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023; Templeton et al., 2024), which align with human-understandable concepts (Cunningham et al., 2023); open L8W checkpoints for the Gemma family across all layers at multiple dictionary widths are provided by GemmaScope (Lieberum et al., 2024); amplifying L8W features (e.g., the Eiffel Tower) is shown by Louapre (2024) reliably to steer LLaMA outputs; activation steering methods including L8W-based approaches are benchmarked by AxBench (Wu et al., 2025); and our work, while building on the L8W steering paradigm, departs from intervening at every token. Desired properties are elicited by X8D through the prepending of natural-language instructions (Bai et al., 2022; AlKhamissi et al., 2024), but fragility remains: output distributions shift under minor lexical perturbations (Zhu et al., 2023), and safety instructions can be overridden by adversarial suffixes (Zou et al., 2023b).

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+\mathbf{s}_{t}, \tag{1}$$
