We introduced Stochastic Token Steering (STS) and Stochastic Block Steering (SBS), two training-free interventions that replace dense, every-token activation steering with sparse random application governed by a single parameter $p$. Across two model families and both suppression and elicitation tasks, steering a fraction of tokens recovers most of the full-steering behavioral shift while improving the fluency-control tradeoff, and the best-performing magnitude rises as $p$ falls. Effective inference-time control need not act at every token.

Our evaluation covers two behavioral tasks (toxicity reduction, emotion steering) on two model families. Generalization to other steering targets (e.g., hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, multi-attribute control) remains unvalidated. We use classifier-based evaluation, which may not capture all dimensions of behavioral change; human evaluation is beyond this paper's scope. The method inherits SAE-based steering limitations: it requires a pretrained SAE with identifiable behavior-relevant features, and steering quality depends on SAE dictionary quality and the contrastive corpora used for feature discovery. Experiments use a single decoding configuration; interactions with other decoding settings (higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, beam search) and between gate-level and sampling-level randomness remain unexplored.

#### Intended use and dual-use considerations.

This work develops a training-free method for inference-time behavioral control of language models, primarily to reduce harmful generation (e.g., toxicity) and shift behavior toward beneficial targets (e.g., emotional regulation). The mechanism could be inverted to amplify harmful behaviors: SAE features identified for toxicity reduction could be steered in the opposite direction to elicit toxicity. This dual-use concern is shared by all activation-steering methods (Turner et al., 2024; Rimsky et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2026). The methods require white-box access to model activations and a trained SAE, and do not enable new attacks on deployed black-box systems. We believe the net effect of interpretable, training-free behavioral control is positive, particularly where retraining is infeasible.

#### Use of sensitive data.

Toxicity reduction experiments use prompts and continuations from RealToxicityPrompts (Gehman et al., 2020), released under terms permitting such use. We generate no fresh toxic content beyond what benchmark prompts elicit and collect or release no new toxic data. Toxicity classification uses the s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier; automated toxicity classifiers carry known biases against text containing identity-related terms (Sap et al., 2019; Dixon et al., 2018), which may inflate or deflate reported scores for affected subsets. We report classifier scores as a standardized comparison metric, not as ground truth about harmfulness.

#### Qualitative examples.

Appendix B.2 reproduces verbatim model outputs containing toxic, offensive, and emotionally distressing content to characterize the method, including its failure modes, prefaced by content warnings in the appendix and at the front of the paper. We excluded examples containing identity-targeted slurs, even where benchmark prompts elicited them.

Content Warning.
This paper studies inference-time control of language model behavior, including the reduction of toxic generation. The appendix contains examples of toxic, offensive, and emotionally distressing model outputs that are shown to illustrate the method. Reader discretion is advised.

Behavioral control over large language models (LLMs)—reducing toxicity, enforcing a persona, adjusting refusal—is a significant deployment concern (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022). The default mechanism, the system prompt, is fragile: output distributions shift under minor lexical perturbation, adversarial suffixes override alignment priors, and prompt steerability is asymmetric and bounded (Mizrahi et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023b; Wolf et al., 2024).

Activation steering instead injects a steering direction into an intermediate residual stream during generation (Turner et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2023a). Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) provide an interpretable basis by decomposing activations into sparse features whose decoder directions can be amplified to promote or suppress a target behavior (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023; Louapre, 2024; Templeton et al., 2024).

Standard implementations apply the selected direction at every generated token, but stronger or more frequent intervention can degrade generation quality (Turner et al., 2024; Louapre, 2024). We therefore ask: how much of dense steering's behavioral effect remains when only a fraction of token positions are steered? We replace deterministic every-token intervention with stochastic gating and measure behavioral and fluency effects across intervention ratios, introducing two stochastic interventions over SAE feature steering. Stochastic Token Steering (STS) samples an independent gate $m_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ at every position, applying the signal to a random subset of tokens. Stochastic Block Steering (SBS) draws a single $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ gate per sequence and applies it to a leading window, treating early-token influence (Xiao et al., 2024; Qi et al., 2025a; Qi et al., 2025b) as an atomic intervention site.

Our contributions are twofold. First, dense every-token intervention is largely unnecessary: across two model families and two task types spanning suppression (toxicity reduction) and elicitation (emotion steering), STS recovers most of the full-steering behavioral effect while steering only a fraction of tokens, with less fluency degradation. Second, the best-performing steering magnitude rises as the intervention ratio falls, revealing a consistent interaction between intervention frequency and per-token strength. The method reduces inference-time behavioral control to a single interpretable sparsity parameter $p$, requires no reward model or learned gating policy, and adds only an activation vector addition during inference.

Activation steering adds contrastive-activation-derived directions to intermediate representations (Turner et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2023a); SAE-based methods intervene through decoder directions of behavior-associated sparse features (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023; Louapre, 2024; Templeton et al., 2024). These methods generally apply a fixed intervention at every generation step; we apply it to only a subset of token positions.

The closest concurrent work, SIA, sparsifies logit-space intervention using a separately trained value model to select positions (Hu et al., 2026), requiring auxiliary-model queries during decoding; its reported protocol additionally uses best-of-$N$ generation and reward-model scoring. Our method gates a fixed direction from a pretrained SAE at an intermediate residual stream, requires no learned selector, and generates a single completion with only a lightweight activation update when the gate fires. Given differences in intervention space, training, inference, and evaluation, the results are not directly comparable; we treat SIA as related work, with a detailed comparison in Appendix A.

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be an $L$-layer decoder-only transformer. For a tokenized input $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T})$, let $\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ denote the residual-stream activation at layer $\ell$ and position $t$. Following common practice in activation steering (Louapre, 2024), we inject a steering signal into the residual stream at a single intermediate layer $\ell$:

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+\mathbf{s}_{t},$
| | (1)

where the steering signal $\mathbf{s}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is defined in Sec. 3.2. Editing at an intermediate layer lets the signal propagate through the remaining layers and be integrated into a coherent representation before the next token is generated.

### 3.1 Steering Direction Discovery via SAE

We use a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) trained on residual-stream activations at layer $\ell$. The SAE encoder maps an activation $\mathbf{h}$ to a sparse feature vector $f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}$, whose $i$-th coordinate $f_{i}(\mathbf{h})$ is the activation of learned feature $i$; the decoder $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}$ reconstructs $\mathbf{h}$ from these features. To isolate behavior-discriminative features, we encode a positive set $\mathcal{P}$ exhibiting the target behavior and a neutral set $\mathcal{N}$ of matched controls, and compute each feature's mean activation differential:

| | $\Delta_{i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_{i}(x)-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_{i}(x).$
| | (2)

We select the top-$K$ features by $\Delta_{i}$ and form feature directions $\mathbf{v}_{k}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_{k}}$ for $k=1,\ldots,K$, where $i_{k}$ indexes the $k$-th selected feature. We aggregate these into a single unit-norm steering direction $\mathbf{v}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}/\bigl\lVert\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}\bigr\rVert$, combining features in proportion to how strongly they distinguish the target behavior.

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering

The steering signal at position $t$ is $\mathbf{s}_{t}=m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}$, where $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ is the intervention magnitude, $\mathbf{v}$ is the unit-norm steering direction, and $m_{t}\in\{0,1\}$ is a binary gate deciding whether position $t$ is steered. The standard approach, Full Steering (FS), sets $m_{t}=1$ at every position. We instead treat the gate as a random variable and propose two stochastic alternatives, which control the fraction of steered positions and thereby trade off behavioral strength against fluency.

#### Stochastic Token Steering (STS).

At each position $t$, we sample an independent gate $m_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$:

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v},~m_{t}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p).$
| | (3)

In expectation, a fraction $p$ of positions receive the signal while the rest are left unperturbed. This position-agnostic design makes no assumptions about which tokens are behaviorally relevant; $p$ interpolates smoothly between no intervention ($p{=}0$) and full steering ($p{=}1$).

#### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS).

We treat a leading prompt window of size $W\leq T$ as an atomic steering unit. A single gate $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ is sampled once per sequence:

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}&t\leq W,\\[2.0pt]
\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}&t>W,\end{cases}$
| | (4)

With probability $p$ the entire window is steered coherently; with probability $1{-}p$ it is left intact. This exploits the findings that initial tokens carry disproportionate contextual influence (Xiao et al., 2024) and that early-token intervention alone can steer model behavior (Qi et al., 2025a; Qi et al., 2025b).

### B.1 Prompts

The prompting baselines were developed through iterative prompt engineering to serve as strong comparison points. For toxicity reduction, we tested formulations from simple instructions (“Do not generate toxic content”) to structured rule-based prompts, selecting the variant with the lowest mean toxicity on a held-out set that still produced coherent continuations. For emotion steering, we iterated over phrasing, tone, and directiveness, retaining the prompt that maximized target-emotion probability on a held-out set. The final prompts below are intentionally strong best-effort prompt-only baselines, so that any method surpassing them improves meaningfully over prompt engineering alone.

### C.1 Fluency-Preserving Regularization Details

Additive steering can push the hidden state off the manifold of natural activations, degrading fluency. We therefore apply three guards:

#### Norm Preservation.
Following Turner et al. (2024), rescale the steered activation to the original norm:
$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\frac{\bigl\|\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|}{\bigl\|\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|}\tag{5}$$

#### Activation Clamping.
Following Louapre (2024), clamp the projection onto $\mathbf{v}$ to $[\gamma_{\min},\,\gamma_{\max}]$ with residual correction:
$$s_{t}=\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\mathbf{v},\quad\hat{s}_{t}=\mathrm{clamp}(s_{t},\;\gamma_{\min},\;\gamma_{\max})\tag{6}$$
$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}+(\hat{s}_{t}-s_{t})\,\mathbf{v}\tag{7}$$
The lower bound $\gamma_{\min}\geq 0$ suppresses residual feature activation already present.

#### Repetition Penalty.
We apply a standard repetition penalty (Keskar et al., 2019; Louapre, 2024) at decoding, discounting previously generated tokens without modifying hidden representations.

#### Effect of Fluency Preservation.
On Gemma-2-2B toxicity reduction, enabling preservation reduces perplexity from roughly 82 to 30 and cuts Rep-3 and Rep-4 roughly threefold, with non-overlapping error bars. The steering intervention is identical in both conditions. We enable fluency preservation by default in all experiments.

#### Setup.

We evaluate on toxicity reduction, a suppression task on RealToxicityPrompts (Gehman et al., 2020), and emotion steering, an elicitation task on GoEmotions (Demszky et al., 2020), mapping fine-grained annotations to Ekman (1992) basic emotions with fear and sadness as targets. We use LLaMA-3.1-8B (Dubey et al., 2024) and Gemma-2 2B (Riviere et al., 2024), steering with an SAE at an intermediate layer and evaluating SBS at window sizes $W\in\{32,64\}$. Every steering method is paired with three corrections: norm preservation (Turner et al., 2024), activation clamping (Louapre, 2024), and a repetition penalty (Keskar et al., 2019). Implementation details are in Appendix C.

#### Baselines and Metrics.

Baselines: (1) No Steering, (2) Full Steering ($p{=}1$), (3) Prompting (task-specific instruction prepended; Appendix B). Effectiveness metrics: mean toxicity reduction and mean probability gain relative to no steering, scored by a RoBERTa toxicity classifier and a DistilRoBERTa emotion classifier (Appendix C). Quality metrics: GPT-2 perplexity and Rep-$n$ (fraction of $n$-grams in a generation that recur).

| | $\Delta_{i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_{i}(x)-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_{i}(x).$

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering

The steering signal is $\mathbf{s}_{t}=m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}$, with intervention magnitude $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$, unit-norm direction $\mathbf{v}$, and binary gate $m_{t}\in\{0,1\}$. Full Steering (FS) sets $m_{t}=1$ at every position; we instead make the gate random, proposing two stochastic alternatives.

#### Stochastic Token Steering (STS).

At each position $t$, sample an independent gate $m_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$:

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v},~m_{t}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p).$
| | (3)

In expectation a fraction $p$ of positions are steered; $p$ interpolates between no intervention ($p{=}0$) and full steering ($p{=}1$).

#### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS).

Treat a leading prompt window of size $W\leq T$ as an atomic unit, sampling one gate $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ per sequence:

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}&t\leq W,\\[2.0pt]
\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}&t>W,\end{cases}$
| | (4)

With probability $p$ the entire window is steered; with probability $1{-}p$ it is left intact, exploiting that initial tokens carry disproportionate contextual influence (Xiao et al., 2024) and that early-token intervention alone can steer behavior (Qi et al., 2025a; Qi et al., 2025b).

Behavioral control over LLMs—reducing toxicity, enforcing a persona, adjusting refusal—is a significant deployment concern (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022). Prompt-based steering, the default mechanism, is fragile: output distributions shift under minor lexical perturbation, adversarial suffixes override alignment priors, and prompt steerability is asymmetric and bounded (Mizrahi et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023b; Wolf et al., 2024).

Activation steering injects a steering direction into an intermediate residual stream during generation (Turner et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2023a). Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) provide an interpretable basis by decomposing activations into sparse features whose decoder directions can be amplified to promote or suppress a target behavior (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023; Louapre, 2024; Templeton et al., 2024).

Standard implementations apply the direction at every generated token, and stronger or more frequent intervention can degrade generation quality (Turner et al., 2024; Louapre, 2024). We ask: how much of dense steering's behavioral effect remains when only a fraction of token positions are steered? We replace deterministic every-token intervention with stochastic gating and measure behavioral and fluency effects across intervention ratios.

We introduce two stochastic interventions over SAE feature steering. Stochastic Token Steering (STS) samples an independent gate $m_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ at every position, applying the signal to a random subset of tokens. Stochastic Block Steering (SBS) draws a single $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ gate per sequence, applied to a leading window, treating early-token influence (Xiao et al., 2024; Qi et al., 2025a; Qi et al., 2025b) as an atomic intervention site.

Our contributions are twofold. First, dense every-token intervention is largely unnecessary: across two model families and two task types spanning suppression (toxicity reduction) and elicitation (emotion steering), STS recovers most of the full-steering behavioral effect while steering only a fraction of tokens, with less fluency degradation. Second, the best-performing steering magnitude rises as the intervention ratio falls, revealing a consistent interaction between intervention frequency and per-token strength. The method reduces inference-time behavioral control to a single interpretable sparsity parameter $p$, requiring no reward model or learned gating policy and adding only an activation vector addition during inference.

Inference-time steering spans prompt-based control, activation-level interventions, and decoding-time methods. Dense activation steering methods—ActAdd (Turner et al., 2024), ITI (Li et al., 2023), CAA (Rimsky et al., 2024), Representation Engineering (Zou et al., 2023a), and SAE-based feature steering (Cunningham et al., 2023; Templeton et al., 2024; Louapre, 2024)—all intervene at every generated token; our method departs from this.

#### Prompt-Based Behavioral Control.

Prompt engineering prepends natural-language instructions to elicit properties such as reduced toxicity or increased helpfulness (Bai et al., 2022; AlKhamissi et al., 2024). It is simple and architecture-agnostic but fragile: output distributions shift under minor lexical perturbations (Zhu et al., 2023), and adversarial suffixes can override safety instructions (Zou et al., 2023b).

#### Dense Activation Steering.

These methods intervene in the residual stream uniformly at every generated token. ActAdd (Turner et al., 2024) computes a steering vector as the difference of mean activations on contrastive prompt pairs, added at every forward pass. ITI (Li et al., 2023) shifts activations along directions of attention heads linearly predictive of truthfulness. CAA (Rimsky et al., 2024) averages contrastive vectors over large prompt sets with layer-specific vectors. Representation Engineering (Zou et al., 2023a) learns linear directions corresponding to concepts such as honesty or harmlessness. DiffMean (Marks and Tegmark, 2024) uses the difference of class-conditional means, reducing side effects versus naive contrastive approaches. Style Vectors (Konen et al., 2024) extract and apply style-specific directions at every decoding step. In-Context Vectors (Liu et al., 2024) extract latent directions from in-context demonstrations to make in-context learning more controllable. All apply the identified direction at every generated position.

#### Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Steering.

SAEs decompose dense, polysemantic activations into a dictionary of more monosemantic features (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023; Templeton et al., 2024). Cunningham et al. (2023) show SAEs trained on residual stream activations recover interpretable features. GemmaScope (Lieberum et al., 2024) provides open SAE checkpoints for the Gemma family across all layers at multiple dictionary widths. Louapre (2024) shows that amplifying SAE features for specific concepts (e.g., the Eiffel Tower) reliably steers LLaMA outputs. Wu et al. (2025) introduce AxBench, a benchmark for activation steering methods with standardized comparisons of effectiveness and side effects. We build on SAE steering but depart from intervening at every token.

#### Detoxification.

All existing detoxification methods correct at every decoding step. DExperts (Liu et al., 2021) re-weights token probabilities using an expert (non-toxic) and anti-expert (toxic) model. PPLM (Dathathri et al., 2020) backpropagates through a toxicity classifier to update hidden states. Self-Debiasing (Schick et al., 2021) prompts the model to generate toxic text and suppresses the resulting probabilities. GeDi (Krause et al., 2021) uses class-conditional language models as generative discriminators. RealToxicityPrompts (Gehman et al., 2020) shows all such methods incur some fluency cost. We instead use SAE-derived directions applied at only a random subset of tokens.

#### Selective and Sparse Steering.

Most closely related, Hu et al. (2026) propose Sparse Inference-time Alignment (SIA), which identifies "critical junctions" via model entropy and steers only there. SIA is reward-guided decoding: it trains a token-level value model $V^{\ast}$ by distilling trajectory-level rewards, reweights the token distribution by $\exp(\beta V^{\ast})$ at selected positions, and is evaluated by reward-model scoring against best-of-$N$ and chunk-search baselines. Steering 20–80% of tokens achieves superior alignment–efficiency trade-offs over dense intervention.

SIA differs from our method in intervention space, training requirements, and inference procedure: it trains a separate value model, queries learned guidance during decoding, and uses reward-model evaluation with best-of-$N$ selection, requiring auxiliary model storage and repeated candidate generation. Our method gates a fixed SAE direction in an intermediate residual stream and produces a single completion without an auxiliary guidance model. Given differing evaluation protocols, results are not directly commensurable; we treat SIA as related work, not a baseline.

Qi et al. (2025a) argue safety alignment is concentrated in early token positions, and Song et al. (2025) focus steering on initial tokens for weak-to-strong decoding. SIA finds position-based gating competitive for safety alignment at low intervention ratios but degrading on helpfulness tasks, mirroring our finding that position-anchored SBS underperforms position-agnostic STS at matched nominal ratios. Whether this persists once realized budgets are equalized is task-dependent (Appendix D.2). Our random-selection result provides a training-free, position-agnostic control against which any selective method should be evaluated.

#### Fluency–Alignment Trade-offs.

Inference-time steering degrades generation quality: Turner et al. (2024) observe large steering magnitudes produce disfluent text; Rimsky et al. (2024) study the trade-off between behavioral shift and coherence loss; Wu et al. (2025) measure it across methods. We add that sparse application improves this trade-off: intervening at fewer positions keeps the residual stream closer to its native distribution, yielding better fluency at matched behavioral shift.

### D.1 Steering Magnitude Calibration

We calibrate the steering magnitude $\alpha$ per model under full steering ($p{=}1$). Figures 5 and 6 show steering effectiveness, perplexity, and repetition versus $\alpha$. Effectiveness rises with $\alpha$ to a saturation region, beyond which generation quality degrades sharply: perplexity is stable at low magnitudes but inflects sharply as $\alpha$ grows, with spikes in Rep-3 and Rep-4. Per task, we select the $\alpha$ maximizing effectiveness just below this inflection: $\alpha=2,2.5,2$ for LLaMA 3.1-8B on toxicity reduction, fear, and sadness, and $\alpha=35,30,35$ for Gemma-2 2B. $\alpha$ is calibrated once at $p{=}1$ and held fixed across all stochastic settings, so sparsity results do not benefit from per-$p$ re-tuning.

### D.3 Residual Stream Shift

We measure the intervention-induced shift in the residual stream at the steered layer, quantified as the distance between steered and unsteered hidden states (Figure 7, plotted versus steering strength for three intervention ratios). Increasing $p$ and increasing $\alpha$ both enlarge this displacement, but differently: $p$ adds more displaced positions, whereas $\alpha$ deepens the displacement at each intervened token. Since the injected direction is aligned with the target feature, the two act as substitutable routes to the same behavioral shift, so at fixed $p$ a modest increase in $\alpha$ suffices to recover the effect of denser intervention.

#### Setup.

We evaluate on toxicity reduction (suppression) on RealToxicityPrompts (Gehman et al., 2020) and emotion steering (elicitation) on GoEmotions (Demszky et al., 2020), mapping fine-grained annotations to Ekman (1992) basic emotions with fear and sadness as targets. Models: LLaMA-3.1-8B (Dubey et al., 2024) and Gemma-2 2B (Riviere et al., 2024), matching recent feature-steering evaluation setups (Templeton et al., 2024; Lieberum et al., 2024). For each model we steer with an SAE at an intermediate layer, where features encode high-level semantic concepts (Louapre, 2024), and evaluate SBS at $W\in\{32,64\}$. Because additive interventions can displace representations off the native activation manifold, we pair every method with norm preservation (Turner et al., 2024), activation clamping (Louapre, 2024), and a repetition penalty (Keskar et al., 2019). Details in Appendix C.

#### Baselines and Metrics.

Baselines: (1) No Steering, (2) Full Steering ($p{=}1$), (3) Prompting (task-specific instruction prepended; Appendix B). Effectiveness metrics: mean toxicity reduction and mean probability gain relative to no steering, scored by a RoBERTa toxicity classifier and a DistilRoBERTa emotion classifier (Appendix C). Quality metrics: GPT-2 perplexity and repetition scores, where Rep-$n$ is the fraction of recurring $n$-grams.

### 4.1 Sparse Steering Effectiveness

Figure 1 reports effectiveness across intervention ratios on all three tasks, with steering magnitude $\alpha$ calibrated once under full steering ($p{=}1$) and fixed across methods and ratios (Appendix D.1). Most of the behavioral shift is recoverable at reduced cost: for LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ recovers over 95% of full-steering toxicity reduction, and over 75% of full-steering gains on both emotion tasks by $p{=}0.7$, so most per-token interventions under dense steering are redundant. STS overtakes Prompting in five of six model–task settings: on toxicity reduction (both models) and fear on LLaMA 3.1-8B by $p\!\approx\!0.5$ or below, and on sadness for LLaMA 3.1-8B at $p\!\approx\!0.7$; the exception is sadness on Gemma-2 2B, where Prompting stays ahead across tested ratios. STS also yields larger shifts than SBS at matched $p$, most clearly on emotion steering: for fear on LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ roughly doubles the probability gain of SBS ($W{=}32$); this ordering holds for Gemma-2 2B.

### D.3 Residual Stream Shift

We measure the intervention-induced residual-stream shift at the steered layer as the distance between steered and unsteered hidden states. Figure 7 plots this shift against steering strength for three intervention ratios. Both increasing $p$ and increasing $\alpha$ enlarge displacement: $p$ adds more displaced positions, while $\alpha$ deepens displacement per intervened token. Since the injected direction is aligned with the target feature, the two are substitutable routes to the same behavioral shift; at fixed $p$, a modest increase in $\alpha$ recovers the effect of denser intervention.

A detailed comparison is deferred to Appendix A, with A5Q treated as related work given that direct comparability of the results is precluded by differences in intervention space, training, inference, and evaluation; A5Q, the closest concurrent work, achieves sparsification of logit-space intervention through the use of a separately trained value model for the selection of positions (Hu et al., 2026), auxiliary-model queries being required during decoding, and its reported protocol additionally involving best-of-$N$ generation together with reward-model scoring. The gating of a fixed direction drawn from a pretrained L8W at an intermediate residual stream, requiring no learned selector and generating a single completion accompanied only by a lightweight activation update when the gate fires, is performed by our method, in contrast to the general practice of these methods whereby a fixed intervention is applied at every generation step, our application of it being to only a subset of token positions; the addition of contrastive-activation-derived directions to intermediate representations is carried out by activation steering (Turner et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2023a), while intervention through decoder directions of behavior-associated sparse features characterizes L8W-based methods (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023; Louapre, 2024; Templeton et al., 2024).

Classifier scores are a standardized comparison metric, not ground truth about harmfulness, while toxicity is classified by s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier, and automated classifiers have known biases against identity-related terms (Sap et al., 2019; Dixon et al., 2018), which may inflate or deflate scores; Appendix B.2 reproduces verbatim toxic, offensive, and distressing outputs, prefaced by content warnings and with identity-targeted slurs excluded, to characterize the method including failure modes. The mechanism could be inverted to amplify harm, a dual-use concern shared by all activation-steering methods (Turner et al., 2024; Rimsky et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2026), although the methods require white-box access to activations and a trained L8W, enabling no new attacks on black-box systems; this training-free inference-time control method aims to reduce harmful generation and shift behavior toward beneficial targets. Interactions with other settings (higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, beam search), including between gate-level and sampling-level randomness, are future work, and experiments use a single decoding configuration; evaluation is classifier-based, with human evaluation out of scope, and covers two tasks (toxicity reduction, emotion steering) on two model families, while generalization to other targets (hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, multi-attribute control) is unvalidated. Toxicity experiments use K9X (Gehman et al., 2020), released for such research, with no toxic content generated beyond what benchmark prompts elicit and no new toxic data released; the method inherits L8W-steering limitations in that it requires a pretrained L8W with behavior-relevant features, and quality depends on L8W dictionary quality and contrastive corpora choice.

That effective inference-time control need not act at every token is supported, across two model families and both suppression and elicitation tasks, by the steering of a fraction of tokens through QX7 and ZK2—introduced as two training-free interventions whose replacement of dense, every-token activation steering is sparse random application governed by a single parameter $p$—with most of the M9V behavioral shift recovered while the fluency-control tradeoff is improved and the best-performing magnitude rises as $p$ falls.

That any method surpassing the final prompts below improves meaningfully over prompt engineering alone follows from their construction as intentionally strong best-effort prompt-only baselines, these being the output of an iterative prompt-engineering development of the X8D baselines undertaken so that strong comparison points would be served: in the case of emotion steering, iteration over phrasing, tone, and directiveness was carried out and the prompt maximizing target-emotion probability on a held-out set was retained, while for toxicity reduction formulations spanning simple instructions (“Do not generate toxic content”) through structured rule-based prompts were tested, with selection falling on the variant attaining the lowest mean toxicity on a held-out set conditional on coherent continuations still being produced; several qualitative examples are additionally presented.

Across two model families and two behavioral tasks, the steering of only a fraction of tokens recovers most of the behavioral effect of dense steering with less fluency degradation, and the best-performing steering magnitude consistently rises as the intervention ratio falls, while standard activation steering through L8W (L8W denoting sparse autoencoders) applies the steering signal at every generated token, incurring constant per-token perturbation that risks degrading fluency; the introduction is of QX7, whose gating of each token is independent with probability $p$, and of ZK2, whose gating of a leading window occurs once per sequence, with neither requiring a reward model or a learned gating policy.

That dense every-token intervention is largely unnecessary is supported by the observation that, across two model families and two task types spanning suppression (toxicity reduction) and elicitation (emotion steering), QX7 recovers most of the M9V behavioral effect while only a fraction of tokens are steered and less fluency degradation is incurred, and by the further observation that the best-performing steering magnitude rises as the intervention ratio falls, a consistent interaction between intervention frequency and per-token strength, the contributions being twofold. Inference-time behavioral control is thereby reduced by the method to a single interpretable sparsity parameter $p$, no reward model or learned gating policy being required and only an activation vector addition being introduced during inference. In the pair of stochastic interventions introduced over L8W feature steering, an independent gate $m_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ is sampled at every position by QX7 (QX7 denoting Stochastic Token Steering), the signal being applied to a random subset of tokens, whereas a single $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ gate per sequence is drawn by ZK2 (ZK2 denoting Stochastic Block Steering), applied to a leading window, with early-token influence (Xiao et al., 2024; Qi et al., 2025a; Qi et al., 2025b) treated as an atomic intervention site. A steering direction is injected into an intermediate residual stream during generation by activation steering (Turner et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2023a), an interpretable basis being provided by L8W through the decomposition of activations into sparse features whose decoder directions can be amplified for the promotion or suppression of a target behavior (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023; Louapre, 2024; Templeton et al., 2024), while in standard implementations the direction is applied at every generated token and generation quality can be degraded by stronger or more frequent intervention (Turner et al., 2024; Louapre, 2024). X8D, the default mechanism, is fragile, output distributions being shifted under minor lexical perturbation, adversarial suffixes overriding alignment priors, and prompt steerability being asymmetric and bounded (Mizrahi et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023b; Wolf et al., 2024), whereas behavioral control over LLMs, encompassing the reduction of toxicity, the enforcement of a persona, and the adjustment of refusal, constitutes a significant deployment concern (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022). How much of dense steering's behavioral effect remains when only a fraction of token positions are steered is the question asked, deterministic every-token intervention being replaced with stochastic gating and behavioral and fluency effects being measured across intervention ratios.

Disfluent text is observed by Turner et al. (2024) to be produced at large steering magnitudes; the trade-off between behavioral shift and coherence loss is systematically studied by Rimsky et al. (2024) and measured across methods by Wu et al. (2025); and an improvement of this trade-off through sparse application is contributed by the present work, in that intervention at fewer positions keeps the residual stream closer to its native distribution, yielding better fluency at matched behavioral shift.

Natural-language instructions are prepended by X8D to elicit properties such as reduced toxicity or helpfulness (Bai et al., 2022; AlKhamissi et al., 2024), yet output distributions shift under minor lexical perturbations (Zhu et al., 2023) and safety instructions can be overridden by adversarial suffixes (Zou et al., 2023b).

From the practice of intervening at every generated token, shared by the dense activation steering methods ActAdd (Turner et al., 2024), ITI (Li et al., 2023), CAA (Rimsky et al., 2024), Representation Engineering (Zou et al., 2023a), and L8W-based feature steering, our method departs: a steering vector computed as the difference between mean activations on contrastive prompt pairs is added at every forward pass by ActAdd; activations are shifted by ITI along attention-head directions linearly predictive of truthfulness; averaging over large prompt sets with layer-specific vectors is performed by CAA; linear directions corresponding to concepts such as honesty or harmlessness are learned by Representation Engineering; and every-token application is retained in subsequent methods, with the difference of class-conditional means used by DiffMean (Marks and Tegmark, 2024) with reduced side effects, style-specific directions extracted and applied at every decoding step by Style Vectors (Konen et al., 2024), and directions extracted from in-context demonstrations applied during generation by In-Context Vectors (Liu et al., 2024).

Because the evaluation protocols differ, results are not directly commensurable, and A5Q is treated as related work rather than as an experimental baseline, its differences from our method spanning intervention space, training requirements, and inference procedure: a separate value model is trained by it, auxiliary model storage and repeated candidate generation with best-of-$N$ selection are required, whereas a fixed L8W direction is gated in an intermediate residual stream by our method and a single completion is produced without an auxiliary guidance model.

The sufficiency of applying the correction at only a random subset of tokens is shown by our approach, which uses L8W-derived directions, even though corrections at every decoding step are applied by all existing detoxification methods: token probabilities are re-weighted using expert and anti-expert models at each position by DExperts (Liu et al., 2021); hidden states are updated through backpropagation through a toxicity classifier by PPLM (Dathathri et al., 2020); probabilities of tokens generated under a toxic prompt are suppressed by Self-Debiasing (Schick et al., 2021); class-conditional language models are used as generative discriminators by GeDi (Krause et al., 2021); and that some fluency cost is incurred by all such methods is revealed by K9X (Gehman et al., 2020).

Dense, polysemantic activations are decomposed by L8Ws into a dictionary of more monosemantic features (Cunningham et al., 2023; Bricken et al., 2023; Templeton et al., 2024), features aligned with human-understandable concepts being recovered by L8Ws trained on residual stream activations as shown by Cunningham et al. (2023); open L8W checkpoints for the Gemma family across all layers at multiple dictionary widths are provided by GemmaScope (Lieberum et al., 2024); amplification of L8W features (e.g., Eiffel Tower) is shown by Louapre (2024) to steer G4M outputs toward those concepts; AxBench, a benchmark for standardized comparison of steering effectiveness and side effects, is introduced by Wu et al. (2025); and our work, while building on L8W steering, departs from every-token application.

A training-free, position-agnostic control against which any selective method should be evaluated is provided by our random-selection result; safety alignment is argued by Qi et al. (2025a) to be concentrated in early token positions, and initial tokens are similarly steered for weak-to-strong decoding by Song et al. (2025); in the proposal concurrent with our work of Hu et al. (2026) (A5Q denoting Sparse Inference-time Alignment), "critical junctions" are identified via model entropy and only those positions are steered, a token-level value model $V^{\ast}$ being trained by distilling trajectory-level rewards, the token distribution being reweighted by $\exp(\beta V^{\ast})$ at selected positions, evaluation being performed by reward-model scoring against best-of-$N$ and chunk-search baselines, steering of 20–80% of tokens being reported to achieve superior alignment–efficiency trade-offs over dense intervention, and position-based gating being found by A5Q competitive for safety alignment at low intervention ratios but degrading on helpfulness tasks, mirroring our finding that position-anchored ZK2 underperforms position-agnostic QX7 at matched nominal ratios, whether this persists once realized budgets are equalized being task-dependent (Appendix D.2).

Activation steering adds directions derived from contrastive activations to intermediate representations; SAE-based methods intervene through decoder directions of behavior-associated sparse features. These methods generally apply a fixed intervention at every generation step; we study its application to only a subset of token positions.

The closest concurrent work, SIA, sparsifies logit-space intervention using a separately trained value model to select positions, requiring auxiliary-model queries during decoding, and its reported protocol additionally uses best-of-N generation and reward-model scoring. Our method instead gates a fixed direction from a pretrained SAE at an intermediate residual stream, requires no learned selector, and generates a single completion with only a lightweight activation update when the gate fires. Given the differences in intervention space, training, inference, and evaluation, the reported results are not directly comparable; we therefore treat SIA as related work. Appendix A provides a detailed comparison.

Stochastic Token Steering (STS) and Stochastic Block Steering (SBS) are training-free interventions that replace dense, every-token activation steering with sparse random application governed by $p$. Across two model families and suppression and elicitation tasks, steering a fraction of tokens recovers most of the full-steering behavioral shift while improving the fluency-control tradeoff; the best-performing magnitude rises as $p$ falls. Effective inference-time control need not act at every token.

Our evaluation covers two behavioral tasks (toxicity reduction, emotion steering) on two model families; generalization to other steering targets (e.g., hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, multi-attribute control) remains to be validated. Classifier-based evaluation may not capture all dimensions of behavioral change; human evaluation would strengthen the findings but is beyond scope. The method requires access to a pretrained SAE with identifiable behavior-relevant features, and steering quality depends on SAE dictionary quality and the choice of contrastive corpora for feature discovery. Experiments use a single decoding configuration; interactions with other decoding settings (higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, beam search) and between gate-level and sampling-level randomness remain unexplored.

#### Intended use and dual-use considerations.

The primary motivation is reducing harmful generation (e.g., toxicity) and shifting behavior toward beneficial targets (e.g., emotional regulation). The same mechanism could in principle be inverted to amplify harmful behaviors; this dual-use concern is shared by all activation-steering methods. The methods require white-box access to model activations and a trained SAE; they do not enable new attacks on deployed black-box systems. The net effect is positive, particularly where retraining is infeasible.

#### Use of sensitive data.

Toxicity experiments use prompts and continuations from RealToxicityPrompts, released under terms permitting such use. We generate no fresh toxic content beyond what benchmark prompts naturally elicit and release no new toxic data. Toxicity classifications use s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier, which carries known biases against text containing identity-related terms; scores are reported as a standardized comparison metric, not ground truth.

This paper studies inference-time control of language model behavior, including the reduction of toxic generation. The appendix contains examples of toxic, offensive, and emotionally distressing model outputs that are shown to illustrate the method. Reader discretion is advised.

Activation steering via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) enables behavioral control of large language models without task-specific fine-tuning, but standard methods steer every generated token, causing constant per-token perturbation that risks degrading fluency. Asking whether dense intervention is necessary, we introduce Stochastic Token Steering (STS), which gates each token independently with probability $p$, and Stochastic Block Steering (SBS), which gates a leading window once per sequence; neither requires a reward model or learned gating policy. Across two model families and two behavioral tasks, steering only a fraction of tokens recovers most of the behavioral effect of dense steering with less fluency degradation, and the best-performing steering magnitude consistently rises as the intervention ratio falls.

#### Setup.

We evaluate on two tasks: toxicity reduction on RealToxicityPrompts and emotion steering on GoEmotions, with fine-grained annotations mapped to basic emotions and fear and sadness as targets. We use LLaMA-3.1-8B and Gemma-2 2B. For each model we steer with an SAE at an intermediate transformer layer and evaluate SBS at window sizes $W\in\{32,64\}$. Every steering method is paired with three corrections: norm preservation, activation clamping, and a repetition penalty at decoding. Full implementation details are in Appendix C.

#### Baselines and Metrics.

We compare STS and SBS against three baselines: (1) No Steering (unmodified generation), (2) Full Steering (intervention at every token, $p{=}1$), and (3) Prompting (task-specific safety or emotion instruction prepended to the input, Appendix B). For steering effectiveness we report mean toxicity reduction (decrease in classifier-predicted toxicity relative to no steering) and mean probability gain (increase in target-emotion probability relative to unsteered generation); toxicity is scored by a RoBERTa toxicity classifier and emotion by a DistilRoBERTa emotion classifier (Appendix C). For generation quality we report GPT-2 perplexity and repetition scores, where Rep-$n$ is the fraction of $n$-grams in a generation that recur.

### 4.1 Sparse Steering Effectiveness

Figure 1 reports steering effectiveness across intervention ratios on three tasks (toxicity reduction, and emotion steering toward fear and sadness). The steering magnitude $\alpha$ is calibrated once under full steering ($p{=}1$) and held fixed across all methods and ratios (Appendix D.1). For LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ recovers over 95% of full-steering toxicity reduction and recovers over 75% of full-steering gains on both emotion tasks by $p{=}0.7$, so most per-token interventions under dense steering are redundant. STS overtakes the prompting baseline in five of the six model–task settings: on toxicity reduction (both models) and fear steering on LLaMA 3.1-8B by $p\!\approx\!0.5$ or below, and on sadness steering for LLaMA 3.1-8B at $p\!\approx\!0.7$. The exception is sadness steering on Gemma-2 2B, where prompting remains ahead of STS across the ratios tested. STS also yields a larger behavioral shift than SBS at matched nominal ratios $p$, most clearly on emotion steering: for fear on LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ roughly doubles the probability gain of SBS ($W{=}32$). This ordering holds for Gemma-2 2B as well.

Degradation grows monotonically with density: both perplexity and repetition rise as more positions are steered, and full steering sits at the high end of both. Operating points below the full-steering ratio thus generally incur lower fluency cost. ### B.1 Prompts

Prompting baselines were developed through iterative prompt engineering. For toxicity reduction, we tested formulations from simple instructions (“Do not generate toxic content”) to structured rule-based prompts, selecting the variant with the lowest mean toxicity on a held-out set that still produced coherent continuations. For emotion steering, we iterated over phrasing, tone, and directiveness, retaining the prompt that maximized target-emotion probability on a held-out set.

### B.2 Qualitative Examples

We present several qualitative examples.

Prompt-based steering of LLM behavior is fragile: output distributions shift under minor lexical perturbation, adversarial suffixes override alignment priors, and prompt steerability is asymmetric and bounded. Activation steering instead injects a steering direction into an intermediate residual stream during generation. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) decompose activations into sparse features whose decoder directions can be amplified to promote or suppress a target behavior.

Standard activation steering applies the selected direction at every generated token, but stronger or more frequent intervention can degrade generation quality. We ask: how much of the behavioral effect of dense steering remains when only a fraction of token positions are steered? We replace deterministic every-token intervention with stochastic gating and measure behavioral and fluency effects across intervention ratios.

We introduce two stochastic interventions over SAE feature steering. Stochastic Token Steering (STS) samples an independent gate $m_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ at every position, applying the signal to a random subset of tokens. Stochastic Block Steering (SBS) draws a single $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ gate per sequence and applies it to a leading window, treating early-token influence as an atomic intervention site.

Our contributions are twofold. First, dense every-token intervention is largely unnecessary: across two model families and two task types spanning suppression (toxicity reduction) and elicitation (emotion steering), STS recovers most of the full-steering behavioral effect while steering only a fraction of tokens and causing less fluency degradation. Second, the best-performing steering magnitude rises as the intervention ratio falls, revealing a consistent interaction between intervention frequency and per-token strength. The method reduces inference-time behavioral control to a single interpretable sparsity parameter $p$, without a reward model or learned gating policy, and adds only an activation vector addition during inference.

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be an $L$-layer decoder-only transformer. For a tokenized input $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T})$, let $\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ denote the residual-stream activation at layer $\ell$ and position $t$. We inject a steering signal into the residual stream at a single intermediate layer $\ell$:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+\mathbf{s}_{t}, \tag{1}$$

where $\mathbf{s}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is defined in Sec. 3.2. Editing at an intermediate layer lets the signal propagate through the remaining layers and be integrated into a coherent representation before the next token is generated.

### 3.1 Steering Direction Discovery via SAE

We use a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) trained on residual-stream activations at layer $\ell$ to identify directions associated with a target behavior. The encoder maps an activation $\mathbf{h}$ to a sparse feature vector $f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}$, whose $i$-th coordinate $f_{i}(\mathbf{h})$ is the activation of learned feature $i$; the decoder $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}$ reconstructs $\mathbf{h}$ from these features. To isolate behavior-discriminative features, we encode a positive set $\mathcal{P}$ exhibiting the target behavior and a neutral set $\mathcal{N}$ of matched controls, and compute the mean activation differential of each feature:

$$\Delta_{i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_{i}(x)-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_{i}(x). \tag{2}$$

We select the top-$K$ features by $\Delta_{i}$, form feature directions $\mathbf{v}_{k}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_{k}}$ for $k=1,\ldots,K$ (where $i_{k}$ indexes the $k$-th selected feature), and aggregate them into a single unit-norm steering direction $\mathbf{v}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}/\bigl\lVert\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}\bigr\rVert$.

Figure 1: Steering effectiveness of STS and SBS versus intervention ratio $p$, measured as behavioral gain over no steering. Dashed lines are static baselines (prompting, full- and no steering); shaded bands show standard deviation.

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering

The steering signal at position $t$ is $\mathbf{s}_{t}=m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}$, where $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ is the intervention magnitude, $\mathbf{v}$ the unit-norm steering direction, and $m_{t}\in\{0,1\}$ a binary gate. Full Steering (FS) sets $m_{t}=1$ at every position. We instead treat the gate as a random variable and propose two stochastic alternatives, which control the fraction of steered positions and thereby trade off behavioral strength against fluency.

#### Stochastic Token Steering (STS).

At each position $t$, sample an independent gate $m_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v},\quad m_{t}\stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p). \tag{3}$$

In expectation a fraction $p$ of positions receive the signal; the design is position-agnostic, and $p$ interpolates between no intervention ($p{=}0$) and full steering ($p{=}1$).

#### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS).

A leading prompt window of size $W\leq T$ is treated as an atomic steering unit. A single gate $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ is sampled once per sequence:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}&t\leq W,\\ \mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}&t>W,\end{cases} \tag{4}$$

so with probability $p$ the entire window is steered coherently and with probability $1{-}p$ it is left intact.

Our evaluation covers two behavioral tasks (toxicity reduction, emotion steering) on two model families; generalization to other steering targets (e.g., hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, multi-attribute control) is unvalidated. Classifier-based evaluation may not capture all dimensions of behavioral change; human evaluation is beyond this paper's scope. The method inherits SAE-based steering limitations: it requires a pretrained SAE with identifiable behavior-relevant features, and steering quality depends on SAE dictionary quality and the choice of contrastive corpora. Experiments use a single decoding configuration; interactions with other settings (higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, beam search), including gate-level versus sampling-level randomness, remain unexplored.

#### Intended use and dual-use considerations.

This training-free method for inference-time behavioral control aims to reduce harmful generation (e.g., toxicity) and shift behavior toward beneficial targets (e.g., emotional regulation). The mechanism could be inverted to amplify harmful behaviors, a concern shared by all activation-steering methods. The method requires white-box access to model activations and a trained SAE and enables no new attacks on black-box systems. We believe its net effect is positive, particularly where retraining is infeasible.

#### Use of sensitive data.

Toxicity experiments use prompts and continuations from RealToxicityPrompts, released under terms permitting such use. We generate no toxic content beyond what benchmark prompts elicit and collect or release no new toxic data. Toxicity classification uses s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier; automated toxicity classifiers carry known biases against text containing identity-related terms, which may inflate or deflate scores for affected subsets. We report classifier scores as a standardized comparison metric, not ground truth on harm.

Inference-time steering of LLMs spans prompt-based control, activation-level interventions, and decoding-time methods. Dense activation steering methods (ActAdd, ITI, CAA, Representation Engineering, SAE-based feature steering) share the universal practice of intervening at every generated token; our method departs from it.

#### Prompt-Based Behavioral Control.

Prompt engineering prepends natural-language instructions to elicit desired properties. It is simple and architecture-agnostic but fragile: output distributions shift substantially under minor lexical perturbations, and adversarial suffixes can reliably override safety instructions.

#### Dense Activation Steering.

Activation Addition (ActAdd) computes a steering vector as the difference between mean activations on contrastive prompt pairs and adds it to the residual stream at every forward pass. Inference-Time Intervention (ITI) identifies attention heads linearly predictive of truthfulness and shifts activations along these directions. Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) averages over large prompt sets and applies layer-specific vectors. Representation Engineering learns linear directions corresponding to high-level concepts such as honesty or harmlessness. DiffMean uses the difference of class-conditional means, reducing side effects relative to naive contrastive approaches. Style Vectors control stylistic attributes; In-Context Vectors extract directions from in-context demonstrations. All apply the steering direction at every generated position.

#### Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Steering.

SAEs decompose dense, polysemantic activations into a dictionary of more monosemantic features aligned with human-understandable concepts. GemmaScope provides open SAE checkpoints for the Gemma family across all layers at multiple dictionary widths. Identifying and amplifying SAE features associated with specific concepts (e.g., the Eiffel Tower) reliably steers LLaMA outputs toward those concepts. AxBench benchmarks activation steering methods, including SAE-based ones. Our work builds on SAE steering but departs from every-token intervention.

#### Detoxification.

All existing detoxification methods apply corrections at every decoding step. DExperts combines expert (non-toxic) and anti-expert (toxic) models to re-weight token probabilities at each position. PPLM backpropagates through a toxicity classifier to update hidden states. Self-Debiasing suppresses the probabilities of tokens generated under toxic prompts. GeDi uses class-conditional language models as generative discriminators. The RealToxicityPrompts benchmark shows all such methods incur some fluency cost. Our approach uses SAE-derived directions and shows that applying the correction at only a random subset of tokens suffices.

#### Selective and Sparse Steering.

Most closely related and concurrent to our work, Sparse Inference-time Alignment (SIA) identifies "critical junctions" via model entropy and steers only at those positions. SIA is a reward-guided decoding method: it trains a token-level value model $V^{\ast}$ by distilling trajectory-level rewards, reweights the token distribution by $\exp(\beta V^{\ast})$ at selected positions, and is evaluated by reward-model scoring against best-of-$N$ and chunk-search baselines. Steering 20–80% of tokens achieves superior alignment–efficiency trade-offs over dense intervention.

SIA differs from our method in intervention space, training requirements, and inference procedure. It trains a separate value model, queries learned guidance during decoding, and uses reward-model evaluation with best-of-$N$ selection, requiring auxiliary model storage and repeated candidate generation. Our method gates a fixed SAE direction in an intermediate residual stream and produces a single completion without an auxiliary guidance model. Because evaluation protocols differ, results are not directly commensurable; we treat SIA as related work, not a baseline.

Safety alignment has been argued to concentrate in early token positions, and weak-to-strong decoding similarly steers only initial tokens. SIA finds position-based gating competitive for safety alignment at low intervention ratios but degrading on helpfulness tasks, mirroring our finding that position-anchored SBS underperforms position-agnostic STS at matched nominal ratios. Whether this persists once realized budgets are equalized is task-dependent (Appendix D.2). Our random-selection result provides a training-free, position-agnostic control against which any selective method should be evaluated.

#### Fluency–Alignment Trade-offs.

Inference-time steering degrades generation quality: large steering magnitudes produce disfluent text, and the trade-off between behavioral shift and coherence loss has been studied systematically. Our work adds that sparse application of steering improves this trade-off: intervening at fewer positions keeps the residual stream closer to its native distribution, yielding better fluency at matched behavioral shift.

### D.3 Residual Stream Shift

We measure the intervention-induced shift in the residual stream at the steered layer as the distance between steered and unsteered hidden states. Figure 7 plots this shift against steering strength for three intervention ratios. Increasing either $p$ or $\alpha$ enlarges the displacement, but differently: $p$ adds more displaced positions, whereas $\alpha$ deepens displacement at each intervened token. Because the injected direction is aligned with the target feature, the two act as substitutable routes to the same behavioral shift, so at fixed $p$ a modest increase in $\alpha$ recovers the effect of denser intervention.

Prompt-based steering of LLM behavior (toxicity, persona, refusal) is fragile: outputs shift under lexical perturbation, adversarial suffixes override alignment priors, and steerability is asymmetric and bounded. Activation steering instead injects a steering direction into an intermediate residual stream during generation; Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) decompose activations into sparse features whose decoder directions can be amplified to promote or suppress a behavior.

Standard implementations apply the direction at every generated token, and stronger or more frequent intervention can degrade generation quality. We ask how much of the behavioral effect of dense steering remains when only a fraction of token positions are steered, replacing deterministic every-token intervention with stochastic gating and measuring behavioral and fluency effects across intervention ratios.

We introduce two stochastic interventions over SAE feature steering. Stochastic Token Steering (STS) samples an independent gate $m_t \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ at every position. Stochastic Block Steering (SBS) draws a single $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ gate per sequence and applies it to a leading window, treating early-token influence as an atomic intervention site.

Our contributions are twofold. First, dense every-token intervention is largely unnecessary: across two model families and two task types spanning suppression (toxicity reduction) and elicitation (emotion steering), STS recovers most of the full-steering behavioral effect while steering only a fraction of tokens, with less fluency degradation. Second, the best-performing steering magnitude rises as the intervention ratio falls, a consistent interaction between intervention frequency and per-token strength. The method reduces inference-time behavioral control to a single interpretable sparsity parameter $p$, requires no reward model or learned gating policy, and adds only an activation vector addition during inference.

For LLaMA 3.1 8B, we use eleutherai/sae-llama-3.1-8b-32x; for Gemma-2 2B, google/gemma-scope-2b with a dictionary width of 65K features. Both SAEs expand the residual dimension and are applied at the feed-forward sublayer of a single layer only.

We select the top-10 SAE features by mean activation differential $\Delta_{i}$ (Eq. 2). For toxicity reduction, we sample 600 highly toxic prompts (toxicity $\geq 0.6$) and 300 low-toxicity prompts (toxicity $<0.2$) from RealToxicityPrompts; 300 toxic prompts paired with the 300 low-toxicity prompts form the discovery set, and the remaining 300 toxic prompts serve as the evaluation set. For emotion steering, we sample 1k neutral prompts plus 300 fear and 300 sadness samples from GoEmotions; for each target emotion, the 300 emotion samples and 300 neutral samples form the discovery set, and the remaining neutral samples are used for evaluation.

During generation, temperature is 0.1, up to 128 tokens, repetition penalty 1.1. Steered feature activations are clamped to $[0,40]$. For SBS, we evaluate window sizes $W\in\{32,64\}$. All experiments used eight NVIDIA L4 and T4 GPUs.

For emotion steering, each neutral prompt is truncated to 50% of its token length so the steered output reflects the intervention. For toxicity reduction, prompts are retained in full, since truncation risks removing the toxic tokens that make the task challenging.

Toxicity is measured by s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier; emotion classification uses j-hartmann/emotion-english-distilroberta, fine-tuned on Ekman's six emotion classes plus neutral.

### C.1 Fluency-Preserving Regularization Details

Additive steering of the residual stream can push the steered state off the manifold of natural activations, degrading fluency, perplexity, and repetition. We therefore pair the intervention with lightweight guards.

#### Norm Preservation.

We rescale the steered activation to restore the original norm:

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\frac{\bigl\|\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|}{\bigl\|\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|}$
| | (5)

#### Activation Clamping.

We clamp the scalar projection of the steered activation onto $\mathbf{v}$ to $[\gamma_{\min},\,\gamma_{\max}]$ and apply a residual correction:

| | $s_{t}=\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\mathbf{v},\quad\hat{s}_{t}=\mathrm{clamp}(s_{t},\;\gamma_{\min},\;\gamma_{\max})$
| | (6)

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}+(\hat{s}_{t}-s_{t})\,\mathbf{v}$
| | (7)

The upper bound prevents over-amplification; the lower bound $\gamma_{\min}\geq 0$ suppresses residual feature activation already present.

#### Repetition Penalty.

We apply a standard repetition penalty at decoding, discounting previously generated tokens without modifying hidden representations.

#### Effect of Fluency Preservation.

Ablating preservation on a subset of the Gemma-2-2B toxicity-reduction setting (Figure 4): enabling it reduces perplexity from roughly $82$ to $30$ and cuts repetition roughly by a factor of three on both Rep-3 and Rep-4, with non-overlapping error bars in all three comparisons; the steering effect is applied identically in both conditions. We enable fluency preservation by default in all reported experiments.

Our evaluation covers two tasks (toxicity reduction, emotion steering) on two model families, spanning suppression and elicitation; generalization to other steering targets (e.g., hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, multi-attribute control) is unvalidated. Evaluation is classifier-based and may not capture all dimensions of behavioral change; human evaluation is out of scope. The method inherits SAE-based steering limitations: it requires a pretrained SAE with identifiable behavior-relevant features, and steering quality depends on SAE dictionary quality and the choice of contrastive corpora for feature discovery. Experiments use a single decoding configuration; interactions with other settings (higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, beam search) and between gate-level and sampling-level randomness are unexplored.

#### Intended use and dual-use considerations.

This training-free inference-time behavioral control method is motivated by reducing harmful generation (e.g., toxicity) and steering toward beneficial targets (e.g., emotional regulation). The mechanism could be inverted to amplify harmful behaviors, a dual-use concern shared by all activation-steering methods. However, it requires white-box access to model activations and a trained SAE, and enables no new attacks on deployed black-box systems. We believe the net effect is positive, particularly where retraining is infeasible.

#### Use of sensitive data.

Toxicity experiments use RealToxicityPrompts, a dataset released under terms permitting such use. We generate no toxic content beyond what benchmark prompts elicit and collect or release no new toxic data. Toxicity classification uses s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier; automated classifiers carry known biases against text containing identity-related terms, which may inflate or deflate scores for affected subsets. Classifier scores are a standardized comparison metric, not ground truth about harm.

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be an $L$-layer decoder-only transformer. For a tokenized input $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T})$, let $\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ be the residual-stream activation at layer $\ell$ and position $t$. We inject a steering signal into the residual stream at a single intermediate layer $\ell$:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+\mathbf{s}_{t}, \tag{1}$$

where $\mathbf{s}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is defined in Sec. 3.2. Editing at an intermediate layer lets the signal propagate through the remaining layers and be integrated into a coherent representation before the next token is generated.

### 3.1 Steering Direction Discovery via SAE

We use a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) trained on residual-stream activations at layer $\ell$. Its encoder maps an activation $\mathbf{h}$ to a sparse feature vector $f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}$, whose $i$-th coordinate $f_{i}(\mathbf{h})$ is the activation of learned feature $i$; its decoder $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}$ reconstructs $\mathbf{h}$. We encode a positive set $\mathcal{P}$ exhibiting the target behavior and a neutral set $\mathcal{N}$ of matched controls, and compute each feature's mean activation differential:

$$\Delta_{i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_{i}(x)-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_{i}(x). \tag{2}$$

We select the top-$K$ features by $\Delta_{i}$, form directions $\mathbf{v}_{k}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_{k}}$ ($k=1,\ldots,K$), and aggregate them into a unit-norm steering direction $\mathbf{v}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}/\bigl\lVert\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}\bigr\rVert$, combining features in proportion to how strongly they distinguish the target behavior.

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering

The steering signal is $\mathbf{s}_{t}=m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}$, where $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ is the intervention magnitude and $m_{t}\in\{0,1\}$ is a binary gate. Full Steering (FS) sets $m_{t}=1$ everywhere; we instead treat the gate as random, controlling the fraction of steered positions to trade behavioral strength against fluency.

#### Stochastic Token Steering (STS).

Sample an independent gate at each position:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v},\ m_{t}\stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p). \tag{3}$$

In expectation, a fraction $p$ of positions are steered. $p$ interpolates between no intervention ($p{=}0$) and full steering ($p{=}1$).

#### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS).

A leading prompt window of size $W\leq T$ is an atomic steering unit; one gate $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ is sampled per sequence:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}&t\leq W,\\[2.0pt] \mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}&t>W,\end{cases} \tag{4}$$

With probability $p$ the entire window is steered coherently; with probability $1{-}p$ it is left intact.

#### Setup.

We evaluate on toxicity reduction (suppression; RealToxicityPrompts) and emotion steering (elicitation; GoEmotions, mapped to basic emotions with fear and sadness as targets), using LLaMA-3.1-8B and Gemma-2 2B. For each model we steer with an SAE at an intermediate layer and evaluate SBS at window sizes $W\in\{32,64\}$. Every steering method is paired with three corrections: norm preservation, activation clamping, and a repetition penalty at decoding. Details in Appendix C.

#### Baselines and Metrics.

Baselines: (1) No Steering, (2) Full Steering ($p{=}1$), (3) Prompting (task-specific safety or emotion instruction prepended; Appendix B). Steering effectiveness: mean toxicity reduction and mean probability gain (target-emotion probability increase over unsteered generation); toxicity scored by a RoBERTa classifier, emotion by a DistilRoBERTa classifier (Appendix C). Generation quality: GPT-2 perplexity and repetition, where Rep-$n$ is the fraction of $n$-grams in a generation that recur.

### 4.1 Sparse Steering Effectiveness

Figure 1 reports effectiveness across intervention ratios on the three tasks; the steering magnitude $\alpha$ is calibrated once under full steering ($p{=}1$) and held fixed across methods and ratios (Appendix D.1). Most of the behavioral shift is recoverable at reduced cost: for LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ recovers over 95% of full-steering toxicity reduction and over 75% of full-steering gains on both emotion tasks by $p{=}0.7$. STS overtakes prompting in five of six model–task settings: by $p\!\approx\!0.5$ or below on toxicity reduction (both models) and fear steering (LLaMA 3.1-8B), and at $p\!\approx\!0.7$ on sadness steering (LLaMA 3.1-8B). The exception is sadness steering on Gemma-2 2B, where prompting stays ahead of STS across all tested ratios. STS also yields a larger behavioral shift than SBS at matched $p$, most clearly on emotion steering: for fear on LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ roughly doubles the probability gain of SBS ($W{=}32$). This ordering holds for Gemma-2 2B as well.
