### D.3 Residual Stream Shift

We measure the intervention-induced shift in the residual stream at the steered layer, quantified as the distance between steered and unsteered hidden states, as a function of steering strength for three intervention ratios. Increasing $p$ and increasing $\alpha$ both enlarge this displacement, but differently: $p$ adds more displaced positions, whereas $\alpha$ deepens the displacement at each intervened token. Since the injected direction is aligned with the target feature, the two are substitutable routes to the same behavioral shift, so at a fixed $p$ a modest increase in $\alpha$ recovers the effect of denser intervention.

Behavioral control over large language models (LLMs)—reducing toxicity, enforcing a persona, adjusting refusal—is a significant deployment concern. The default mechanism, the system prompt, is fragile: distributions shift under minor lexical perturbation, adversarial suffixes override alignment priors, and prompt-based steerability is asymmetric and bounded.

Activation steering modifies behavior by injecting a steering direction into an intermediate residual stream during generation. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) decompose activations into sparse features whose decoder directions can be amplified to promote or suppress a target behavior.

Standard implementations steer at every generated token. Because stronger or more frequent intervention can degrade generation quality, we ask: how much of the behavioral effect of dense steering remains when only a fraction of token positions are steered? We replace deterministic every-token intervention with stochastic gating and measure behavioral and fluency effects across intervention ratios.

We introduce two stochastic interventions over SAE feature steering. Stochastic Token Steering (STS) samples an independent gate $m_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ at every position, steering a random subset of tokens. Stochastic Block Steering (SBS) draws a single $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ gate per sequence and applies it to a leading window, treating early-token influence as an atomic intervention site.

Contributions are twofold. First, dense every-token intervention is largely unnecessary: across two model families and two task types spanning suppression (toxicity reduction) and elicitation (emotion steering), STS recovers most of the full-steering behavioral effect while steering only a fraction of tokens, with less fluency degradation. Second, the best-performing steering magnitude rises as the intervention ratio falls, revealing a consistent interaction between intervention frequency and per-token strength. The method reduces inference-time behavioral control to a single interpretable sparsity parameter $p$, requires no reward model or learned gating policy, and adds only an activation vector addition during inference.

Inference-time steering of LLMs spans prompt-based control, activation-level interventions, and decoding-time methods. Dense activation steering methods—ActAdd, ITI, CAA, Representation Engineering, and SAE-based feature steering—all intervene at every generated token; our method departs from this.

#### Prompt-Based Behavioral Control.

Prompt engineering prepends natural-language instructions to elicit properties such as reduced toxicity or increased helpfulness. It is simple and architecture-agnostic but fragile: output distributions shift substantially under minor lexical perturbations, and adversarial suffixes can reliably override safety instructions.

#### Dense Activation Steering.

These methods intervene in the residual stream, applying corrections uniformly at every token. ActAdd computes a steering vector as the difference between mean activations on contrastive prompt pairs and adds it to the residual stream at every forward pass. ITI identifies attention heads linearly predictive of truthfulness and shifts activations along these directions. CAA averages over large prompt sets and applies layer-specific vectors. Representation Engineering learns linear directions corresponding to high-level concepts such as honesty or harmlessness. DiffMean uses the difference of class-conditional means, reducing side effects versus naive contrastive approaches. Style Vectors extract style-specific directions applied at every decoding step. In-Context Vectors extract latent directions from in-context demonstrations and apply them during generation. All apply the steering direction at every generated position.

#### Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Steering.

SAEs decompose dense, polysemantic activations into a dictionary of more monosemantic features; SAEs trained on residual stream activations recover interpretable features aligned with human-understandable concepts. GemmaScope provides open SAE checkpoints for the Gemma family across all layers at multiple dictionary widths. Identifying and amplifying SAE features associated with specific concepts (e.g., the Eiffel Tower) reliably steers LLaMA outputs toward those concepts. AxBench is a benchmark for evaluating activation steering methods, including SAE-based approaches, with standardized comparisons of effectiveness and side effects. Our work builds on the SAE steering paradigm but departs from every-token intervention.

#### Detoxification.

All existing detoxification methods apply corrections at every decoding step. DExperts combines an expert (non-toxic) and anti-expert (toxic) model to re-weight token probabilities at each position. PPLM backpropagates through a toxicity classifier to update hidden states during generation. Self-Debiasing prompts the model to generate toxic text and suppresses the resulting token probabilities. GeDi uses class-conditional language models as generative discriminators. Evaluation on RealToxicityPrompts shows all such methods incur some fluency cost. Our approach uses SAE-derived directions and shows that applying the correction at only a random subset of tokens suffices.

#### Selective and Sparse Steering.

Most closely related and concurrent, Sparse Inference-time Alignment (SIA) identifies "critical junctions" via model entropy and steers only at those positions. SIA is reward-guided decoding: it trains a token-level value model $V^{\ast}$ by distilling trajectory-level rewards, reweights the token distribution by $\exp(\beta V^{\ast})$ at selected positions, and is evaluated by reward-model scoring against best-of-$N$ and chunk-search baselines. Steering 20–80% of tokens achieves superior alignment–efficiency trade-offs over dense intervention.

SIA differs from our method in intervention space, training requirements, and inference procedure: it trains a value model from trajectory rewards, queries learned guidance during decoding, uses reward-model evaluation with best-of-$N$ selection, and requires auxiliary model storage and repeated candidate generation. Our method gates a fixed SAE direction in an intermediate residual stream and produces a single completion without an auxiliary guidance model. Because evaluation protocols differ, results are not directly commensurable; we treat SIA as related work, not a baseline.

Safety alignment has been argued to concentrate in early token positions, and weak-to-strong decoding similarly focuses steering on initial tokens. SIA finds position-based gating competitive for safety alignment at low intervention ratios but degrading on helpfulness tasks—a task-dependence mirroring our finding that position-anchored SBS underperforms position-agnostic STS at matched nominal ratios. Whether this persists once realized budgets are equalized is task-dependent (Appendix D.2). Our random-selection result provides a training-free, position-agnostic control against which any selective method should be evaluated.

#### Fluency–Alignment Trade-offs.

Inference-time steering degrades generation quality: large steering magnitudes produce disfluent text, and the trade-off between behavioral shift and coherence loss has been systematically studied and standardized across methods. We add the observation that sparse application improves this trade-off: intervening at fewer positions keeps the residual stream closer to its native distribution, yielding better fluency at matched behavioral shift.

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be an $L$-layer decoder-only transformer. For input $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T})$, let $\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ be the residual-stream activation at layer $\ell$, position $t$. We inject a steering signal at a single intermediate layer $\ell$:

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+\mathbf{s}_{t},$
| | (1)

where $\mathbf{s}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is defined in Sec. 3.2. The intervention is restricted to one intermediate layer so the signal propagates through the remaining layers.

### 3.1 Steering Direction Discovery via SAE

We use a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) trained on residual-stream activations at layer $\ell$. Its encoder maps $\mathbf{h}$ to a sparse feature vector $f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}$, where $f_{i}(\mathbf{h})$ is the activation of feature $i$; the decoder $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}$ reconstructs $\mathbf{h}$. We encode a positive set $\mathcal{P}$ exhibiting the target behavior and a neutral set $\mathcal{N}$ of matched controls, and compute each feature's mean activation differential:

| | $\Delta_{i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_{i}(x)-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_{i}(x).$
| | (2)

We select the top-$K$ features by $\Delta_{i}$, form directions $\mathbf{v}_{k}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_{k}}$, and aggregate them into a unit-norm steering direction $\mathbf{v}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}/\bigl\lVert\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}\bigr\rVert$.

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering

The steering signal is $\mathbf{s}_{t}=m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}$, with magnitude $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$, unit-norm direction $\mathbf{v}$, and binary gate $m_{t}\in\{0,1\}$. Full Steering (FS) sets $m_{t}=1$ everywhere. We propose two stochastic alternatives that control the fraction of steered positions.

#### Stochastic Token Steering (STS).

At each position, sample an independent gate $m_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$:

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v},~m_{t}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p).$
| | (3)

In expectation a fraction $p$ of positions is steered; $p$ interpolates between no intervention ($p{=}0$) and full steering ($p{=}1$).

#### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS).

Treat a leading prompt window of size $W\leq T$ as an atomic unit, sampling one gate $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ per sequence:

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}&t\leq W,\\[2.0pt]
\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}&t>W,\end{cases}$
| | (4)

With probability $p$ the whole window is steered coherently; with probability $1{-}p$ it is left intact.

For LLaMA 3.1 8B we use eleutherai/sae-llama-3.1-8b-32x; for Gemma-2 2B, google/gemma-scope-2b with a dictionary width of 65K features. Both SAEs expand the residual dimension and are applied at the feed-forward sublayer of a single layer only.

We select the top-10 SAE features by mean activation differential $\Delta_{i}$ (Eq. 2). For emotion steering, we sample 1k neutral prompts plus 300 fear and 300 sadness samples from GoEmotions; per emotion, 300 emotion and 300 neutral samples form the discovery set and the remaining neutral samples the evaluation set.

For emotion steering, neutral prompts are truncated to 50% of token length so the continuation reflects the intervention. For toxicity reduction, we retain the full prompt, since truncation could remove the toxic tokens and make the task less challenging.

### C.1 Fluency-Preserving Regularization Details

Additive steering can push the steered state off the manifold of natural activations, degrading fluency, perplexity, and repetition. We therefore apply three guards.

#### Norm Preservation.

We rescale the steered activation to restore the original norm:

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\frac{\bigl\|\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|}{\bigl\|\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|}$
| | (5)

#### Activation Clamping.

We clamp the projection onto $\mathbf{v}$ to $[\gamma_{\min},\,\gamma_{\max}]$ and apply a residual correction:

| | $s_{t}=\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\mathbf{v},\quad\hat{s}_{t}=\mathrm{clamp}(s_{t},\;\gamma_{\min},\;\gamma_{\max})$
| | (6)

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}+(\hat{s}_{t}-s_{t})\,\mathbf{v}$
| | (7)

The upper bound prevents over-amplification; the lower bound $\gamma_{\min}\geq 0$ suppresses residual feature activation.

#### Repetition Penalty.

We apply a standard repetition penalty at decoding, discounting previously generated tokens without modifying hidden representations.

#### Effect of Fluency Preservation.

Ablating preservation on the Gemma-2-2B toxicity-reduction setting (Figure 4): enabling it reduces perplexity from roughly $82$ to $30$ and cuts Rep-3 and Rep-4 by roughly a factor of three, with non-overlapping error bars in all three comparisons. The steering effect is identical in both conditions, so the gains come from keeping generation on-manifold. Fluency preservation is enabled by default in all reported experiments.

#### Prompt-Based Behavioral Control.

Prompt engineering prepends natural-language instructions to elicit properties such as reduced toxicity or increased helpfulness. ### C.1 Fluency-Preserving Regularization Details

Additive steering injects a fixed direction $\mathbf{v}$ (Section 3) into the hidden state at layer $\ell$, but does not guarantee the result stays on the manifold the model decodes fluently; as steering strength grows or the intervention accumulates, the state can drift in norm or direction, degrading fluency, inflating perplexity, and inducing repetition. We therefore pair the intervention with three lightweight guards.

#### Norm Preservation.

We rescale the steered activation to restore the original norm:

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\frac{\bigl\|\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|}{\bigl\|\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|}$ | | (5)

This rotates the representation toward $\mathbf{v}$ without inflating its magnitude, preserving the scale invariants assumed downstream.

#### Activation Clamping.

We clamp the scalar projection of the steered activation onto $\mathbf{v}$ to $[\gamma_{\min},\,\gamma_{\max}]$ and apply a residual correction:

| | $s_{t}=\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\mathbf{v},\quad\hat{s}_{t}=\mathrm{clamp}(s_{t},\;\gamma_{\min},\;\gamma_{\max})$ | | (6)

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}+(\hat{s}_{t}-s_{t})\,\mathbf{v}$ | | (7)

The upper bound prevents over-amplification beyond the feature's natural range; the lower bound $\gamma_{\min}\geq 0$ suppresses residual feature activation in the unsteered representation.

#### Repetition Penalty.

We apply a standard repetition penalty at decoding, discounting previously generated tokens without modifying hidden representations.

# A Coin Flip Per Token: Bernoulli Sparse Steering of Large Language Models

###### Abstract

We introduce Stochastic Token Steering (STS), which gates each token independently with probability $p$, and Stochastic Block Steering (SBS), which gates a leading window once per sequence; neither requires a reward model or learned gating policy. Across two model families and two behavioral tasks, steering only a fraction of tokens recovers most of the behavioral effect of dense steering while incurring less fluency degradation. The best-performing steering magnitude consistently rises as the intervention ratio falls.

## 1 Introduction

Activation steering injects a steering direction into an intermediate residual stream during generation; Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) provide an interpretable basis by decomposing activations into sparse features whose decoder directions can be amplified to promote or suppress a target behavior. Standard implementations apply the selected direction at every generated token, but stronger or more frequent intervention can degrade generation quality. We ask: how much of the behavioral effect of dense steering remains when only a fraction of token positions are steered?

Our contributions are twofold. First, dense every-token intervention is largely unnecessary: across two model families and two task types spanning suppression (toxicity reduction) and elicitation (emotion steering), STS recovers most of the full-steering behavioral effect while steering only a fraction of tokens, and causes less fluency degradation. Second, the best-performing steering magnitude rises as the intervention ratio falls, revealing a consistent interaction between intervention frequency and per-token strength. The method reduces inference-time behavioral control to a single interpretable sparsity parameter $p$, without a reward model or learned gating policy, and adds only an activation vector addition during inference.

## 2 Related Work

Existing activation-steering methods generally apply a fixed intervention at every generation step; we apply it to only a subset of token positions. The closest concurrent work, SIA, sparsifies logit-space intervention using a separately trained value model to select positions, requires auxiliary-model queries during decoding, and uses best-of-$N$ generation and reward-model scoring. Our method instead gates a fixed direction from a pretrained SAE at an intermediate residual stream, requires no learned selector, and generates a single completion with only a lightweight activation update when the gate fires. Given the differences in intervention space, training, inference, and evaluation, the results are not directly comparable; Appendix A provides a detailed comparison.

## 3 Method

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be an $L$-layer decoder-only transformer. For a tokenized input $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T})$, let $\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ denote the residual-stream activation at layer $\ell$ and position $t$. We inject a steering signal into the residual stream at a single intermediate layer $\ell$:

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+\mathbf{s}_{t},$
| | (1)

where $\mathbf{s}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ is defined in Sec. 3.2.

### 3.1 Steering Direction Discovery via SAE

An SAE trained on residual-stream activations at layer $\ell$ maps an activation $\mathbf{h}$ to a sparse feature vector $f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}$, whose $i$-th coordinate $f_{i}(\mathbf{h})$ is the activation of learned feature $i$; the decoder $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}$ reconstructs $\mathbf{h}$ from these features. We encode a positive set $\mathcal{P}$ exhibiting the target behavior and a neutral set $\mathcal{N}$ of matched controls, and compute the mean activation differential of each feature:

| | $\Delta_{i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_{i}(x)-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_{i}(x).$
| | (2)

We select the top-$K$ features by $\Delta_{i}$, form feature directions $\mathbf{v}_{k}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_{k}}$ for $k=1,\ldots,K$, and aggregate them into a single unit-norm steering direction $\mathbf{v}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}/\bigl\lVert\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}\bigr\rVert$.

Figure 1: Steering effectiveness of STS and SBS versus intervention ratio $p$, measured as behavioral gain over no steering. Dashed lines are static baselines (prompting, full- and no steering); shaded bands show standard deviation.

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering

The steering signal at position $t$ is $\mathbf{s}_{t}=m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}$, where $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ is the intervention magnitude and $m_{t}\in\{0,1\}$ is a binary gate. Full Steering (FS) sets $m_{t}=1$ at every position. We propose two stochastic alternatives.

#### Stochastic Token Steering (STS).

At each position $t$, we sample an independent gate $m_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$:

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v},~m_{t}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p).$
| | (3)

In expectation, a fraction $p$ of positions receive the signal; $p$ interpolates between no intervention ($p{=}0$) and full steering ($p{=}1$).

#### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS).

A single gate $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ is sampled once per sequence and applied to a leading prompt window of size $W\leq T$:

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}&t\leq W,\\[2.0pt]
\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}&t>W,\end{cases}$
| | (4)

## 4 Experiments

#### Setup.

We evaluate on toxicity reduction, a suppression task built on RealToxicityPrompts, and emotion steering, an elicitation task built on GoEmotions, taking fear and sadness as targets. We use LLaMA-3.1-8B and Gemma-2 2B, steering with an SAE at an intermediate transformer layer, and evaluate SBS at window sizes $W\in\{32,64\}$. Because additive interventions can displace representations off the model's native activation manifold, we pair every steering method with norm preservation, activation clamping, and a repetition penalty at decoding. Full implementation details are in Appendix C.

#### Baselines and Metrics.

We compare STS and SBS against three baselines: (1) No Steering, (2) Full Steering ($p{=}1$), and (3) Prompting (a task-specific safety or emotion instruction prepended to the input, Appendix B). We report mean toxicity reduction (decrease in classifier-predicted toxicity relative to no steering) and mean probability gain (increase in target-emotion probability relative to unsteered generation); toxicity is scored by a RoBERTa toxicity classifier and emotion by a DistilRoBERTa emotion classifier. For generation quality we report GPT-2 perplexity and repetition scores, where Rep-$n$ is the fraction of $n$-grams in a generation that recur.

### 4.1 Sparse Steering Effectiveness

Figure 1 reports steering effectiveness across intervention ratios on three tasks. We calibrate the steering magnitude $\alpha$ once under full steering ($p{=}1$) and hold it fixed across all methods and ratios (Appendix D.1). For LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ recovers over 95% of full-steering toxicity reduction and over 75% of full-steering gains on both emotion tasks by $p{=}0.7$. STS overtakes the prompting baseline in five of the six model–task settings: on toxicity reduction (both models) and fear steering on LLaMA 3.1-8B by $p\!\approx\!0.5$ or below, and on sadness steering for LLaMA 3.1-8B at $p\!\approx\!0.7$. The exception is sadness steering on Gemma-2 2B, where prompting remains ahead of STS across the ratios we test. STS also yields a larger behavioral shift than SBS at matched nominal ratios $p$: for fear on LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ roughly doubles the probability gain of SBS ($W{=}32$). This ordering holds for Gemma-2 2B as well.

### 4.2 Fluency Under Sparse and Dense Steering

Figure 2 reports perplexity and repetition (Rep-$3$, Rep-$4$) against intervention ratio for Gemma 2-2B on toxicity reduction. Degradation grows monotonically with density: both perplexity and repetition rise as more positions are steered, and full steering sits at the high end of both. Operating points below the full-steering ratio therefore incur lower fluency cost. The trend holds across SBS window sizes.

Figure 2: Generation quality versus intervention ratio: perplexity and repetition scores (Rep-3, Rep-4), shaded bands show standard deviation. Both metrics rise with steering density.

### 4.3 Steering Magnitude and Intervention Ratio

Figure 3 plots the best-performing $\alpha^{*}$ (maximizing behavioral shift subject to fluency preservation) against the intervention ratio for both models. The best-performing steering magnitude rises as the ratio falls: at a fixed magnitude the behavioral effect increases with the ratio, and conversely the ratio required to reach a target effect decreases as per-token strength grows. Appendix D.3 corroborates this: normalized residual-stream displacement grows with $\alpha$ and $p$.

Figure 3: Best-performing steering magnitude $\alpha^{*}$ versus intervention ratio (GoEmotions-fear). At each $p$, $\alpha^{*}$ maximizes target-emotion probability gain subject to fluency preservation.

## 5 Conclusion

STS and SBS are two training-free interventions that replace dense, every-token activation steering with sparse random application governed by a single parameter $p$. Across two model families and both suppression and elicitation tasks, steering a fraction of tokens recovers most of the full-steering behavioral shift while improving the fluency-control tradeoff, and the best-performing magnitude rises as $p$ falls. Effective inference-time control need not act at every token.

## Limitations

Our evaluation covers two behavioral tasks on two model families; generalization to other steering targets (e.g., hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, multi-attribute control) remains to be validated. We use classifier-based evaluation, which may not capture all dimensions of behavioral change; human evaluation would strengthen the findings. The method requires access to a pretrained SAE with identifiable behavior-relevant features, and steering quality depends on SAE dictionary quality and the choice of contrastive corpora. Our experiments use a single decoding configuration; how stochastic steering interacts with other decoding settings (e.g., higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, beam search) remains unexplored.

#### Intended use and dual-use considerations.

The same mechanism could in principle be inverted to amplify harmful behaviors: SAE features identified for toxicity reduction could be steered in the opposite direction to elicit toxicity. However, the methods require white-box access to model activations and to a trained SAE; they do not enable new attacks on deployed black-box systems.

#### Use of sensitive data.

Toxicity reduction experiments use prompts and continuations from RealToxicityPrompts, released under terms permitting such use. We do not generate fresh toxic content beyond what the benchmark prompts naturally elicit, and do not collect or release new toxic data. Toxicity classifications use s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier; automated toxicity classifiers carry known biases against text containing identity-related terms, which may inflate or deflate reported scores for affected subsets. We report classifier scores as a standardized comparison metric, not as ground truth.

#### Qualitative examples.

Appendix B.2 reproduces verbatim model outputs that include toxic, offensive, and emotionally distressing content, prefaced by content warnings. We have excluded examples containing identity-targeted slurs.

## Appendix A Related Work

#### Prompt-Based Behavioral Control.

Prompt engineering prepends natural-language instructions to elicit desired properties, but output distributions shift under minor lexical perturbations and adversarial suffixes can override safety instructions.

#### Dense Activation Steering.

Activation Addition (ActAdd), Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), Representation Engineering, DiffMean, Style Vectors, In-Context Vectors, and SAE-based feature steering all apply a steering direction at every generated position.

#### Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Steering.

SAEs decompose dense, polysemantic activations into a dictionary of more monosemantic features. GemmaScope provides open SAE checkpoints for the Gemma model family across all layers at multiple dictionary widths. AxBench provides standardized comparisons of steering effectiveness and side effects. We build on the SAE steering paradigm but do not apply interventions at every token position.

#### Detoxification.

DExperts, PPLM, Self-Debiasing, and GeDi all apply corrections at every decoding step and incur some fluency cost on RealToxicityPrompts. Our approach uses SAE-derived directions and applies the correction at only a random subset of tokens.

#### Selective and Sparse Steering.

SIA identifies "critical junctions" via model entropy and steers only at those positions: it trains a token-level value model $V^{\ast}$ by distilling trajectory-level rewards, reweights the token distribution by $\exp(\beta V^{\ast})$ at selected positions, and is evaluated by reward-model scoring against best-of-$N$ and chunk-search baselines, reporting that steering 20–80% of tokens achieves superior alignment–efficiency trade-offs over dense intervention. These components require auxiliary model storage and repeated candidate generation; our method gates a fixed SAE direction and produces a single completion. SIA finds position-based gating competitive for safety alignment at low ratios but degrading on helpfulness tasks, mirroring our finding that SBS underperforms STS at matched nominal ratios. Whether this persists once realized budgets are equalized is task-dependent (Appendix D.2). Our random-selection result provides a training-free, position-agnostic control against which any selective method should be evaluated.

#### Fluency–Alignment Trade-offs.

Large steering magnitudes produce disfluent text; sparse application of steering improves this trade-off by keeping the residual stream closer to its native distribution, yielding better fluency at matched behavioral shift.

### C.1 Fluency-Preserving Regularization Details

#### Norm Preservation.

We rescale the steered activation to restore the norm of the original:

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\frac{\bigl\|\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|}{\bigl\|\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\bigr\|}$
| | (5)

#### Activation Clamping.

We clamp the scalar projection of the steered activation onto $\mathbf{v}$ to a range $[\gamma_{\min},\,\gamma_{\max}]$ and apply a residual correction:

| | $s_{t}=\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\mathbf{v},\quad\hat{s}_{t}=\mathrm{clamp}(s_{t},\;\gamma_{\min},\;\gamma_{\max})$
| | (6)

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}+(\hat{s}_{t}-s_{t})\,\mathbf{v}$
| | (7)

The upper bound prevents over-amplification beyond the feature's natural range, while the lower bound $\gamma_{\min}\geq 0$ suppresses residual feature activation already present in the unsteered representation.

#### Repetition Penalty.

We apply a standard repetition penalty at the decoding stage, discounting previously generated tokens without further modifying hidden representations.

#### Effect of Fluency Preservation.

Toggling preservation on, holding all other settings fixed, on a subset of the Gemma-2-2B toxicity-reduction setting reduces perplexity substantially (from roughly $82$ to $30$) and cuts repetition roughly by a factor of three across both Rep-3 and Rep-4, with non-overlapping error bars in all three comparisons. The behavioral steering effect is applied identically in both conditions. We enable fluency preservation by default in all reported experiments.

### D.3 Residual Stream Shift

We measure the shift induced in the residual stream at the steered layer as the distance between steered and unsteered hidden states (Figure 7). Both increasing $p$ and increasing $\alpha$ enlarge this displacement, but differently: $p$ adds more displaced positions, whereas $\alpha$ deepens the displacement at each intervened token. Since the injected direction is aligned with the target feature, the two act as substitutable routes to the same behavioral shift, so at a fixed $p$ a modest increase in $\alpha$ recovers the effect of denser intervention.

# A Coin Flip Per Token: Bernoulli Sparse Steering of Large Language Models

###### Abstract

Standard SAE activation steering perturbs every generated token. We introduce Stochastic Token Steering (STS), gating each token independently with probability \(p\), and Stochastic Block Steering (SBS), drawing one Bernoulli(\(p\)) gate per sequence for a leading window. Neither uses a reward model or learned gate. Across two model families and suppression/elicitation tasks, steering a fraction of tokens recovers most dense-steering behavioral effect with less fluency degradation; the best-performing magnitude rises as intervention ratio falls.

## 1 Introduction

Prompt-based behavioral control is fragile; activation steering injects directions into an intermediate residual stream, and SAE decoder directions give interpretable features to amplify or suppress behavior. Standard implementations steer every token. We test whether dense intervention is necessary by stochastic gating across intervention ratios. Contributions: dense every-token intervention is largely unnecessary across two model families and two task types, STS recovers most full-steering effect while steering fewer tokens and degrading fluency less, and best-performing steering magnitude rises as intervention ratio falls. Control reduces to one sparsity parameter \(p\), with only an activation-vector addition when the gate fires.

## 2 Related Work

Prior activation-steering and SAE feature-steering methods generally apply a fixed intervention at every generation step; we apply it to only a subset of token positions. The closest concurrent method, SIA, sparsifies logit-space intervention using a separately trained value model, auxiliary queries during decoding, best-of-\(N\) generation, and reward-model scoring; ours gates a fixed pretrained-SAE direction in a residual stream and emits one completion, so results are not directly comparable and SIA is treated as related work.

## 3 Method

Let \(\mathcal{M}\) be an \(L\)-layer decoder-only transformer. For \(\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T})\), let \(\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\) be the layer-\(\ell\) residual activation at position \(t\). Steering is injected at one intermediate layer \(\ell\):
\[
\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+\mathbf{s}_{t},
\tag{1}
\]
where \(\mathbf{s}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\) is defined below. Editing an intermediate layer lets the signal propagate through remaining layers before the next token.

### 3.1 Steering Direction Discovery via SAE

An SAE at layer \(\ell\) maps \(\mathbf{h}\) to sparse features \(f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}\), with \(f_i(\mathbf{h})\) the activation of feature \(i\); decoder \(\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}\) reconstructs \(\mathbf{h}\). Encode positive set \(\mathcal{P}\) exhibiting the target behavior and neutral controls \(\mathcal{N}\), and compute
\[
\Delta_{i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_{i}(x)-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_{i}(x).
\tag{2}
\]
Select top-\(K\) features by \(\Delta_i\), form \(\mathbf{v}_{k}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_{k}}\), and aggregate to unit-norm
\(\mathbf{v}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}/\lVert\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}\rVert\).

Figure 1: Steering effectiveness of STS and SBS versus intervention ratio \(p\), measured as behavioral gain over no steering. Dashed lines are static baselines (prompting, full- and no steering); shaded bands show standard deviation.

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering

The signal is \(\mathbf{s}_{t}=m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}\), with magnitude \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), unit-norm direction \(\mathbf{v}\), and gate \(m_t\in\{0,1\}\). Full Steering (FS) sets \(m_t=1\) for all \(t\). The stochastic variants randomize \(m_t\) to trade behavioral strength against fluency.

#### Stochastic Token Steering (STS).

Sample an independent gate at each position:
\[
\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v},\quad m_{t}\stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p).
\tag{3}
\]
Expected steered fraction is \(p\); the design is position-agnostic and interpolates from no intervention (\(p{=}0\)) to full steering (\(p{=}1\)).

#### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS).

Treat a leading window of size \(W\le T\) as one unit with a single per-sequence gate \(m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)\):
\[
\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=
\begin{cases}
\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}&t\le W,\\[2pt]
\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}&t>W,
\end{cases}
\tag{4}
\]
With probability \(p\) the whole window is steered; with probability \(1-p\) it is intact. This uses early tokens as an atomic intervention site.

## 4 Experiments

#### Setup.

Tasks: toxicity reduction (suppression) on RealToxicityPrompts, and emotion steering (elicitation) on GoEmotions mapped to basic emotions with fear and sadness as targets. Models: LLaMA-3.1-8B and Gemma-2 2B. Each uses an SAE at one intermediate layer; SBS is evaluated at \(W\in\{32,64\}\). Every steering method is paired with norm preservation, activation clamping, and repetition penalty. Implementation details are in Appendix C.

#### Baselines and Metrics.

Baselines: No Steering, Full Steering (\(p{=}1\)), and Prompting with a curated task instruction (Appendix B). Effectiveness: mean toxicity reduction relative to no steering, scored by a RoBERTa toxicity classifier; mean target-emotion probability gain relative to unsteered generation, scored by a DistilRoBERTa emotion classifier. Quality: GPT-2 perplexity and Rep-\(n\), the fraction of recurring \(n\)-grams.

### 4.1 Sparse Steering Effectiveness

Figure 1 reports effectiveness across ratios for toxicity reduction and fear/sadness steering, with \(\alpha\) calibrated once at \(p{=}1\) and held fixed (Appendix D.1). For LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at \(p{=}0.5\) recovers over 95% of full-steering toxicity reduction and over 75% of full-steering gains on both emotion tasks by \(p{=}0.7\). STS overtakes prompting in five of six model-task settings: on toxicity for both models and fear for LLaMA by \(p\!\approx\!0.5\) or below, on LLaMA sadness at \(p\!\approx\!0.7\); Gemma sadness remains below prompting across tested ratios. STS exceeds SBS at matched nominal \(p\), most clearly for LLaMA fear where STS at \(p{=}0.5\) roughly doubles SBS (\(W{=}32\)) probability gain; the ordering also holds for Gemma.

### 4.2 Fluency Under Sparse and Dense Steering

Figure 2 reports perplexity, Rep-3, and Rep-4 versus intervention ratio for Gemma-2 2B toxicity reduction. Perplexity and repetition rise monotonically as more positions are steered, with full steering at the high end; sparse operating points generally incur lower fluency cost across SBS window sizes. The required ratio is task-dependent, smaller for toxicity reduction than emotion steering.

## 5 Conclusion

STS and SBS are training-free sparse replacements for dense every-token steering, governed by \(p\). Across two model families and suppression/elicitation tasks, steering a fraction of tokens recovers most full-steering behavioral shift while improving the fluency-control tradeoff, and best-performing magnitude rises as \(p\) falls. Effective inference-time control need not act at every token.

## Limitations

Evaluation covers toxicity reduction and emotion steering on two model families; generalization to hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, and multi-attribute control is unvalidated. Classifier-based evaluation may miss behavioral dimensions; human evaluation is out of scope. The method requires a pretrained SAE with identifiable behavior-relevant features and depends on SAE dictionary quality and contrastive corpora. Experiments use one decoding configuration; interactions with higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, beam search, and sampling-level randomness are unexplored.

#### Intended use and dual-use considerations.

The method is intended for inference-time control such as toxicity reduction and beneficial emotional targets, but the same SAE features could be steered oppositely to amplify harm. This dual-use risk is shared with activation-steering methods. The methods require white-box access to activations and a trained SAE and do not enable new attacks on black-box deployed systems.

#### Use of sensitive data.

Toxicity experiments use RealToxicityPrompts under terms permitting research use; no fresh toxic content is generated beyond benchmark-elicited continuations and no new toxic data are collected or released. Toxicity uses s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier; automated toxicity classifiers have known biases against identity-related terms, which may inflate or deflate subset scores. Classifier scores are standardized metrics, not ground truth.

#### Qualitative examples.

Appendix B.2 contains verbatim toxic, offensive, and emotionally distressing outputs, with content warnings, to characterize behavior including failure modes. Identity-targeted slurs were excluded even when benchmark prompts could elicit them.

Detoxification methods DExperts, PPLM, Self-Debiasing, and GeDi correct every decoding step and incur fluency cost on RealToxicityPrompts. SIA is reward-guided decoding: it trains token-level value model \(V^{*}\) from distilled trajectory rewards, reweights by \(\exp(\beta V^{*})\) at selected positions, uses reward-model scoring against best-of-\(N\) and chunk-search, and reports steering 20–80% of tokens improves alignment-efficiency trade-offs. SIA differs in intervention space, training, inference, and evaluation, requiring auxiliary storage and repeated candidates, so results are not commensurable. Safety alignment is concentrated early; initial-token steering and SIA position gating are competitive for safety at low ratios but degrade on helpfulness, mirroring SBS underperforming position-agnostic STS at matched nominal ratios. Whether this persists at equal realized budgets is task-dependent. Random selection is a training-free position-agnostic control for selective methods. Sparse application keeps the residual stream closer to its native distribution, improving fluency at matched behavioral shift.

### C.1 Fluency-Preserving Regularization Details

Additive steering injects fixed \(\mathbf{v}\) into layer \(\ell\) but does not guarantee staying on the fluent decoding manifold; drift in norm or direction causes degraded fluency, inflated perplexity, and repetition. Guards keep steered activations near the natural regime while preserving behavioral effect.

#### Norm Preservation.

Rescale the steered activation to the original norm:
\[
\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\frac{\|\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\|}{\|\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\|}
\tag{5}
\]
This rotates toward \(\mathbf{v}\) without magnitude inflation.

#### Activation Clamping.

Clamp the projection onto \(\mathbf{v}\) to \([\gamma_{\min},\gamma_{\max}]\) and correct the residual:
\[
s_{t}=\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\mathbf{v},\quad \hat{s}_{t}=\mathrm{clamp}(s_{t},\gamma_{\min},\gamma_{\max})
\tag{6}
\]
\[
\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}+(\hat{s}_{t}-s_{t})\mathbf{v}
\tag{7}
\]
The upper bound prevents over-amplification; \(\gamma_{\min}\ge0\) suppresses residual feature activation already present.

#### Repetition Penalty.

A standard decoding-time repetition penalty discounts previously generated tokens without changing hidden representations.

#### Effect of Fluency Preservation.

Ablating preservation on a Gemma-2-2B toxicity subset, enabling it reduces perplexity from roughly 82 to 30 and cuts Rep-3 and Rep-4 by roughly a factor of three, with non-overlapping error bars, while the behavioral steering effect is applied identically. Fluency preservation is enabled by default in all reported experiments.

### D.3 Residual Stream Shift

Residual shift at the steered layer is the distance between steered and unsteered hidden states. Increasing \(p\) and increasing \(\alpha\) both enlarge displacement: \(p\) adds displaced positions, while \(\alpha\) deepens displacement at intervened tokens. Because the injected direction aligns with the target feature, they are substitutable routes to the same behavioral shift, so at fixed \(p\) a modest \(\alpha\) increase can recover denser intervention.

# A Coin Flip Per Token: Bernoulli Sparse Steering of Large Language Models

###### Abstract

Activation steering via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) enables behavioral control of large language models without task-specific fine-tuning, but standard methods apply the steering signal at every generated token, risking fluency degradation. We introduce Stochastic Token Steering (STS), which gates each token independently with probability $p$, and Stochastic Block Steering (SBS), which gates a leading window once per sequence; neither requires a reward model or learned gating policy. Across two model families and two behavioral tasks, steering only a fraction of tokens recovers most of the behavioral effect of dense steering with less fluency degradation, and the best-performing steering magnitude consistently rises as the intervention ratio falls.

## 1 Introduction

Standard activation-steering implementations apply the selected direction at every generated token, and stronger or more frequent intervention can degrade generation quality. We ask: how much of the behavioral effect of dense steering remains when only a fraction of token positions are steered? STS samples an independent gate $m_t \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ at every position; SBS draws a single $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ gate per sequence and applies it to a leading window, treating early-token influence as an atomic intervention site. Our contributions: (1) dense every-token intervention is largely unnecessary—across two model families and two task types spanning suppression (toxicity reduction) and elicitation (emotion steering), STS recovers most of the full-steering behavioral effect while steering only a fraction of tokens and causing less fluency degradation; (2) the best-performing steering magnitude rises as the intervention ratio falls. The method reduces inference-time behavioral control to a single interpretable sparsity parameter $p$, adding only an activation vector addition during inference.

## 2 Related Work

Activation steering and SAE-based methods generally apply a fixed intervention at every generation step; we study applying it to only a subset of positions. The closest concurrent work, SIA, sparsifies logit-space intervention using a separately trained value model to select positions, requires auxiliary-model queries during decoding, and its reported protocol uses best-of-$N$ generation and reward-model scoring. Our method gates a fixed direction from a pretrained SAE at an intermediate residual stream, requires no learned selector, and generates a single completion with a lightweight activation update when the gate fires. Given these differences, the reported results are not directly comparable; we treat SIA as related work (Appendix A).

## 3 Method

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be an $L$-layer decoder-only transformer. For input $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_T)$, let $\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ be the residual-stream activation at layer $\ell$ and position $t$. We inject a steering signal at a single intermediate layer $\ell$:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)} = \mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)} + \mathbf{s}_t, \tag{1}$$

with $\mathbf{s}_t$ defined in Sec. 3.2. Editing at an intermediate layer lets the signal propagate through the remaining layers before the next token is generated.

### 3.1 Steering Direction Discovery via SAE

We use an SAE trained on residual-stream activations at layer $\ell$. The encoder maps $\mathbf{h}$ to a sparse feature vector $f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}$, where $f_i(\mathbf{h})$ is the activation of feature $i$; the decoder $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}$ reconstructs $\mathbf{h}$. We encode a positive set $\mathcal{P}$ exhibiting the target behavior and a neutral set $\mathcal{N}$ of matched controls, and compute each feature's mean activation differential:

$$\Delta_i = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}} f_i(x) - \frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}} f_i(x). \tag{2}$$

We select the top-$K$ features by $\Delta_i$, form $\mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_k}$, and aggregate into a unit-norm direction $\mathbf{v} = \sum_{k=1}^K \mathbf{v}_k / \lVert \sum_{k=1}^K \mathbf{v}_k \rVert$.

Figure 1: Steering effectiveness of STS and SBS versus intervention ratio $p$, measured as behavioral gain over no steering. Dashed lines are static baselines (prompting, full- and no steering); shaded bands show standard deviation.

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering

The steering signal is $\mathbf{s}_t = m_t \cdot \alpha\, \mathbf{v}$, where $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ is the intervention magnitude, $\mathbf{v}$ the unit-norm direction, and $m_t\in\{0,1\}$ a binary gate. Full Steering (FS) sets $m_t=1$ everywhere; we instead treat the gate as random, trading behavioral strength against fluency.

#### Stochastic Token Steering (STS).

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)} = \mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)} + m_t \cdot \alpha\,\mathbf{v}, \quad m_t \stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p). \tag{3}$$

In expectation a fraction $p$ of positions are steered; this position-agnostic design assumes nothing about which tokens are behaviorally relevant, and $p$ interpolates between no intervention ($p{=}0$) and full steering ($p{=}1$).

#### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS).

A leading window of size $W \le T$ is an atomic steering unit with one gate $m \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ per sequence:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)} = \begin{cases} \mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)} + m \cdot \alpha\,\mathbf{v} & t \le W, \\ \mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)} & t > W. \end{cases} \tag{4}$$

With probability $p$ the entire window is steered coherently; with probability $1-p$ it is left intact.

## 4 Experiments

#### Setup.

We evaluate on toxicity reduction, a suppression task built on RealToxicityPrompts, and emotion steering, an elicitation task built on GoEmotions, mapping the fine-grained annotations onto basic emotions and taking fear and sadness as targets. We use LLaMA-3.1-8B and Gemma-2 2B, steering with an SAE at an intermediate layer and evaluating SBS at $W\in\{32,64\}$. Because additive interventions can displace representations off the model's native activation manifold and induce incoherent or repetitive text, we pair every steering method with norm preservation, activation clamping, and a repetition penalty at decoding. Full details are in Appendix C.

#### Baselines and Metrics.

Baselines: (1) No Steering, (2) Full Steering ($p{=}1$), and (3) Prompting (a curated task-specific safety or emotion instruction prepended to the input; Appendix B). Steering effectiveness: mean toxicity reduction (decrease in classifier-predicted toxicity vs. no steering) and mean probability gain (increase in target-emotion probability vs. unsteered generation); toxicity is scored by a RoBERTa toxicity classifier and emotion by a DistilRoBERTa classifier (Appendix C). Generation quality: GPT-2 perplexity and Rep-$n$, the fraction of $n$-grams in a generation that recur.

### 4.1 Sparse Steering Effectiveness

Figure 1 reports effectiveness across intervention ratios on toxicity reduction and fear and sadness steering. We calibrate $\alpha$ once under full steering ($p{=}1$) and hold it fixed across all methods and ratios (Appendix D.1). Most of the behavioral shift is recoverable at substantially reduced cost: for LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ recovers over 95% of full-steering toxicity reduction and recovers over 75% of full-steering gains on both emotion tasks by $p{=}0.7$, confirming most per-token interventions under dense steering are redundant. STS overtakes the prompting baseline in five of the six model–task settings: on toxicity reduction (both models) and fear on LLaMA 3.1-8B by $p\approx 0.5$ or below, and on sadness for LLaMA 3.1-8B at $p\approx 0.7$; the exception is sadness on Gemma-2 2B, where prompting remains ahead across tested ratios. STS also yields a larger behavioral shift than SBS at matched nominal $p$, most clearly on emotion steering: for fear on LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ roughly doubles the probability gain of SBS ($W{=}32$). This ordering holds for Gemma-2 2B as well.

### 4.2 Fluency Under Sparse and Dense Steering

Figure 2 reports perplexity and repetition (Rep-3, Rep-4) against intervention ratio for Gemma-2 2B on toxicity reduction, with full steering as reference. Degradation grows monotonically with density: perplexity and repetition rise as more positions are steered, and full steering sits at the high end of both, so operating points below the full-steering ratio generally incur lower fluency cost. The required ratio is task dependent (smaller for toxicity reduction than for emotion steering), and the trend holds across SBS window sizes.

Figure 2: Generation quality versus intervention ratio: perplexity and repetition scores (Rep-3, Rep-4); shaded bands show standard deviation. Both metrics rise with steering density.

### 4.3 Steering Magnitude and Intervention Ratio

Figure 3 plots the best-performing $\alpha^*$ (maximizing behavioral shift subject to fluency preservation) against intervention ratio for both models: $\alpha^*$ tends to rise as the ratio falls. At a fixed magnitude the behavioral effect increases with the intervention ratio, and conversely the ratio needed for a target effect decreases as per-token strength grows. Appendix D.3 corroborates this: normalized residual-stream displacement grows with both $\alpha$ and $p$.

## 5 Conclusion

STS and SBS replace dense every-token activation steering with sparse random application governed by a single parameter $p$. Across two model families and both suppression and elicitation tasks, steering a fraction of tokens recovers most of the full-steering behavioral shift while improving the fluency-control tradeoff, and the best-performing magnitude rises as $p$ falls. Effective inference-time control need not act at every token.

## Limitations

Our evaluation covers two tasks on two model families; generalization to other steering targets (e.g., hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, multi-attribute control) remains unvalidated. We use classifier-based evaluation, which may not capture all dimensions of behavioral change; human evaluation is beyond the scope of this short paper. The method requires a pretrained SAE with identifiable behavior-relevant features, and steering quality depends on SAE dictionary quality and the contrastive corpora used for feature discovery. Our experiments use a single decoding configuration; interactions with other decoding settings (higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, beam search) and between gate-level and sampling-level randomness remain unexplored.

#### Intended use and dual-use considerations.

The primary motivation is reducing harmful generation (e.g., toxicity) and shifting behavior toward beneficial targets. The same mechanism could in principle be inverted to amplify harmful behaviors—features identified for toxicity reduction could be steered oppositely to elicit toxicity—a dual-use concern shared by all activation-steering methods. The methods require white-box access to activations and a trained SAE and do not enable new attacks on deployed black-box systems.

#### Use of sensitive data.

Toxicity experiments use prompts and continuations from RealToxicityPrompts; we do not generate fresh toxic content beyond what the benchmark prompts elicit and do not collect or release new toxic data. Toxicity classification uses s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier; automated toxicity classifiers carry known biases against text containing identity-related terms, which may inflate or deflate scores for affected subsets. We report classifier scores as a standardized comparison metric, not as ground truth.

#### Qualitative examples.

Appendix B.2 reproduces verbatim model outputs that include toxic, offensive, and emotionally distressing content, prefaced by content warnings. We excluded examples containing identity-targeted slurs.

## Appendix A Related Work

Dense activation steering methods—ActAdd, ITI, CAA, Representation Engineering, and SAE-based feature steering—share the universal practice of intervening at every generated token; our method departs from it.

#### Prompt-Based Behavioral Control.

Prompt-based control is fragile: output distributions shift under minor lexical perturbations and adversarial suffixes can override safety instructions.

#### Dense Activation Steering.

ActAdd adds the difference between mean activations on contrastive prompt pairs to the residual stream at every forward pass; ITI shifts activations along attention-head directions predictive of truthfulness; CAA averages over large prompt sets with layer-specific vectors; Representation Engineering learns linear directions for high-level concepts. DiffMean uses the difference of class-conditional means; Style Vectors control stylistic attributes; In-Context Vectors extract directions from demonstrations. All apply the direction at every generated position.

#### Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Steering.

SAEs decompose dense, polysemantic activations into a dictionary of more monosemantic features; amplifying behavior-associated features steers outputs. GemmaScope provides open SAE checkpoints for Gemma across layers at multiple dictionary widths; AxBench benchmarks activation steering methods. We depart from the universal every-token practice.

#### Detoxification.

DExperts reweights token probabilities using expert and anti-expert models; PPLM backpropagates through a toxicity classifier to update hidden states; Self-Debiasing suppresses probabilities of tokens the model generates when prompted for toxic text; GeDi uses class-conditional models as generative discriminators. All apply corrections at every decoding step and incur some fluency cost. We use SAE-derived directions applied at only a random subset of tokens.

#### Selective and Sparse Steering.

Concurrent work SIA identifies "critical junctions" via model entropy and steers only there: it trains a token-level value model $V^*$ by distilling trajectory-level rewards, reweights the token distribution by $\exp(\beta V^*)$ at selected positions, and is evaluated by reward-model scoring against best-of-$N$ and chunk-search baselines, reporting that steering 20–80% of tokens achieves superior alignment–efficiency trade-offs over dense intervention. SIA differs in intervention space, training requirements, and inference procedure, and the evaluation protocols are not commensurable. Prior work argues safety alignment is concentrated in early token positions; SIA finds position-based gating competitive for safety alignment at low ratios but degrading on helpfulness tasks—mirroring our finding that position-anchored SBS underperforms position-agnostic STS at matched nominal ratios. Whether this persists at equalized realized budgets is task-dependent (Appendix D.2). Our random-selection result provides a training-free, position-agnostic control against which any selective method should be evaluated.

#### Fluency–Alignment Trade-offs.

Large steering magnitudes produce disfluent text; there is a systematic trade-off between behavioral shift and coherence loss. Sparse application improves this trade-off: intervening at fewer positions keeps the residual stream closer to its native distribution, yielding better fluency at matched behavioral shift.

### C.1 Fluency-Preserving Regularization Details

Additive steering carries no guarantee the steered representation stays on the manifold the model decodes fluently; drift in norm or direction manifests as degraded fluency, inflated perplexity, and repetition. We therefore apply three guards.

#### Norm Preservation.

We rescale the steered activation to restore the original norm:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)} \leftarrow \tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)} \cdot \frac{\lVert \mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)} \rVert}{\lVert \tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)} \rVert} \tag{5}$$

This constrains the intervention to rotate the representation toward $\mathbf{v}$ without inflating its magnitude.

#### Activation Clamping.

We clamp the scalar projection onto $\mathbf{v}$ to $[\gamma_{\min}, \gamma_{\max}]$ and apply a residual correction:

$$s_t = \tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)} \cdot \mathbf{v}, \quad \hat{s}_t = \mathrm{clamp}(s_t, \gamma_{\min}, \gamma_{\max}) \tag{6}$$

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)} \leftarrow \tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)} + (\hat{s}_t - s_t)\,\mathbf{v} \tag{7}$$

The upper bound prevents over-amplification beyond the feature's natural range; $\gamma_{\min} \geq 0$ suppresses residual feature activation already present.

#### Repetition Penalty.

Steering suppresses high-probability continuations, which can drive repetitive sequences; we apply a standard repetition penalty at decoding, discounting previously generated tokens without modifying hidden representations.

#### Effect of Fluency Preservation.

Toggling preservation on a subset of the Gemma-2 2B toxicity-reduction setting (Figure 4): perplexity drops from roughly 82 to 30, and Rep-3 and Rep-4 fall roughly by a factor of three, with non-overlapping error bars in all three comparisons. The steering signal is applied identically in both conditions, so gains reflect staying on the natural manifold, not weakened steering. We enable fluency preservation by default in all reported experiments.

### D.3 Residual Stream Shift

We measure the distance between steered and unsteered hidden states at the steered layer (Figure 7). Both increasing $p$ and increasing $\alpha$ enlarge this displacement, but differently: $p$ adds more displaced positions, whereas $\alpha$ deepens displacement at each intervened token. Since the injected direction is aligned with the target feature, the two are substitutable routes to the same behavioral shift, so at fixed $p$ a modest increase in $\alpha$ recovers the effect of denser intervention.

The best-performing steering magnitude rises consistently as the intervention ratio falls, and, across two model families and two behavioral tasks, most of the behavioral effect of dense steering is recovered, with less fluency degradation incurred, through the steering of only a fraction of tokens, under QX7, in which the gating of each token is performed independently with probability $p$, and under ZK2, in which a leading window is gated once per sequence, with neither of the two requiring a reward model or a learned gating policy.

The interaction of stochastic steering with other decoding settings (e.g., higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, beam search) remains unexplored, our experiments using a single decoding configuration, and steering quality depends on L8W dictionary quality and the choice of contrastive corpora, the method requiring access to a pretrained L8W with identifiable behavior-relevant features; generalization to other steering targets (e.g., hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, multi-attribute control) remains to be validated, our evaluation covering two behavioral tasks on two model families, and human evaluation would strengthen the findings given that the classifier-based evaluation employed may not capture all dimensions of behavioral change.

Because intervention space, training, inference, and evaluation all differ, the results are not directly comparable, and Appendix A provides a detailed comparison. The gating of a fixed direction drawn from a pretrained L8W at an intermediate residual stream is performed by the method presented here, which, requiring no learned selector, generates a single completion in which the only update is a lightweight activation update applied when the gate fires. In A5Q, the closest concurrent work, logit-space intervention is sparsified through the selection of positions by a separately trained value model, with auxiliary-model queries required during decoding and best-of-$N$ generation used together with reward-model scoring. A fixed intervention is generally applied at every generation step by existing activation-steering methods, whereas application is made here to only a subset of token positions.

Effective inference-time control need not act at every token, a conclusion arising from the recovery of most of the M9V behavioral shift, together with an improvement of the fluency-control tradeoff, achieved, across two model families and both suppression and elicitation tasks, by the application of QX7 and ZK2 to a fraction of tokens, with the best-performing magnitude rising as $p$ falls, $p$ being the single parameter by which the replacement of dense, every-token activation steering with sparse random application, carried out by these two training-free interventions, is governed.

Most of the M9V behavioral effect is recovered by QX7 while steering is applied to only a fraction of tokens, with less fluency degradation being caused in comparison, and this holds across two model families and two task types spanning suppression (toxicity reduction) and elicitation (emotion steering), dense every-token intervention being thereby shown to be largely unnecessary; the best-performing steering magnitude, moreover, rises as H9C falls, a consistent interaction between intervention frequency and per-token strength being revealed by this dependence.

The reduction of inference-time behavioral control to a single interpretable sparsity parameter $p$ is effected without a reward model or learned gating policy, only an activation vector addition being introduced during inference.

How much of the behavioral effect of dense steering remains when only a fraction of token positions are steered is the question posed, given that the selected direction is applied at every generated token in standard implementations, whereas stronger or more frequent intervention can degrade generation quality.

Activation steering consists in the injection of a steering direction into an intermediate residual stream during generation; an interpretable basis is furnished by L8W, under which activations are decomposed into sparse features whose decoder directions can be amplified to promote or suppress a target behavior.

Several qualitative examples are presented, and the X8D baselines, developed through iterative prompt engineering, involved the selection, for emotion steering, of the prompt achieving maximization of target-emotion probability on a held-out set, and, for toxicity reduction, of the variant by which the lowest mean toxicity on a held-out set was achieved while coherent continuations were produced.

Large steering magnitudes produce disfluent text; sparse application of steering improves this trade-off by keeping the residual stream closer to its native distribution, yielding better fluency at matched behavioral shift, even as Activation Addition (ActAdd), Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), Representation Engineering, DiffMean, Style Vectors, In-Context Vectors, and L8W-based feature steering all apply a steering direction at every generated position, and the corrections of DExperts, PPLM, Self-Debiasing, and GeDi are applied at every decoding step, incurring some fluency cost on K9X, whereas the approach taken here uses L8W-derived directions and applies the correction at only a random subset of tokens.
