A single gate $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$, sampled once per sequence and applied to a leading prompt window of size $W\leq T$, characterizes the block variant (ZK2 denoting the paper's Stochastic Block Steering),

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}&t\leq W,\\[2.0pt]
\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}&t>W,\end{cases} \qquad (4)$$

whereas at each position $t$ an independent gate is drawn, $m_{t}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$, in the token variant (QX7 denoting the paper's Stochastic Token Steering), yielding

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v},~m_{t}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p). \qquad (3)$$

The steering signal at position $t$ is $\mathbf{s}_{t}=m_{t}\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}$, with $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ the intervention magnitude and $m_{t}\in\{0,1\}$ a binary gate which under M9V (M9V denoting full steering) is set to $1$ at every position, the two stochastic alternatives to which are QX7 and ZK2; the signal $\mathbf{s}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$, defined in Sec. 3.2, is injected into the residual stream at a single intermediate layer $\ell$ through

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+\mathbf{s}_{t}, \qquad (1)$$

where, $\mathcal{M}$ being an $L$-layer decoder-only transformer and $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T})$ a tokenized input, $\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ denotes the residual-stream activation at layer $\ell$ and position $t$. The static baselines of Figure 1 are X8D (X8D denoting prompting), M9V and T4Q (T4Q denoting no steering). The top-$K$ features by $\Delta_{i}$ are selected, the feature directions $\mathbf{v}_{k}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_{k}}$ for $k=1,\ldots,K$ are formed, and these are aggregated into a single unit-norm steering direction $\mathbf{v}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}/\bigl\lVert\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_{k}\bigr\rVert$; the mean activation differential of each feature is computed, from the encoding of a positive set $\mathcal{P}$ exhibiting the target behavior and a neutral set $\mathcal{N}$ of matched controls, as

$$\Delta_{i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_{i}(x)-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_{i}(x), \qquad (2)$$

and, under the L8W-based steering-direction discovery of Sec. 3.1, an L8W trained on residual-stream activations at layer $\ell$ maps an activation $\mathbf{h}$ to a sparse feature vector $f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}$, whose $i$-th coordinate $f_{i}(\mathbf{h})$ is the activation of learned feature $i$, the decoder $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}$ reconstructing $\mathbf{h}$ from these features.

# A Coin Flip Per Token: Bernoulli Sparse Steering of Large Language Models

Nima Eshraghi, Lovedeep Gondara, Yuqing Huang, Sagarika Suresh, Leizer Teran, Jithin Pradeep (The Vanguard Group, Inc.); Xiaotong (Tone) Xu, Fanny Chevalier (University of Toronto). Emails as listed.

Abstract: SAE activation steering controls LLMs without task-specific fine-tuning, but standard dense steering perturbs every generated token and can degrade fluency. We introduce Stochastic Token Steering (STS), gating each token i.i.d. with probability $p$, and Stochastic Block Steering (SBS), one Bernoulli($p$) gate for a leading window; neither uses a reward model or learned gate. Across two model families and suppression/elicitation tasks, steering a fraction of tokens recovers most dense-steering behavioral effect with less fluency loss; the best-performing magnitude rises as intervention ratio falls.

## 1 Introduction

LLM behavioral control—toxicity reduction, persona, refusal—is deployment-critical. System prompts are fragile: distributions shift under lexical perturbation, adversarial suffixes override alignment priors, and prompt steerability is asymmetric/bounded. Activation steering injects a direction into an intermediate residual stream; SAEs give sparse interpretable decoder directions to amplify/suppress behavior. Standard practice applies the direction every token, leaving open whether persistent intervention is needed given quality degradation at stronger/frequent intervention. Question: how much dense-steering effect remains when only a fraction of positions are steered? Contributions: dense every-token intervention is largely unnecessary across two families and suppression (toxicity) plus elicitation (emotion); STS recovers most full-steering effect while steering few tokens and degrading fluency less. Across settings, best-performing steering magnitude rises as intervention ratio falls, showing frequency–strength interaction. Inference-time control becomes one interpretable sparsity parameter $p$, no reward model/learned gate, only an activation-vector addition.

## 2 Related Work

Activation steering adds contrastive directions to intermediate representations; SAE methods use decoder directions of behavior-associated sparse features. Both generally fix intervention at every generation step; we steer only subsets. Closest concurrent SIA sparsifies logit-space intervention with a separately trained value model selecting positions, requires auxiliary-model queries during decoding, and reports best-of-$N$ plus reward-model scoring. We gate a fixed pretrained-SAE direction in an intermediate residual stream, need no learned selector, and generate one completion with a lightweight activation update when the gate fires. Different intervention space, training, inference and evaluation make results not directly comparable; SIA is related work (App. A).

## 3 Method

Let $\mathcal M$ be an $L$-layer decoder-only transformer; for $\mathbf x=(x_1,\dots,x_T)$, $\mathbf h_t^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^d$ is the residual activation at layer $\ell$, position $t$. Inject at one intermediate layer:
$$\tilde{\mathbf h}_t^{(\ell)}=\mathbf h_t^{(\ell)}+\mathbf s_t,\tag{1}$$
with $\mathbf s_t$ in Sec. 3.2. Single intermediate-layer intervention lets signal propagate through remaining layers before next-token generation.

### 3.1 Steering Direction Discovery via SAE

An SAE at layer $\ell$ maps $\mathbf h$ to sparse $f(\mathbf h)\in\mathbb R^{d_{\rm sae}}$; $f_i(\mathbf h)$ is feature $i$ activation; decoder $\mathbf W_{\rm dec}\in\mathbb R^{d_{\rm sae}\times d}$ reconstructs $\mathbf h$. Encode positive set $\mathcal P$ exhibiting target behavior and neutral matched controls $\mathcal N$; feature differential
$$\Delta_i=\frac1{|\mathcal P|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal P}f_i(x)-\frac1{|\mathcal N|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal N}f_i(x).\tag{2}$$
Select top-$K$ by $\Delta_i$; $\mathbf v_k=\mathbf W_{{\rm dec},i_k}$, $k=1..K$; aggregate unit-norm $\mathbf v=\sum_k\mathbf v_k/\|\sum_k\mathbf v_k\|$, weighting by behavior discrimination.

Figure 1: STS/SBS effectiveness vs intervention ratio $p$ as behavioral gain over no steering; dashed static baselines (prompting, full/no steering); bands SD.

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering

$\mathbf s_t=m_t\cdot\alpha\mathbf v$, $\alpha\in\mathbb R$ magnitude, $\mathbf v$ unit-norm, $m_t\in\{0,1\}$ gate. Full Steering (FS): $m_t=1\ \forall t$. We randomize gates to control steered fraction and trade behavioral strength vs fluency.

#### Stochastic Token Steering (STS).
$$\tilde{\mathbf h}_t^{(\ell)}=\mathbf h_t^{(\ell)}+m_t\cdot\alpha\mathbf v,\quad m_t\stackrel{iid}{\sim}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p).\tag{3}$$
Expected fraction $p$ steered; rest unperturbed. Position-agnostic; $p$ interpolates no intervention ($p{=}0$) to full steering ($p{=}1$).

#### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS).
Leading prompt window size $W\le T$ is atomic; one $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ per sequence:
$$\tilde{\mathbf h}_t^{(\ell)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf h_t^{(\ell)}+m\cdot\alpha\mathbf v&t\le W,\\ \mathbf h_t^{(\ell)}&t>W,\end{cases}\tag{4}$$
With probability $p$ whole window steered coherently; else intact. Exploits disproportionate early-token influence and early-token steering sufficiency.

## 4 Experiments

Setup: tasks with opposite goals: toxicity reduction (suppression; RealToxicityPrompts) and emotion steering (elicitation; GoEmotions mapped to Ekman basics; targets fear, sadness). Models: LLaMA-3.1-8B and Gemma-2 2B, distinct families/scales, matching recent feature-steering evaluations. Each steered with an SAE at an intermediate layer where SAE features encode high-level semantics; SBS $W\in\{32,64\}$. Because additive interventions can move representations off-manifold causing incoherence/repetition, every method pairs with norm preservation, activation clamping, decoding repetition penalty (App. C).

Baselines/metrics: No Steering; Full Steering ($p{=}1$); Prompting (curated safety/emotion instruction, App. B). Effectiveness: mean toxicity reduction (classifier toxicity decrease vs no steering) and mean target-emotion probability gain vs unsteered; RoBERTa toxicity and DistilRoBERTa emotion classifiers (App. C). Quality: GPT-2 perplexity; Rep-$n$ = fraction of $n$-grams recurring.

### 4.1 Sparse Steering Effectiveness

Fig. 1 spans toxicity reduction and fear/sadness steering. $\alpha$ calibrated once under FS ($p{=}1$), fixed across methods/ratios (App. D.1). Most behavioral shift is recoverable at lower cost: LLaMA-3.1-8B STS at $p{=}0.5$ recovers >95% full-steering toxicity reduction and >75% of full-steering gains on both emotions by $p{=}0.7$; most dense per-token interventions are redundant. STS overtakes prompting in five of six model–task settings: toxicity (both models) and LLaMA fear by $p\approx0.5$ or below (≥half tokens unperturbed); LLaMA sadness crossover at $p\approx0.7$; exception Gemma-2 2B sadness, prompting stays ahead across tested ratios. STS exceeds SBS at matched nominal $p$, clearest on emotions: LLaMA fear STS $p{=}0.5$ roughly doubles SBS ($W{=}32$) probability gain; ordering holds for Gemma-2 2B.

### 4.2 Fluency Under Sparse and Dense Steering

Fig. 2: Gemma-2-2B toxicity perplexity and Rep-3/Rep-4 vs ratio, FS reference. Perplexity and repetition rise monotonically as more positions are steered; FS is high end. Sparse operating points generally sit below FS cost; required ratio is task-dependent (smaller for toxicity than emotion, Sec. 4.1); trend holds across SBS $W$, not method-specific.

Figure 2: quality vs ratio: perplexity and Rep-3/Rep-4 rise with steering density; bands SD.

### 4.3 Steering Magnitude and Intervention Ratio

Fig. 3 plots best-performing $\alpha^*$ (max behavioral shift subject to fluency preservation) vs ratio for both models. $\alpha^*$ tends to rise as ratio falls. At fixed magnitude, behavioral effect increases with intervention ratio; ratio needed for target effect decreases as per-token strength grows. App. D.3: normalized residual displacement grows with $\alpha$ and $p$.

Figure 3: $\alpha^*$ vs intervention ratio (GoEmotions-fear); at each $p$, $\alpha^*$ maximizes target-emotion gain subject to fluency preservation.

## 5 Conclusion

STS/SBS are training-free sparse replacements for dense every-token steering via one parameter $p$. Across two families and suppression/elicitation, steering a token fraction recovers most full-steering shift with better fluency-control tradeoff; best magnitude rises as $p$ falls. Effective inference-time control need not act every token.

## Limitations

Evaluation covers two tasks (toxicity reduction, emotion steering) and two families; though spanning suppression/elicitation, generalization to hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, multi-attribute control is unvalidated. Classifier evaluation may miss behavioral dimensions; human evaluation is out of scope. Method inherits SAE-steering limits: needs pretrained SAE with identifiable behavior-relevant features; quality depends on SAE dictionary and contrastive corpora. Experiments use one decoding configuration; interactions with higher temperature, nucleus sampling, beam search, and gate-level vs sampling-level randomness are unexplored.

Intended use/dual-use: training-free inference-time control aimed at reducing harmful generation (toxicity) and shifting toward beneficial targets (emotional regulation). Same mechanism could be inverted to amplify harm (toxicity features steered oppositely); concern shared by activation steering, not specific here. Methods require white-box activations and trained SAE; no new black-box attacks. Net effect viewed positive where retraining infeasible.

Sensitive data: RealToxicityPrompts prompts/continuations used under permitted research terms; no fresh toxic content beyond benchmark-elicited, no new toxic data collected/released. Toxicity uses s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier; automated toxicity classifiers have known identity-term biases that may inflate/deflate subset scores. Scores are standardized metrics, not ground truth harm.

Qualitative examples: App. B.2 has verbatim toxic/offensive/distressing outputs for honest characterization incl. failure modes, with warnings in appendix/front. Identity-targeted slur examples excluded even if benchmark-elicited; harm outweighs marginal value.

## Appendix A Related Work

Inference-time steering spans prompt control, activation interventions, decoding methods. Dense activation steering—ActAdd, ITI, CAA, Representation Engineering, SAE feature steering—shares universal every-token intervention; we depart.

Prompt-Based Behavioral Control: prepended natural-language instructions for toxicity/helpfulness are simple and architecture-agnostic but fragile to lexical perturbation and adversarial suffixes overriding safety instructions.

Dense Activation Steering: residual-stream corrections at every token. ActAdd: steering vector = difference of mean activations on contrastive prompt pairs, added every forward pass. ITI: shifts attention-head activations linearly predictive of truthfulness. CAA: averages contrastive prompts and applies layer-specific vectors. Representation Engineering learns linear directions for high-level concepts (honesty, harmlessness). DiffMean uses difference of class-conditional means with reduced side effects vs naive contrastive. Style Vectors extract/apply style directions each decoding step. In-Context Vectors extract latent directions from demonstrations and apply during generation. Common assumption: once direction found, apply at every position.

Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Steering: SAEs decompose dense polysemantic activations into more monosemantic dictionaries. Residual-stream SAEs recover interpretable human-aligned features. GemmaScope provides open Gemma SAE checkpoints across layers/widths. Amplifying concept-associated SAE features (e.g., Eiffel Tower) steers LLaMA outputs. AxBench standardizes activation-steering comparisons incl. SAE effectiveness/side effects. We build on SAE steering but not every-token application.

Detoxification: all existing methods correct every decoding step. DExperts reweights token probabilities each position using expert non-toxic and anti-expert toxic LMs. PPLM backpropagates through toxicity classifier to update hidden states during generation. Self-Debiasing prompts model to generate toxic text then suppresses resulting token probabilities. GeDi uses class-conditional LMs as generative discriminators. RealToxicityPrompts shows all incur fluency cost. We use SAE directions and show random-subset correction suffices.

Selective and Sparse Steering: concurrent SIA identifies “critical junctions” via model entropy and steers only there. It is reward-guided decoding: trains token-level value model $V^*$ by distilling trajectory-level rewards, reweights token distribution by $\exp(\beta V^*)$ at selected positions, evaluated by reward-model scoring against best-of-$N$ and chunk-search. Reports steering 20–80% tokens gives superior alignment–efficiency trade-offs over dense intervention. SIA differs in intervention space, training, inference: separate value model from trajectory rewards, learned guidance queries during decoding, reward-model evaluation with best-of-$N$; needs auxiliary storage and repeated candidates. We gate fixed SAE direction in intermediate residual stream, single completion, no auxiliary guidance model; protocols not commensurable, treated as related work not baseline. Safety alignment concentrated early; weak-to-strong steering focuses initial tokens. SIA finds position gating competitive for safety at low ratios but degrades on helpfulness; mirrors SBS underperforming position-agnostic STS at matched nominal ratios. Under equalized realized budgets persistence is task-dependent (App. D.2). Random selection is a training-free position-agnostic control for selective methods.

Fluency–Alignment Trade-offs: large steering magnitudes produce disfluent text; behavioral shift vs coherence loss is systematic; standardized measurements exist across methods. We add: sparse application improves trade-off—fewer interventions keep residual stream nearer native distribution, yielding better fluency at matched behavioral shift.

### C.1 Fluency-Preserving Regularization Details

Additive steering injects fixed $\mathbf v$ into layer-$\ell$ hidden state; simple/controllable but no guarantee of staying on fluent decoding manifold. As strength grows or intervention accumulates, steered state drifts in norm/direction from natural activations, causing degraded fluency, inflated perplexity, repetition. Guards keep steered activation near natural regime while preserving behavior.

Norm Preservation:
$$\tilde{\mathbf h}_t^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf h}_t^{(\ell)}\cdot\frac{\|\mathbf h_t^{(\ell)}\|}{\|\tilde{\mathbf h}_t^{(\ell)}\|}\tag{5}$$
Rotates toward $\mathbf v$ without inflating magnitude, preserving scale invariants downstream.

Activation Clamping:
$$s_t=\tilde{\mathbf h}_t^{(\ell)}\cdot\mathbf v,\quad \hat s_t=\mathrm{clamp}(s_t,\gamma_{\min},\gamma_{\max})\tag{6}$$
$$\tilde{\mathbf h}_t^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf h}_t^{(\ell)}+(\hat s_t-s_t)\mathbf v\tag{7}$$
Upper bound prevents over-amplification beyond feature range; lower $\gamma_{\min}\ge0$ suppresses residual feature activation already present.

Repetition Penalty: steering suppresses high-probability continuations and can induce repetitive fallback; standard decoding-time repetition penalty discounts previously generated tokens without further hidden-state modification.

Effect of Fluency Preservation: ablation toggling preservation with all else fixed on Gemma-2-2B toxicity subset (Fig. 4). Preservation reduces perplexity roughly $82\to30$ and cuts Rep-3/Rep-4 by ~factor three, non-overlapping error bars in all three. Behavioral steering applied identically, so gains reflect on-manifold generation not weakened steering. Enabled by default in all reported experiments.

# A Coin Flip Per Token: Bernoulli Sparse Steering of Large Language Models

Nima Eshraghi, Lovedeep Gondara, Yuqing Huang, Sagarika Suresh, Leizer Teran, Jithin Pradeep (The Vanguard Group, Inc.); Xiaotong (Tone) Xu, Fanny Chevalier (University of Toronto)

###### Abstract

Activation steering via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) applies the steering signal at every generated token, risking fluency loss. We introduce Stochastic Token Steering (STS), gating each token independently with probability $p$, and Stochastic Block Steering (SBS), gating a leading window once per sequence; neither needs a reward model or learned gating policy. Across two model families and two tasks, steering a fraction of tokens recovers most of dense steering's behavioral effect with less fluency degradation; the best-performing steering magnitude consistently rises as the intervention ratio falls.

## 1 Introduction

Activation steering injects a steering direction into an intermediate residual stream during generation. SAEs provide an interpretable basis: activations decompose into sparse features whose decoder directions can be amplified to promote or suppress a target behavior. Standard implementations apply the direction at every generated token, though stronger or more frequent intervention can degrade generation quality. We ask: how much of the behavioral effect of dense steering remains when only a fraction of token positions are steered? We replace deterministic every-token intervention with stochastic gating.

STS samples an independent gate $m_t\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ at every position; SBS draws one $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ gate per sequence applied to a leading window, exploiting early-token influence.

Contributions: (1) dense every-token intervention is largely unnecessary: across two model families and both suppression (toxicity reduction) and elicitation (emotion steering), STS recovers most of the full-steering effect steering only a fraction of tokens, with less fluency degradation; (2) across our settings, the best-performing steering magnitude rises as the intervention ratio falls—a consistent frequency–strength interaction. The method reduces inference-time control to a single interpretable sparsity parameter $p$, needs no reward model or learned gating policy, and adds only an activation vector addition at inference.

## 2 Related Work

Activation steering adds contrastive-activation directions to intermediate representations; SAE-based methods intervene through decoder directions of behavior-associated sparse features. Both generally apply a fixed intervention at every generation step; we apply it to a subset of positions.

Closest concurrent work, SIA, sparsifies logit-space intervention using a separately trained value model to select positions, requiring auxiliary-model queries during decoding, best-of-$N$ generation and reward-model scoring. We gate a fixed pretrained-SAE direction at an intermediate residual stream, require no learned selector, and generate one completion with only a lightweight activation update when the gate fires. Given differences in intervention space, training, inference, and evaluation, results are not directly comparable (Appendix A).

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}+\mathbf{s}_t,$ | (1)

with $\mathbf{s}_t\in\mathbb{R}^d$ defined in Sec. 3.2. Intermediate-layer editing lets the signal propagate through remaining layers into a coherent representation.

An SAE trained on layer-$\ell$ residual activations maps $\mathbf{h}$ to a sparse feature vector $f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}$; decoder $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}$ reconstructs $\mathbf{h}$. To isolate behavior-discriminative features, encode a positive set $\mathcal{P}$ and neutral set $\mathcal{N}$ and compute each feature's mean activation differential:

| | $\Delta_i=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_i(x)-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_i(x).$ | (2)

Select top-$K$ features by $\Delta_i$, form $\mathbf{v}_k=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_k}$, $k=1,\ldots,K$, and aggregate into unit-norm $\mathbf{v}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_k/\bigl\|\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbf{v}_k\bigr\|$.

#### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS).

A leading window of size $W\le T$ is one atomic unit; a single gate $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ per sequence:

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}+m\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}&t\le W,\\[2.0pt]\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}&t>W,\end{cases}$ | (4)

With probability $p$ the whole window is steered coherently, else left intact, exploiting the disproportionate contextual influence of initial tokens.

## 4 Experiments

#### Setup.

Two tasks with opposite goals: toxicity reduction (suppression; RealToxicityPrompts) and emotion steering (elicitation; GoEmotions, fine-grained labels mapped to Ekman basic emotions, targets fear and sadness). Models: LLaMA-3.1-8B and Gemma-2 2B. Each is steered with an SAE at an intermediate layer (where SAE features encode high-level semantics); SBS at $W\in\{32,64\}$. Every steering method is paired with three lightweight corrections: norm preservation, activation clamping, and a decoding-time repetition penalty (App. C).

#### Baselines and Metrics.

Baselines: (1) No Steering, (2) Full Steering ($p{=}1$), (3) Prompting (curated task-specific instruction, App. B). Effectiveness: mean toxicity reduction (classifier-predicted toxicity decrease vs. no steering; RoBERTa toxicity classifier) and mean probability gain (target-emotion probability increase; DistilRoBERTa emotion classifier). Quality: GPT-2 perplexity and Rep-$n$ (fraction of $n$-grams in a generation that recur).

### 4.1 Sparse Steering Effectiveness

Figure 1: effectiveness across ratios on toxicity reduction and fear/sadness steering; $\alpha$ is calibrated once at $p{=}1$ and held fixed (App. D.1). Most behavioral shift is recoverable at reduced cost: LLaMA-3.1-8B STS at $p{=}0.5$ recovers over 95% of full-steering toxicity reduction, and over 75% of full-steering gains on both emotion tasks by $p{=}0.7$—most per-token interventions under dense steering are redundant. STS yields a larger behavioral shift than SBS at matched nominal $p$, clearest on emotion steering: fear on LLaMA at $p{=}0.5$, STS roughly doubles the probability gain of SBS ($W{=}32$); the ordering holds for Gemma-2 2B.

## 5 Conclusion

STS and SBS are training-free interventions replacing dense every-token steering with sparse random application via a single parameter $p$: across two model families and suppression/elicitation tasks, steering a fraction of tokens recovers most of the full-steering shift with a better fluency–control tradeoff; best-performing magnitude rises as $p$ falls.

## Limitations

Evaluation covers two tasks (toxicity reduction, emotion steering) on two model families; generalization to other targets (hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, multi-attribute control) is unvalidated. Classifier-based evaluation may miss dimensions of behavioral change; human evaluation is out of scope. The method inherits SAE-steering limitations: it needs a pretrained SAE with identifiable behavior-relevant features, and quality depends on SAE dictionary quality and contrastive-corpus choice. A single decoding configuration is used; interaction with other settings (higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, beam search) and between gate-level and sampling-level randomness is unexplored.

#### Intended use and dual-use considerations.

Motivation is reducing harmful generation (toxicity) and shifting behavior toward beneficial targets (emotional regulation), but the same mechanism could be inverted—toxicity-reduction features steered oppositely to elicit toxicity. This dual-use concern is shared by all activation-steering methods. The methods require white-box access to activations and a trained SAE; they enable no new attacks on black-box systems. We believe advancing interpretable, training-free control is net positive, especially where retraining is infeasible.

#### Use of sensitive data.

Toxicity experiments use RealToxicityPrompts, released for toxic-language research; we generate no fresh toxic content beyond what prompts elicit and release none. Toxicity uses s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier; automated classifiers carry known biases against identity-related terms, which may inflate or deflate scores for affected subsets. Classifier scores are a standardized comparison metric, not ground truth on harmfulness.

#### Qualitative examples.

Appendix B.2 reproduces verbatim outputs containing toxic, offensive, and emotionally distressing content (with content warnings), to characterize the method including failure modes. Examples with identity-targeted slurs were excluded even where prompts would have elicited them.

## Appendix A Related Work

Inference-time steering spans prompt-based control, activation-level interventions, and decoding-time methods. Dense steering methods—ActAdd, ITI, CAA, Representation Engineering, SAE-based feature steering—all intervene at every generated token; our method departs from this.

#### Prompt-Based Behavioral Control.

Prompt engineering prepends natural-language instructions to elicit properties like reduced toxicity or helpfulness. Simple and architecture-agnostic but fragile: output distributions shift substantially under minor lexical perturbations, and adversarial suffixes reliably override safety instructions.

#### Dense Activation Steering.

ActAdd computes a steering vector as the difference of mean activations on contrastive prompt pairs, added to the residual stream every forward pass. ITI identifies attention heads linearly predictive of truthfulness and shifts activations along those directions. CAA averages over large prompt sets with layer-specific vectors. Representation Engineering learns linear directions for high-level concepts such as honesty or harmlessness. DiffMean uses the difference of class-conditional means, reducing side effects vs. naive contrastive approaches. Style Vectors control stylistic attributes; In-Context Vectors extract latent directions from in-context demonstrations to make ICL more controllable. All apply the direction at every generated position.

#### Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Steering.

SAEs decompose dense polysemantic activations into more monosemantic features; SAEs trained on residual-stream activations recover interpretable, human-understandable concepts. GemmaScope provides open SAE checkpoints for Gemma across all layers at multiple widths. Amplifying SAE features tied to specific concepts (e.g., the Eiffel Tower) reliably steers LLaMA outputs toward them. AxBench benchmarks activation-steering methods, including SAE-based ones, on effectiveness and side effects. We build on SAE steering but depart from every-token application.

#### Detoxification.

All existing detoxification methods correct at every decoding step: DExperts combines expert (non-toxic) and anti-expert (toxic) LMs to re-weight token probabilities; PPLM backpropagates through a toxicity classifier to update hidden states; Self-Debiasing prompts the model to generate toxic text and suppresses resulting probabilities; GeDi uses class-conditional LMs as generative discriminators. RealToxicityPrompts evaluation shows all incur some fluency cost. We use SAE-derived directions and show correction at a random subset of tokens suffices.

#### Selective and Sparse Steering.

Concurrent SIA identifies "critical junctions" via model entropy and steers only there: a reward-guided decoding method training a token-level value model $V^{*}$ by distilling trajectory-level rewards, reweighting the token distribution by $\exp(\beta V^{*})$ at selected positions, evaluated by reward-model scoring against best-of-$N$ and chunk-search baselines; steering 20–80% of tokens achieves superior alignment–efficiency trade-offs over dense intervention. SIA differs in intervention space, training, and inference: it trains a value model from trajectory rewards, queries learned guidance during decoding, and reports reward-model evaluation with best-of-$N$ selection, requiring auxiliary storage and repeated candidate generation. We gate a fixed SAE direction in an intermediate residual stream and produce a single completion without auxiliary guidance; different evaluation protocols make results not directly commensurable.

Safety alignment is concentrated in early token positions; steering initial tokens also underlies weak-to-strong decoding. SIA finds position-based gating competitive for safety alignment at low ratios but degrading on helpfulness tasks—mirroring our finding that position-anchored SBS underperforms position-agnostic STS at matched nominal ratios. Whether this persists at equalized realized budgets is task-dependent (App. D.2). Our random-selection result is a training-free, position-agnostic control against which any selective method should be evaluated.

#### Fluency–Alignment Trade-offs.

Large steering magnitudes produce disfluent text; the behavioral-shift/coherence-loss trade-off is documented across methods. We add that sparse application improves this trade-off: intervening at fewer positions keeps the residual stream closer to its native distribution, giving better fluency at matched behavioral shift.

### C.1 Fluency-Preserving Regularization Details

Additive steering can push the residual stream off the model's native manifold as magnitude grows or intervention accumulates, manifesting as degraded fluency, inflated perplexity, and repetition. Three guards counter this:

#### Norm Preservation.

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}\cdot\frac{\|\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}\|}{\|\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}\|}$ | (5)

Rotates the representation toward $\mathbf{v}$ without inflating magnitude.

#### Activation Clamping.

Clamp the projection onto $\mathbf{v}$ to $[\gamma_{\min},\gamma_{\max}]$ with residual correction:

| | $s_t=\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}\cdot\mathbf{v},\quad\hat{s}_t=\mathrm{clamp}(s_t,\gamma_{\min},\gamma_{\max})$ | (6)

| | $\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}+(\hat{s}_t-s_t)\,\mathbf{v}$ | (7)

The upper bound prevents over-amplification; $\gamma_{\min}\geq0$ suppresses residual feature activation already present.

#### Repetition Penalty.

Steering suppresses high-probability continuations, inviting repetitive sequences; a standard decoding-stage repetition penalty discounts previously generated tokens without modifying hidden states.

#### Effect of Fluency Preservation.

Ablation on Gemma-2-2B toxicity reduction, all else fixed: enabling preservation cuts perplexity from roughly 82 to 30 and reduces repetition roughly threefold on Rep-3 and Rep-4, with non-overlapping error bars in all three comparisons. The behavioral intervention is identical in both conditions—gains reflect staying on-manifold, not weaker steering. Fluency preservation is on by default in all reported experiments.

# A Coin Flip Per Token: Bernoulli Sparse Steering of Large Language Models

###### Abstract

Activation steering via SAEs controls LLM behavior without fine-tuning, but standard methods steer every token, risking fluency loss. We introduce Stochastic Token Steering (STS), gating each token independently with probability $p$, and Stochastic Block Steering (SBS), gating a leading window once per sequence; neither needs a reward model or learned gate. Across two model families and two tasks, steering a fraction of tokens recovers most of dense steering's behavioral effect with less fluency degradation, and the best-performing steering magnitude consistently rises as the intervention ratio falls.

## 1 Introduction

Activation steering injects a direction into an intermediate residual stream during generation; SAEs provide an interpretable basis, decomposing activations into sparse features whose decoder directions are amplified to promote or suppress a behavior. Standard implementations apply the direction at every token; stronger or more frequent intervention can degrade generation quality. We ask: how much of dense steering's behavioral effect remains when only a fraction of positions are steered?

STS samples an independent gate $m_t\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ per position; SBS draws one $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ gate per sequence applied to a leading window, treating early-token influence as an atomic site.

Contributions: (1) dense intervention is largely unnecessary—across two model families and two tasks spanning suppression (toxicity reduction) and elicitation (emotion steering), STS recovers most of full steering's effect while steering a fraction of tokens and degrading fluency less; (2) the best-performing steering magnitude rises as the intervention ratio falls, a consistent frequency–strength interaction. The method reduces control to one interpretable sparsity parameter $p$, needs no reward model or learned gate, and adds only a vector addition at inference.

## 2 Related Work

Activation steering adds contrastive-derived directions to intermediate representations; SAE methods steer via decoder directions of behavior-associated features. These apply a fixed intervention at every generation step; we steer only a subset of positions.

Closest concurrent work, SIA, sparsifies logit-space intervention using a separately trained value model to select positions, requiring auxiliary-model queries during decoding plus best-of-$N$ generation and reward-model scoring. Our method gates a fixed pretrained-SAE direction at an intermediate residual stream, needs no learned selector, and generates one completion with a lightweight activation update. Given differing intervention space, training, inference, and evaluation, results are not directly comparable (Appendix A).

## 3 Method

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be an $L$-layer decoder-only transformer. For input $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_T)$, let $\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ be the residual activation at layer $\ell$, position $t$. We inject a steering signal at a single intermediate layer $\ell$:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}+\mathbf{s}_t,\tag{1}$$

with $\mathbf{s}_t\in\mathbb{R}^d$ defined in Sec. 3.2. Editing an intermediate layer lets the signal propagate through remaining layers into a coherent representation.

### 3.1 Steering Direction Discovery via SAE

An SAE trained on layer-$\ell$ residual activations maps $\mathbf{h}$ to sparse features $f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}$; decoder $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}$ reconstructs $\mathbf{h}$. Encode a positive set $\mathcal{P}$ exhibiting the behavior and neutral controls $\mathcal{N}$, and compute each feature's mean activation differential:

$$\Delta_i=\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\textstyle\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_i(x)-\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\textstyle\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_i(x).\tag{2}$$

Select top-$K$ features by $\Delta_i$, form $\mathbf{v}_k=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_k}$, and aggregate into a unit-norm direction $\mathbf{v}=\sum_{k=1}^K\mathbf{v}_k/\lVert\sum_{k=1}^K\mathbf{v}_k\rVert$.

Figure 1: Steering effectiveness of STS and SBS versus intervention ratio $p$, as behavioral gain over no steering. Dashed lines: static baselines (prompting, full/no steering); bands: standard deviation.

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering

The signal at $t$ is $\mathbf{s}_t=m_t\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}$, with magnitude $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$, unit-norm $\mathbf{v}$, and binary gate $m_t\in\{0,1\}$. Full Steering (FS) sets $m_t=1$ everywhere; we randomize the gate, trading behavioral strength against fluency.

#### Stochastic Token Steering (STS).

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}+m_t\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v},\quad m_t\stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p).\tag{3}$$

In expectation a fraction $p$ of positions are steered; position-agnostic, $p$ interpolates from no intervention ($p{=}0$) to full steering ($p{=}1$).

#### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS).

A leading window of size $W\le T$ is steered atomically via one per-sequence gate $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}+m\cdot\alpha\,\mathbf{v}&t\le W,\\\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}&t>W.\end{cases}\tag{4}$$

With probability $p$ the window is steered coherently, else intact; exploits the disproportionate contextual influence of initial tokens.

## 5 Conclusion

STS and SBS are training-free interventions replacing dense every-token steering with sparse random application governed by one parameter $p$. Across two model families and both suppression and elicitation, steering a fraction of tokens recovers most of the full-steering shift with a better fluency trade-off; best-performing magnitude rises as $p$ falls. Effective inference-time control need not act at every token.

## Limitations

Evaluation covers two tasks on two model families; generalization to other targets (hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, multi-attribute control) is unvalidated. Classifier-based evaluation may miss dimensions of behavioral change; human evaluation is out of scope. The method inherits SAE-steering limitations: it needs a pretrained SAE with identifiable behavior-relevant features, and quality depends on SAE dictionary quality and contrastive corpora. Experiments use one decoding configuration; interactions with other settings (higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, beam search) and between gate-level and sampling-level randomness are unexplored.

#### Intended use and dual-use considerations.

The training-free method targets reducing harmful generation (toxicity) and shifting behavior toward beneficial targets, but could in principle be inverted to amplify harmful behaviors—features found for toxicity reduction could be steered oppositely. This dual-use concern is shared by all activation-steering methods. The methods require white-box access to activations and a trained SAE; they enable no new attacks on deployed black-box systems. We judge the net effect positive, especially where retraining is infeasible.

#### Use of sensitive data.

Toxicity experiments use RealToxicityPrompts, built and licensed for toxic-language research; we generate no fresh toxic content beyond what benchmark prompts elicit and release no new toxic data. Toxicity scoring uses s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier; automated toxicity classifiers carry known biases against text with identity-related terms, which may inflate or deflate scores for affected subsets. With differing evaluation protocols, results are not commensurable; SIA is related work, not a baseline.

Safety alignment has been argued to concentrate in early token positions, and weak-to-strong decoding similarly steers initial tokens. SIA finds position-based gating competitive for safety at low ratios but degrading on helpfulness—mirroring our finding that position-anchored SBS underperforms position-agnostic STS at matched nominal ratios; whether this persists at equalized realized budgets is task-dependent (Appendix D.2). Our random-selection result is a training-free, position-agnostic control against which any selective method should be evaluated.

#### Fluency–Alignment Trade-offs.

Large steering magnitudes produce disfluent text; the behavioral-shift/coherence trade-off has been systematically studied and standardized. Sparse application improves the trade-off: intervening at fewer positions keeps the residual stream closer to its native distribution, giving better fluency at matched behavioral shift.

### C.1 Fluency-Preserving Regularization Details

Additive steering carries no guarantee that the steered state stays on the fluently decodable manifold; as strength grows or intervention accumulates, drift in norm or direction manifests as degraded fluency, inflated perplexity, repetition. We add lightweight guards.

#### Norm Preservation.

Rescale the steered activation to the original norm:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}\cdot\frac{\|\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}\|}{\|\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}\|}\tag{5}$$

constraining intervention to rotate toward $\mathbf{v}$ without inflating magnitude.

#### Activation Clamping.

Clamp the projection onto $\mathbf{v}$ to $[\gamma_{\min},\gamma_{\max}]$ with residual correction:

$$s_t=\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}\cdot\mathbf{v},\quad\hat{s}_t=\mathrm{clamp}(s_t,\gamma_{\min},\gamma_{\max})\tag{6}$$

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}+(\hat{s}_t-s_t)\,\mathbf{v}\tag{7}$$

The upper bound prevents over-amplification; $\gamma_{\min}\geq0$ suppresses residual feature activation already present.

#### Repetition Penalty.

Steering suppresses high-probability continuations, risking repetitive fallback; a standard decoding-time repetition penalty discounts previously generated tokens without modifying hidden states.

#### Effect of Fluency Preservation.

Ablating preservation (all else fixed) on Gemma-2-2B toxicity reduction: enabling it cuts perplexity from roughly $82$ to $30$ and repetition roughly threefold on Rep-3 and Rep-4, with non-overlapping error bars. The steering effect is identical in both conditions, so gains reflect staying on-manifold, not weaker steering. Preservation is on by default in all experiments.

# A Coin Flip Per Token: Bernoulli Sparse Steering of Large Language Models

###### Abstract
SAE-based activation steering usually perturbs every generated token, which risks fluency loss. Is dense intervention necessary? We introduce two gates:
- **Stochastic Token Steering (STS):** each token is gated independently with probability $p$.
- **Stochastic Block Steering (SBS):** a leading window is gated once per sequence.

Neither needs a reward model or a learned gating policy. Across two model families and two behavioral tasks, steering a fraction of tokens recovers most of dense steering's effect with less fluency degradation. The best-performing steering magnitude rises as the intervention ratio falls.

## 1 Introduction
Prompt-based behavioral control (toxicity, persona, refusal) is fragile. Outputs shift under minor lexical perturbation, adversarial suffixes override alignment, and steerability is asymmetric and bounded. Activation steering instead injects a direction into an intermediate residual stream. SAEs give an interpretable basis: decoder directions of sparse features can be amplified to promote or suppress a behavior. Standard implementations steer every token, though stronger or more frequent intervention degrades generation quality. We ask how much of the dense effect remains when only a fraction of positions are steered.

STS samples $m_t\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ per position. SBS draws one $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ gate per sequence for a leading window, treating early-token influence as an atomic intervention site.

Contributions:
1. Across two model families, a suppression task (toxicity) and an elicitation task (emotion), STS recovers most of the full-steering effect while steering a fraction of tokens, with less fluency degradation.
2. The best-performing magnitude rises as the ratio falls.

Control reduces to one interpretable parameter $p$, with only an activation vector addition at inference.

## 2 Related Work
Activation steering adds contrastive directions to intermediate representations. SAE methods intervene through decoder directions of behavior-associated features. Both intervene at every step.

Concurrent SIA sparsifies logit-space intervention using a separately trained value model queried during decoding, plus best-of-$N$ generation and reward-model scoring. We gate a fixed pretrained-SAE direction in the residual stream, with no learned selector and a single completion. Results are not directly comparable, so SIA is treated as related work (App. A).

## 3 Method
$\mathcal{M}$ is an $L$-layer decoder-only transformer, and $\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ is the residual activation at layer $\ell$, position $t$ of $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_T)$. We intervene at a single intermediate layer, so the signal propagates through the remaining layers:
$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}+\mathbf{s}_t\quad(1)$$

### 3.1 Steering Direction Discovery via SAE
The SAE at layer $\ell$ has encoder $f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}$ and decoder $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}$. Given a positive set $\mathcal{P}$ and a matched neutral set $\mathcal{N}$:
$$\Delta_i=\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\textstyle\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_i(x)-\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_i(x)\quad(2)$$
The top-$K$ features by $\Delta_i$ give $\mathbf{v}_k=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_k}$, combined as $\mathbf{v}=\sum_k\mathbf{v}_k/\lVert\sum_k\mathbf{v}_k\rVert$.

Figure 1: STS/SBS behavioral gain over no steering vs. $p$. Dashed lines: prompting, full and no steering. Bands: std.

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering
The signal is $\mathbf{s}_t=m_t\,\alpha\mathbf{v}$, with magnitude $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ and gate $m_t\in\{0,1\}$. Full Steering (FS) sets $m_t=1$ for all $t$.

#### Stochastic Token Steering (STS).
$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}+m_t\alpha\mathbf{v},\ m_t\overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)\quad(3)$$
STS is position-agnostic. $p$ interpolates between no intervention ($p{=}0$) and FS ($p{=}1$).

#### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS).
One gate $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ is drawn per sequence over a leading window $W\le T$:
$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}+m\alpha\mathbf{v}&t\le W\\ \mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}&t>W\end{cases}\quad(4)$$
This exploits the outsized influence of initial tokens.

## 4 Experiments
#### Setup.
- **Tasks:** toxicity reduction (suppression, RealToxicityPrompts) and emotion steering (elicitation, GoEmotions mapped to Ekman basic emotions; targets fear and sadness).
- **Models:** LLaMA-3.1-8B and Gemma-2 2B, each with an SAE at an intermediate layer.
- **SBS windows:** $W\in\{32,64\}$.
- **Corrections (all methods):** norm preservation, activation clamping, decoding repetition penalty (App. C).

#### Baselines and Metrics.
- **Baselines:** No Steering; FS ($p{=}1$); Prompting with a curated instruction (App. B).
- **Effectiveness:** mean toxicity reduction (RoBERTa classifier) and mean target-emotion probability gain (DistilRoBERTa), both relative to no steering.
- **Quality:** GPT-2 perplexity; Rep-$n$, the fraction of recurring $n$-grams.

### 4.1 Sparse Steering Effectiveness
$\alpha$ is calibrated once at $p{=}1$ and held fixed across methods and ratios (App. D.1).

On LLaMA 3.1-8B, STS at $p{=}0.5$ recovers >95% of full-steering toxicity reduction, and by $p{=}0.7$ it recovers >75% of full-steering gains on both emotion tasks. Most dense per-token interventions are therefore redundant.

STS beats prompting in 5 of 6 model–task settings:
- by $p\approx0.5$ or below on toxicity (both models) and LLaMA fear;
- at $p\approx0.7$ on LLaMA sadness;
- not at any tested ratio on Gemma-2 2B sadness.

STS yields a larger shift than SBS at matched nominal $p$, clearest on emotion. On LLaMA fear, STS at $p{=}0.5$ roughly doubles the gain of SBS ($W{=}32$). The same ordering holds on Gemma-2 2B.

### 4.2 Fluency Under Sparse and Dense Steering
On Gemma-2 2B toxicity, perplexity, Rep-3 and Rep-4 rise monotonically with steering density, with FS at the high end. Sparse operating points therefore generally cost less fluency. The ratio required is task dependent (smaller for toxicity than emotion). The trend holds across SBS window sizes.

Figure 2: Perplexity and Rep-3/Rep-4 vs. ratio. Bands: std.

### 4.3 Steering Magnitude and Intervention Ratio
The best-performing $\alpha^*$ (maximal behavioral shift subject to fluency preservation) rises as $p$ falls, for both models. At fixed $\alpha$, the effect grows with $p$; the ratio needed for a target effect falls as $\alpha$ grows. Residual displacement corroborates this (App. D.3).

Figure 3: $\alpha^*$ vs. ratio (GoEmotions-fear); at each $p$, $\alpha^*$ maximizes probability gain subject to fluency preservation.

## 5 Conclusion
Training-free STS and SBS replace dense steering with sparse random application governed by $p$. A fraction of tokens recovers most of the effect with a better fluency–control tradeoff. Control need not act at every token.

## Limitations
- **Scope:** two tasks, two model families. Other targets (hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, multi-attribute control) remain unvalidated.
- **Evaluation:** classifier-based, so it may miss dimensions of behavioral change; no human evaluation.
- **SAE dependence:** requires a pretrained SAE with identifiable behavior-relevant features; quality depends on the dictionary and the contrastive corpora.
- **Decoding:** a single configuration. Interactions with higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, beam search, and between gate-level and sampling-level randomness are unexplored.

#### Intended use and dual-use considerations.
The method targets harm reduction and beneficial behavior shifts. Features could be steered inversely, e.g. to elicit toxicity, a concern shared by all activation steering. It needs white-box access and an SAE, so it enables no new attacks on black-box systems. We judge the net effect positive, especially where retraining is infeasible.

#### Use of sensitive data.
RealToxicityPrompts permits this research use. We collect and release no new toxic data beyond what the prompts elicit. s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier has known biases against identity terms; scores are comparison metrics, not ground truth.

#### Qualitative examples.
App. B.2 gives verbatim toxic or distressing outputs, including failure modes, with content warnings. Identity-targeted slurs are excluded.

## Appendix A Related Work
#### Prompt-Based Behavioral Control.
Prepended instructions are simple and architecture-agnostic but fragile. Outputs shift under minor lexical perturbation, and adversarial suffixes reliably override safety instructions.

#### Dense Activation Steering.
All of these apply the identified direction at every generated position:
- **ActAdd:** adds the mean activation difference of contrastive prompt pairs every forward pass.
- **ITI:** shifts activations of attention heads linearly predictive of truthfulness.
- **CAA:** averages over large prompt sets with layer-specific vectors.
- **Representation Engineering:** learns linear directions for concepts such as honesty.
- **DiffMean:** uses class-conditional mean differences, with fewer side effects.
- **Style Vectors:** control stylistic attributes.
- **In-Context Vectors:** extract directions from demonstrations.

#### Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Steering.
SAEs decompose polysemantic activations into more monosemantic, human-interpretable features. GemmaScope provides open SAEs for every Gemma layer at multiple widths. Amplifying concept features (e.g., the Eiffel Tower) reliably steers LLaMA. AxBench benchmarks steering effectiveness and side effects, including SAE methods.

#### Detoxification.
All prior methods correct at every decoding step:
- **DExperts:** reweights tokens with expert/anti-expert LMs.
- **PPLM:** backpropagates through a toxicity classifier.
- **Self-Debiasing:** suppresses self-generated toxic probabilities.
- **GeDi:** uses class-conditional LMs as discriminators.

On RealToxicityPrompts all incur fluency cost. We use SAE directions and show a random token subset suffices.

#### Selective and Sparse Steering.
SIA (concurrent) is reward-guided decoding:
- finds "critical junctions" via entropy;
- distils trajectory rewards into a token-level value model $V^{\ast}$;
- reweights selected positions by $\exp(\beta V^{\ast})$;
- is evaluated by reward-model scoring against best-of-$N$ and chunk search.

Steering 20–80% of tokens beats dense intervention. SIA needs auxiliary model storage and repeated candidate generation; we use a fixed SAE direction, a single completion, and no guidance model. Protocols differ, so results are not commensurable.

Other work concentrates safety alignment or weak-to-strong steering in early tokens. SIA finds position-based gating competitive for safety at low ratios but degrading on helpfulness. This mirrors our SBS underperforming STS at matched nominal ratios; whether that persists at equal realized budgets is task-dependent (App. D.2). Random selection gives a training-free, position-agnostic control for evaluating selective methods.

#### Fluency–Alignment Trade-offs.
Large magnitudes cause disfluency, with a documented shift–coherence trade-off. Sparse application keeps the residual stream closer to its native distribution, yielding better fluency at matched shift.

# A Coin Flip Per Token: Bernoulli Sparse Steering of Large Language Models

###### Abstract

SAE-based activation steering usually applies its signal at every generated token, a constant perturbation that risks fluency. We introduce Stochastic Token Steering (STS), gating each token independently with probability $p$, and Stochastic Block Steering (SBS), gating a leading window once per sequence. Neither needs a reward model or learned gating policy. Across two model families and two behavioral tasks, steering a fraction of tokens recovers most of dense steering's behavioral effect with less fluency degradation. The best-performing steering magnitude consistently rises as the intervention ratio falls.

## 1 Introduction

Prompt-based behavioral control (toxicity, persona, refusal) is fragile: outputs shift under minor lexical perturbation, adversarial suffixes override alignment, and steerability is asymmetric and bounded. Activation steering injects a direction into an intermediate residual stream. SAEs give an interpretable basis, with decoder directions amplified to promote or suppress behavior. Standard implementations steer every token, though stronger or more frequent intervention can degrade quality. We ask how much of dense steering's effect remains when only a fraction of positions are steered.

STS samples $m_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ per position. SBS draws one $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ gate per sequence for a leading window, treating early-token influence as an atomic site.

Contributions:
1. Across two model families and suppression (toxicity) and elicitation (emotion) tasks, STS recovers most of the full-steering effect while steering a fraction of tokens, with less fluency loss.
2. The best-performing magnitude rises as the intervention ratio falls.

Control reduces to one interpretable parameter $p$, adding only a vector addition at inference.

## 2 Related Work

Contrastive and SAE-based steering apply a fixed intervention at every step. Concurrent SIA sparsifies logit-space intervention using a separately trained value model to select positions. It needs auxiliary-model queries during decoding and reports best-of-$N$ generation with reward-model scoring. We gate a fixed pretrained-SAE direction with no learned selector and produce a single completion. Results are not directly comparable, so SIA is treated as related work (Appendix A).

## 3 Method

For an $L$-layer decoder-only transformer $\mathcal{M}$, input $\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{T})$, and residual activation $\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$, we steer a single intermediate layer $\ell$, so later layers integrate the signal:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+\mathbf{s}_{t}.\quad(1)$$

### 3.1 Steering Direction Discovery via SAE

The SAE encoder gives sparse features $f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}$, and the decoder is $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}$. With positive set $\mathcal{P}$ and matched neutral set $\mathcal{N}$:

$$\Delta_{i}=\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\textstyle\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_{i}(x)-\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_{i}(x).\quad(2)$$

We take the top-$K$ features by $\Delta_i$, set $\mathbf{v}_{k}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_{k}}$, and form $\mathbf{v}=\sum_{k}\mathbf{v}_{k}/\lVert\sum_{k}\mathbf{v}_{k}\rVert$.

Figure 1: STS/SBS behavioral gain over no steering vs. $p$; dashed lines are prompting, full and no steering; bands are std.

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering

$\mathbf{s}_{t}=m_{t}\alpha\mathbf{v}$, with magnitude $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ and gate $m_t\in\{0,1\}$. Full Steering (FS) sets $m_t=1$ everywhere.

#### Stochastic Token Steering (STS).

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m_{t}\alpha\mathbf{v},~m_{t}\stackrel{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p).\quad(3)$$

A fraction $p$ of positions is steered in expectation. STS is position-agnostic and interpolates from no steering ($p{=}0$) to FS ($p{=}1$).

#### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS).

One gate $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ per sequence over a leading window $W\leq T$:

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}+m\alpha\mathbf{v}&t\leq W,\\[2.0pt]\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}&t>W.\end{cases}\quad(4)$$

This exploits the disproportionate influence of initial tokens.

## 4 Experiments

#### Setup.

Tasks:
- Toxicity reduction (suppression) on RealToxicityPrompts.
- Emotion steering (elicitation) on GoEmotions, mapped to Ekman basic emotions, with fear and sadness as targets.

Models: LLaMA-3.1-8B and Gemma-2 2B, each steered via an SAE at an intermediate layer. SBS uses $W\in\{32,64\}$. Every method adds norm preservation, activation clamping, and a decoding repetition penalty, since additive steering can push representations off-manifold (Appendix C).

#### Baselines and Metrics.

Baselines: No Steering, Full Steering ($p{=}1$), and Prompting with a curated instruction (Appendix B). Effectiveness metrics are mean toxicity reduction vs. no steering (RoBERTa classifier) and mean target-emotion probability gain (DistilRoBERTa). Quality metrics are GPT-2 perplexity and Rep-$n$, the fraction of recurring $n$-grams.

### 4.1 Sparse Steering Effectiveness

$\alpha$ is calibrated once at $p{=}1$ and fixed across methods and ratios (App. D.1). For LLaMA 3.1-8B:
- STS at $p{=}0.5$ recovers >95% of full-steering toxicity reduction.
- By $p{=}0.7$ it recovers >75% of full-steering gains on both emotion tasks, so most dense interventions are redundant.

STS beats prompting in 5 of 6 model–task settings:
- At $p\approx0.5$ or below for toxicity (both models) and LLaMA fear.
- At $p\approx0.7$ for LLaMA sadness.
- Never on Gemma-2 2B sadness, where prompting stays ahead at all tested ratios.

STS beats SBS at matched nominal $p$, most clearly on emotion; for LLaMA fear at $p{=}0.5$ it roughly doubles SBS ($W{=}32$) gain. The ordering holds for Gemma-2 2B too.

### 4.2 Fluency Under Sparse and Dense Steering

Figure 2 shows perplexity, Rep-3 and Rep-4 vs. ratio (Gemma 2–2B, toxicity). Degradation grows monotonically with density, and FS is worst on both. Sparse operating points generally cost less fluency than FS. The required ratio is task-dependent (smaller for toxicity than emotion). The trend holds across SBS window sizes.

Figure 2: Perplexity and Rep-3/4 vs. intervention ratio (std bands); both rise with density.

### 4.3 Steering Magnitude and Intervention Ratio

The best $\alpha^{*}$ (max behavioral shift subject to fluency preservation) rises as $p$ falls for both models. At fixed $\alpha$, effect grows with $p$; the ratio needed for a target effect falls as strength grows. Normalized residual displacement grows with $\alpha$ and $p$ (App. D.3).

Figure 3: $\alpha^{*}$ vs. intervention ratio (GoEmotions-fear).

## 5 Conclusion

STS and SBS are training-free, governed by one parameter $p$. Steering a fraction of tokens recovers most of the full-steering shift with a better fluency–control tradeoff. The best magnitude rises as $p$ falls.

## Limitations

- Coverage: two tasks on two model families. Other targets (hallucination, persona, multi-attribute) are unvalidated.
- Evaluation is classifier-based; human evaluation is beyond scope.
- SAE dependence: requires a pretrained SAE with identifiable features. Quality depends on dictionary quality and contrastive corpora.
- A single decoding configuration; interactions with higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, beam search, and gate- vs. sampling-level randomness are unexplored.

#### Intended use and dual-use considerations.

The aim is reducing harm (e.g., toxicity) and steering toward beneficial targets. The mechanism could be inverted to elicit toxicity, a concern shared by all activation steering. It needs white-box access and a trained SAE, so it enables no new attacks on black-box systems. We judge the net effect positive, especially where retraining is infeasible.

#### Use of sensitive data.

RealToxicityPrompts is research-licensed. We generate no toxic content beyond what prompts elicit and release no new toxic data. s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier carries known biases against identity terms, so scores are a comparison metric, not ground truth.

### C.1 Fluency-Preserving Regularization Details

Additive steering can drift the state off-manifold in norm or direction, inflating perplexity and repetition.

#### Norm Preservation.

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\|\mathbf{h}_{t}^{(\ell)}\|/\|\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\|\quad(5)$$

This rotates toward $\mathbf{v}$ without inflating magnitude.

#### Activation Clamping.

$$s_{t}=\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\cdot\mathbf{v},\ \hat{s}_{t}=\mathrm{clamp}(s_{t},\gamma_{\min},\gamma_{\max})\quad(6)$$
$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}^{(\ell)}+(\hat{s}_{t}-s_{t})\mathbf{v}\quad(7)$$

The upper bound prevents over-amplification; $\gamma_{\min}\geq0$ suppresses residual feature activation.

#### Repetition Penalty.

Steering suppresses high-probability continuations, causing repetition, so a standard decoding-time penalty is applied.

#### Effect of Fluency Preservation.

On a Gemma-2-2B toxicity subset, preservation cuts perplexity from ~82 to ~30 and Rep-3/Rep-4 by ~3×, with non-overlapping error bars. Steering is applied identically in both conditions. It is enabled by default.

# A Coin Flip Per Token: Bernoulli Sparse Steering of Large Language Models

###### Abstract
SAE-based activation steering usually perturbs every generated token, which risks degrading fluency. We ask whether dense intervention is necessary. Stochastic Token Steering (STS) gates each token independently with probability $p$. Stochastic Block Steering (SBS) gates a leading window once per sequence. Neither needs a reward model or a learned gating policy. Across two model families and two behavioral tasks, steering a fraction of tokens recovers most of the dense-steering effect with less fluency degradation. The best-performing steering magnitude consistently rises as the intervention ratio falls.

## 1 Introduction
Prompt-based behavioral control (toxicity, persona, refusal) is fragile:
- outputs shift under minor lexical perturbation;
- adversarial suffixes override alignment;
- steerability is asymmetric and bounded.

Activation steering instead injects a direction into an intermediate residual stream, and SAEs supply interpretable decoder directions for amplifying or suppressing behaviors. Standard implementations steer every generated token, yet stronger or more frequent intervention can degrade quality. We ask how much of the dense-steering effect remains when only a fraction of positions are steered.

Contributions:
- **STS** samples $m_t\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ per position. **SBS** samples one $\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ gate per sequence over a leading window, treating early-token influence as an atomic site.
- **Dense intervention is largely unnecessary.** Across two model families and both suppression (toxicity) and elicitation (emotion) tasks, STS recovers most of the full-steering effect while steering a fraction of tokens, with less fluency degradation.
- **Magnitude–frequency interaction.** The best-performing magnitude rises as the intervention ratio falls.
- **Simplicity.** Control reduces to one interpretable parameter $p$, with no reward model or learned gate. Inference overhead is only an activation vector addition.

## 2 Related Work
Activation steering adds contrastive directions to intermediate representations, and SAE methods use decoder directions of behavior-associated features. Both typically intervene at every step. The concurrent SIA sparsifies logit-space intervention with a separately trained value model that selects positions and is queried during decoding; its protocol adds best-of-$N$ generation and reward-model scoring. We gate a fixed pretrained-SAE direction with no learned selector and generate a single completion. Results are not directly comparable (Appendix A).

## 3 Method
Let $\mathcal{M}$ be an $L$-layer decoder-only transformer with input $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_T)$ and residual activation $\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^d$. We intervene at a single intermediate layer $\ell$, so the signal propagates through the remaining layers:
$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}+\mathbf{s}_t.\quad(1)$$

### 3.1 Steering Direction Discovery via SAE
The SAE at layer $\ell$ has encoder $f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}$ and decoder $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}$. Given a positive set $\mathcal{P}$ and a matched neutral set $\mathcal{N}$:
$$\Delta_i=\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_i(x)-\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_i(x).\quad(2)$$
We take the top-$K$ features by $\Delta_i$, set $\mathbf{v}_k=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_k}$, and form $\mathbf{v}=\sum_k\mathbf{v}_k/\lVert\sum_k\mathbf{v}_k\rVert$ (unit norm).

### 3.2 Stochastic Activation Steering
The signal is $\mathbf{s}_t=m_t\alpha\mathbf{v}$, with magnitude $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ and gate $m_t\in\{0,1\}$. Full Steering (FS) sets $m_t=1$ for all $t$.

#### Stochastic Token Steering (STS).
$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}+m_t\alpha\mathbf{v},\ m_t\overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p).\quad(3)$$
A fraction $p$ of positions is steered in expectation. The scheme is position-agnostic: $p=0$ is no steering and $p=1$ is FS.

#### Stochastic Block Steering (SBS).
Over a leading window $W\le T$, one gate $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ is drawn per sequence:
$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}+m\alpha\mathbf{v}&t\le W\\\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}&t>W\end{cases}\quad(4)$$
The whole window is steered coherently with probability $p$. This exploits the disproportionate influence of initial tokens and the finding that early-token intervention alone can steer behavior.

## 4 Experiments
#### Setup.
- **Tasks:** toxicity reduction (suppression, RealToxicityPrompts) and emotion steering (elicitation, GoEmotions mapped to Ekman basic emotions; targets fear and sadness).
- **Models:** LLaMA-3.1-8B and Gemma-2 2B, each with an SAE at an intermediate layer.
- **SBS windows:** $W\in\{32,64\}$.
- **Guards:** all methods use norm preservation, activation clamping, and a decoding repetition penalty (Appendix C).

#### Baselines and Metrics.
- **Baselines:** No Steering; Full Steering ($p=1$); Prompting (curated safety/emotion instruction, Appendix B).
- **Effectiveness:** mean toxicity reduction vs. no steering (RoBERTa classifier); mean target-emotion probability gain (DistilRoBERTa classifier).
- **Quality:** GPT-2 perplexity; Rep-$n$, the fraction of $n$-grams that recur.

### 4.1 Sparse Steering Effectiveness
Fig. 1 plots STS/SBS gain over no steering vs. $p$, with dashed lines for prompting, full and no steering, and std bands. $\alpha$ is calibrated once at $p=1$ and fixed across methods and ratios (App. D.1).
- **Recovery (LLaMA 3.1-8B):** STS at $p=0.5$ recovers >95% of full-steering toxicity reduction, and >75% of full-steering gains on both emotion tasks by $p=0.7$. Most dense per-token interventions are redundant.
- **Vs. prompting:** STS beats prompting in 5/6 model–task settings:
  - by $p\approx0.5$ or below on toxicity (both models) and LLaMA fear;
  - at $p\approx0.7$ on LLaMA sadness;
  - never on Gemma-2 2B sadness within the tested ratios.
- **STS vs. SBS:** at matched nominal $p$, STS beats SBS, most clearly on emotion. On LLaMA fear, STS at $p=0.5$ roughly doubles the SBS ($W=32$) gain; Gemma-2 2B shows the same ordering.

### 4.2 Fluency Under Sparse and Dense Steering
Fig. 2 plots perplexity, Rep-3 and Rep-4 vs. $p$ for Gemma-2 2B toxicity (std bands).
- Degradation grows monotonically with density, and full steering is highest.
- Sparse operating points generally cost less fluency.
- The required ratio is task-dependent: smaller for toxicity than for emotion.
- The trend holds across SBS window sizes.

### 4.3 Steering Magnitude and Intervention Ratio
Fig. 3 (GoEmotions-fear, both models) shows the best $\alpha^*$ (maximizing target-emotion gain subject to fluency preservation) rising as $p$ falls. At fixed $\alpha$, the effect grows with $p$. Conversely, the $p$ needed for a target effect falls as per-token strength grows. Residual-stream displacement grows with both $\alpha$ and $p$ (App. D.3).

## 5 Conclusion
STS and SBS replace dense steering with training-free, sparse random application governed by $p$. Effective inference-time control need not act at every token.

## Limitations
- **Scope:** two tasks and two model families. Other targets (hallucination reduction, persona enforcement, multi-attribute control) are unvalidated.
- **Evaluation:** classifier-based evaluation may miss dimensions of behavioral change; there is no human evaluation.
- **SAE dependence:** the method inherits SAE-steering limits. It needs a pretrained SAE with identifiable behavior features, and quality depends on dictionary quality and the contrastive corpora.
- **Decoding:** one decoding configuration only. Interactions with higher temperatures, nucleus sampling and beam search, and between gate-level and sampling-level randomness, are unexplored.

#### Intended use and dual-use considerations.
The aim is to reduce harmful generation and shift behavior toward beneficial targets. The mechanism can be inverted (e.g., steering toxicity features to elicit toxicity), as with all activation steering. It needs white-box activation access and a trained SAE, so it enables no new attacks on deployed black-box systems. We judge the net effect positive, especially where retraining is infeasible.

#### Use of sensitive data.
RealToxicityPrompts is licensed for toxic-language research. We generate no toxic content beyond what the prompts elicit and release no new toxic data. s-nlp/roberta_toxicity_classifier, like automated toxicity classifiers generally, is biased against identity-related terms, which may inflate or deflate subset scores. Scores are a comparison metric, not ground truth about harm.

## Appendix A Related Work
Dense methods (ActAdd, ITI, CAA, Representation Engineering, SAE feature steering) all intervene at every generated token; we depart from this.

#### Prompt-Based Behavioral Control.
Prepended instructions are simple and architecture-agnostic but fragile: outputs shift under minor lexical perturbations, and adversarial suffixes override safety instructions.

#### Dense Activation Steering.
- **ActAdd:** mean activation difference over contrastive prompt pairs, added at every forward pass.
- **ITI:** shifts activations of attention heads linearly predictive of truthfulness.
- **CAA:** averages over large prompt sets; layer-specific vectors.
- **Representation Engineering:** linear directions for high-level concepts (honesty, harmlessness).
- **DiffMean:** difference of class-conditional means; fewer side effects than naive contrastive approaches.
- **Style Vectors:** style-specific directions applied at each decoding step.
- **In-Context Vectors:** latent directions from in-context demonstrations, for controllable ICL.

All apply the identified direction at every position.

#### Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Steering.
- SAEs decompose polysemantic activations into more monosemantic features; residual-stream SAEs recover human-interpretable features.
- GemmaScope provides open SAEs for all Gemma layers at multiple widths.
- Amplifying concept features (e.g., the Eiffel Tower) reliably steers LLaMA.
- AxBench benchmarks steering methods, including SAE-based ones, on effectiveness and side effects.

#### Detoxification.
All existing methods correct at every step:
- **DExperts:** expert/anti-expert reweighting.
- **PPLM:** backprop through a toxicity classifier into hidden states.
- **Self-Debiasing:** suppresses probabilities of self-generated toxic text.
- **GeDi:** class-conditional LMs as generative discriminators.

On RealToxicityPrompts all incur some fluency cost. We use SAE directions and correct only a random token subset.

#### Selective and Sparse Steering.
SIA (concurrent) identifies "critical junctions" via model entropy and steers only there. It is reward-guided decoding:
- trains a token-level value model $V^{\ast}$ by distilling trajectory-level rewards;
- reweights the token distribution by $\exp(\beta V^{\ast})$ at selected positions;
- is evaluated by reward-model scoring against best-of-$N$ and chunk-search baselines.

Steering 20–80% of tokens beats dense intervention on alignment–efficiency. SIA needs auxiliary model storage and repeated candidate generation; we produce a single completion without auxiliary guidance. Because protocols differ, SIA is not an experimental baseline.

Safety alignment is concentrated in early tokens, and weak-to-strong decoding steers initial tokens. SIA finds position-based gating competitive for safety at low ratios but degrading on helpfulness. This mirrors our finding that position-anchored SBS underperforms position-agnostic STS at matched nominal ratios; whether that persists at equalized realized budgets is task-dependent (App. D.2). Random selection is a training-free, position-agnostic control against which selective methods should be evaluated.

#### Fluency–Alignment Trade-offs.
Large magnitudes yield disfluent text, and the shift–coherence trade-off has been studied and benchmarked across methods. Sparse application improves this trade-off by keeping the residual stream closer to its native distribution, giving better fluency at matched behavioral shift.

### C.1 Fluency-Preserving Regularization Details
Additive steering does not guarantee staying on the manifold the model decodes fluently. With large strength, or accumulation across tokens, norm and direction drift raise perplexity and repetition.

$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}\leftarrow\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}\cdot\|\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}\|/\|\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}\|\quad(5)$$

The upper bound prevents over-amplification beyond the feature's natural range. The lower bound $\gamma_{\min}\ge0$ suppresses residual feature activation already present.
