### D.3 Residual Stream Shift
Fig. 7 plots the normalized steered-vs-unsteered displacement at the steered layer vs. $\alpha$ for three values of $p$ (std band). Both enlarge it: $p$ adds displaced positions, while $\alpha$ deepens per-token displacement. They are substitutable routes, so at fixed $p$ a modest increase in $\alpha$ recovers the effect of denser intervention.

Control need not act at every token: most of the effect, with a better fluency–control tradeoff, is recovered when application is restricted to a fraction of tokens, dense steering being replaced by sparse random application governed by $p$ in the training-free QX7 and ZK2.

Concurrent A5Q is treated as related work (App. A), direct comparability of results being absent: logit-space intervention is sparsified by A5Q through a separately trained value model queried during decoding, together with best-of-$N$ generation and reward-model scoring, whereas intervention at every step is common both to activation steering, under which contrastive directions are added to intermediate representations, and to L8W methods, which intervene through decoder directions of behavior-associated features; gating of a fixed pretrained-L8W direction in the residual stream is instead performed by us, with no learned selector and a single completion.

Qualitative examples are presented; intentionally strong, the X8D baselines come from iterative engineering—emotion having phrasing, tone and directiveness varied and the one maximizing held-out target probability kept, toxicity variants ranging from simple ("Do not generate toxic content") to rule-based and the one with lowest mean held-out toxicity and coherent output kept.

The net effect is judged positive, especially where retraining is infeasible. The appendix contains toxic, offensive, and emotionally distressing outputs. A single decoding configuration having been used, interactions with higher temperatures, nucleus sampling, beam search, and those between gate-level and sampling-level randomness are left unexplored. Position-agnosticism is exhibited by QX7 (QX7 denoting the paper's stochastic token steering), under which the gated update
$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}+m_t\alpha\mathbf{v},\ m_t\overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)\quad(3)$$
is applied, with $p$ interpolating between the absence of any intervention ($p{=}0$) and M9V ($p{=}1$). The outsized influence of initial tokens is what is exploited by the alternative construction, in which one gate $m\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$ is drawn per sequence over a leading window $W\le T$:
$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}=\begin{cases}\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}+m\alpha\mathbf{v}&t\le W\\ \mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}&t>W\end{cases}\quad(4)$$
this construction being ZK2 (ZK2 denoting the paper's stochastic block steering). The signal in all cases is $\mathbf{s}_t=m_t\,\alpha\mathbf{v}$, of magnitude $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ and gate $m_t\in\{0,1\}$, and M9V (M9V denoting full steering) is obtained by the setting of $m_t=1$ for all $t$, the intervention itself being carried out at a single intermediate layer of $\mathcal{M}$, an $L$-layer decoder-only transformer in which $\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ is the residual activation at layer $\ell$, position $t$ of $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_T)$, so that the signal propagates through the remaining layers:
$$\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{h}_t^{(\ell)}+\mathbf{s}_t\quad(1)$$
The top-$K$ features by $\Delta_i$ give $\mathbf{v}_k=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec},i_k}$, combined as $\mathbf{v}=\sum_k\mathbf{v}_k/\lVert\sum_k\mathbf{v}_k\rVert$, the quantity $\Delta_i$ being computed, given a positive set $\mathcal{P}$ and a matched neutral set $\mathcal{N}$, as
$$\Delta_i=\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\textstyle\sum_{x\in\mathcal{P}}f_i(x)-\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{N}}f_i(x)\quad(2)$$
where the L8W at layer $\ell$ has encoder $f(\mathbf{h})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}}$ and decoder $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{dec}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{sae}}\times d}$.

{"id":"q7","type":"why","claims":["c4"],"pair":null,"question":"Why does STS yield a larger behavioral shift than SBS at the same nominal p?","answer":"At the same p, SBS steers far fewer tokens: only a leading window of W tokens can ever be steered, so its realized ratio is roughly p·W divided by generation length. {"id":"q8","type":"why","claims":["c1","c5"],"pair":null,"question":"Why are the reported sparse-steering recovery numbers, if anything, an underestimate of what STS could achieve at low p?","answer":"Alpha was calibrated at p=1 and held fixed for all ratios. {"id":"q9","type":"why","claims":["c6"],"pair":null,"question":"Why does steering effectiveness saturate as alpha increases in the full-steering alpha sweeps, rather than growing without bound?","answer":"Norm preservation rescales the steered activation back to the original norm, so larger alpha only rotates the state toward v, approaching a limit. {"id": "q47", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": "p2", "question": "For Gemma-2 2B STS on toxicity reduction, does raising p from 0.7 to 0.9 add more effect than raising it from 0.1 to 0.3?", "answer": "No. Going from 0.7 to 0.9 adds only about 0.011 (0.252 to 0.263), while going from 0.1 to 0.3 adds about 0.071 (0.122 to 0.193). {"id": "q49", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c4", "c7", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "A team proposes a learned token selector that steers about 30% of tokens on Gemma-2 2B toxicity, under the paper's alpha and decoding settings, and reaches a toxicity reduction of 0.18. {"id": "q52", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c6", "c3", "c5"], "pair": "p3", "question": "If the alpha calibrated under full steering (p=1) is applied at p=0.5, should generation be expected to stay in the stable fluency region?", "answer": "Yes. {"id": "q53", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c6", "c3", "c5"], "pair": "p3", "question": "If the best-performing alpha* found for a low ratio such as p=0.3 is applied under full steering (p=1), should generation be expected to stay in the stable fluency region?", "answer": "No. alpha* rises as p falls, so the low-p alpha* exceeds the value that suits p=1. {"id": "q54", "type": "why", "claims": ["c5", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Norm preservation rescales each steered activation back to its original norm. {"id": "q55", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper's construction of the steering direction combine the top-10 features in proportion to their mean activation differentials? {"id": "q56", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper directly show that alpha* rises as p falls for toxicity reduction and sadness steering? {"id": "q57", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the preservation ablation establish which of the three guards (norm preservation, clamping, repetition penalty) is responsible for the fluency gain? {"id": "q58", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c7", "c5", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that behavioral control is governed by the single parameter p with no other per-setting tuning? {"id": "q59", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c4", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Appendix A says SIA's finding that position-based gating is competitive for safety mirrors the paper's results. {"id": "q60", "type": "why", "claims": ["c3", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Why should SBS be expected to show less fluency degradation than STS at the same nominal p?", "answer": "Fluency degradation grows monotonically with the share of positions steered. {"id": "q62", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c1", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "If Gemma's STS fear gain at p=0.5 had been about 90% of its p=0.9 value, as toxicity's is, which statement in the paper would lose its Gemma support?", "answer": "The claim that the required ratio is task dependent, smaller for toxicity than for emotion steering, would lose its Gemma support. {"id": "q63", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Would STS be expected to show toxicity reductions of similar size (around 0.2 on Gemma) if it were evaluated on low-toxicity prompts instead of the paper's prompts with toxicity ≥0.6? {"id": "q64", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c4", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "A team needs a sad tone maintained throughout every output, including the final tokens of a 128-token generation. {"id": "q65", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c1", "c5", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "The high recovery of the full-steering effect at reduced p was measured with alpha calibrated in the saturation region of the p=1 alpha sweep. {"id": "q66", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c4", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Would STS's advantage over SBS at matched nominal p necessarily survive if each method were given its own best-performing alpha* for its density, rather than the shared fixed alpha? {"id": "q67", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c5", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "The paper argues that alpha can substitute for p because both enlarge residual displacement. ANSWER Q15: Yes. For guarded Gemma-2 2B toxicity steering, perplexity rises monotonically with intervention density, so STS at \(p=0.5\) should have lower perplexity than Full Steering at \(p=1\).

ANSWER Q16: Not settled. The paper shows that sparse steering is more fluent than denser or full steering, but it does not report a direct fluency comparison between STS and the prompting baseline at the crossover ratios.

ANSWER Q17: Not settled. The paper says prompting remains ahead of STS across the tested sparse ratios for Gemma sadness, but it does not explicitly establish that prompting exceeds the separate Full Steering baseline at \(p=1\).

ANSWER Q18: Yes, it should generally remain stable. The magnitude was selected to remain just below the fluency-degradation inflection even at \(p=1\), and lowering \(p\) reduces accumulated residual displacement and empirically lowers fluency degradation.

ANSWER Q19: The contrast that STS produces a single completion without repeated candidate generation or best-of-\(N\) selection would be lost. That single-completion inference procedure is a central distinction from SIA’s reported protocol.

ANSWER Q20: Contradicted. The matched-budget results say STS retains an advantage on toxicity reduction over much of the range, while SBS is particularly competitive on fear elicitation; thus they do not generally show position-anchored gating as especially competitive on the safety-like task.

ANSWER Q21: Yes. SBS with \(W=32,p=0.9\) achieves toxicity reduction \(0.230\), compared with only \(0.108\) for \(W=64,p=0.5\), despite their similar realized ratios of \(0.274\) and \(0.261\).

ANSWER Q22: If the window covered every generated position, each SBS sequence would be entirely steered with probability \(p\) and entirely unsteered with probability \(1-p\), giving an average realized ratio of approximately \(p\). At \(p=1\) it would equal Full Steering; below 1 it would be a sequence-level mixture of Full Steering and No Steering rather than token-level sparsity.

ANSWER Q1: Contradicted. STS is stronger at matched nominal \(p\), but Table 1 shows that after matching realized intervention budgets, SBS can be competitive or better on fear elicitation, so no universal ordering holds.

ANSWER Q2: SBS uses one sequence-level Bernoulli gate, producing a mixture of fully window-steered and entirely unsteered sequences. STS averages many independent token-level gates within each sequence, so its realized intervention fraction concentrates more tightly around \(p\), reducing between-sequence variation.

ANSWER Q3: The statement that toxicity reduction requires a smaller intervention ratio than emotion steering would lose its strongest low-\(p\) Gemma support. The substantial \(0.122\) reduction at \(p=0.1\) shows toxicity responding at very low density; a near-zero result would remove that evidence.

ANSWER Q4: It would be surprising that short early windows achieve effects comparable to random steering with similar or larger budgets. For example, SBS \(W=32,p=0.9\) achieves \(0.230\) toxicity reduction at a realized ratio of \(0.274\), versus STS’s \(0.193\) at \(0.287\).

ANSWER Q5: Pick SBS \(W=64,p=0.5\) based on the reported means. Its realized ratio is slightly lower than STS at \(p=0.3\) (\(0.261\) versus \(0.287\)), yet its fear probability gain is larger (\(0.092\) versus \(0.055\)), although their uncertainty intervals overlap.

ANSWER Q6: Behavioral response saturates even though residual displacement continues growing. With fixed \(\alpha\), additional steered positions can move representations farther without yielding proportional classifier-score gains, especially near the task’s achievable ceiling.

ANSWER Q7: Figure 2 shows that, for Gemma toxicity reduction, perplexity and repetition increase with intervention density and Full Steering lies at the high-cost end. Thus STS at \(p\approx0.5\), which beats prompting, should have lower fluency cost than \(p=1\).

ANSWER Q8: No, not specifically with the reported pipeline. Its classifier predicts Ekman’s six basic emotions plus neutral and has no gratitude class, though gratitude might be evaluated only indirectly if mapped to a broader class such as joy.

ANSWER Q9: Contradicted. The top features are selected using their mean activation differentials, but the direction is an unweighted normalized sum of their decoder vectors; Equation 2’s differential values are not used as combination weights.

ANSWER Q10: Generations are capped at 128 tokens but do not necessarily reach that length. Because the realized ratio divides by the actual number of generated tokens, steering up to 64 positions occupies more than \(64/128\) of shorter completions.

ANSWER Q11: No. STS samples fresh Bernoulli gates, and the decoding setup may also involve sampling despite its low temperature, so repeated runs need not match without fixed seeds, fixed gate masks, or deterministic decoding.

ANSWER Q12: The interpretation that intervention frequency and per-token strength are substitutable would lose support. In particular, there would be no evidence that fixed-\(\alpha\) sparse results understate low-\(p\) performance because sparse settings benefit from a larger retuned \(\alpha\).

ANSWER Q13: Not necessarily. At \(p=0.01\), many sequences may receive no intervention at all, while making \(\alpha\) extremely large risks off-manifold activations, clamping or behavioral saturation, repetition, and poor fluency; the paper does not test or guarantee this regime.

ANSWER Q14: No. The increase from \(p=0.7\) to \(0.9\) is \(0.263-0.252=0.011\), whereas the increase from \(p=0.1\) to \(0.3\) is \(0.193-0.122=0.071\).

ANSWER Q15: SBS generally realizes a smaller intervention ratio because it can affect only a bounded leading window, even when its sequence-level gate fires. Since fluency degradation rises with steering density, this lower effective budget should usually cost less fluency than STS at the same nominal \(p\).

ANSWER Q16: Yes. STS at \(p=0.5\) achieves \(0.237\) toxicity reduction versus \(0.263\) at \(p=0.9\), while steering only \(49.2\%\) rather than \(86.9\%\) of positions; the paper’s monotonic fluency trend therefore favors \(p=0.5\).

ANSWER Q17: Yes. The gain from \(p=0.7\) to \(0.9\) is \(0.251-0.165=0.086\), compared with \(0.055-0.012=0.043\) from \(p=0.1\) to \(0.3\).

ANSWER Q18: The model is autoregressive, so steering one position can alter the generated token and hence the context used at every later position. The intermediate-layer intervention also propagates through subsequent layers, allowing its behavioral influence to persist beyond the directly steered position.

ANSWER Q19: The fairness of the reported toxicity-reduction results would be most compromised. Using evaluation prompts to discover the direction would leak test-set information into the intervention, weakening claims that STS generalizes to held-out toxic prompts and unfairly favoring it over baselines.

ANSWER Q20: Yes. STS produces a toxicity reduction of \(0.122\pm0.021\), compared with \(0.065\pm0.021\) for SBS \(W=32,p=0.3\), despite their reasonably similar realized ratios.

ANSWER Q21: No, not as the paper’s SAE-based method. STS itself learns no gate or policy, but it requires a pretrained SAE with suitable features; training a new SAE would mean the overall deployment process was no longer training-free.

ANSWER Q22: Extrapolating the approximately linear all-or-none mixture gives a realized ratio of about \(0.274/0.9\approx0.304\) and toxicity reduction of about \(0.230/0.9\approx0.256\) at \(p=1\). That is nearly STS \(p=0.9\)’s \(0.263\) reduction, but with only about \(30\%\) rather than \(86.9\%\) of positions steered.

{"id": "q3", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c7", "c1"], "pair": "p2", "question": "If K were raised from 10 to 20 under the paper's construction of the steering direction, would the magnitude of the signal injected at a steered position change for a fixed alpha?", "answer": "No. The summed decoder directions are divided by their norm, so v is always unit-norm. ANSWER Q1: Steering effectiveness saturates because classifier probabilities and achievable behavioral shifts are bounded, while clamping and norm preservation limit effective activation changes. Beyond the useful range, larger α mainly pushes representations off-manifold and degrades fluency rather than producing proportional behavioral gains.

ANSWER Q2: Yes. STS achieves a mean toxicity reduction of 0.122 at realized ratio 0.108, versus 0.065 for SBS \(W=32\) at realized ratio 0.086.

ANSWER Q3: Not settled. Toxicity reduction and fear probability gain are different metrics with different baselines and scales, so the similar numerical values do not establish equal effectiveness across tasks.

ANSWER Q4: Not settled. The authors developed a strong best-effort baseline through held-out prompt engineering, but they cannot establish that no other prompt could perform better.

ANSWER Q5: This follows from the finding that behavioral effect increases with intervention ratio at fixed α, together with \(p=1\) being Full Steering. If STS already beats prompting near \(p=0.7\), Full Steering should also beat it.

ANSWER Q6: Independent Bernoulli gating has gate-count variance proportional to \(p(1-p)\), which peaks at \(p=0.5\) and decreases as \(p\) approaches 0 or 1. Variation in which positions are selected also contributes to output variability.

ANSWER Q7: It would undermine the explanation that increasing α deepens each intervened token’s residual displacement and can therefore compensate for a lower intervention ratio. The claimed substitutability of per-token strength and intervention frequency would lack its proposed mechanistic support.

ANSWER Q8: Yes. At \(p=0.9\), increasing \(W\) from 32 to 64 raises the reported fear gain from 0.070 to 0.135, nearly doubling it.

ANSWER Q9: Contradicted. STS deliberately selects positions randomly and makes no assumptions about which tokens are behaviorally relevant, so the paper demonstrates redundancy without identifying a dispensable set of positions.

ANSWER Q10: Yes, under the paper’s additive definition. With a unit-norm direction and no norm preservation or clamping, the immediate displacement at a gated position is \(\lVert\alpha\mathbf v\rVert=|\alpha|\), so it is mathematically unbounded as α grows.

ANSWER Q11: Contradicted. Table 1 provides one realized-ratio column and explicitly says those ratios are shared across both tasks, rather than reporting task-specific realized ratios that could be compared.

ANSWER Q12: At low \(p\), fewer positions are perturbed, so there is less cumulative off-manifold drift and fluency damage. The fluency constraint therefore permits a stronger perturbation at each selected position before perplexity or repetition becomes unacceptable.

ANSWER Q13: Not settled. The method avoids some vector additions when gates do not fire, but the paper reports no latency, throughput, or wall-clock measurements showing a meaningful speedup over Full Steering.

ANSWER Q14: The single-completion contrast would be lost. The paper distinguishes STS from SIA partly because STS does not require best-of-\(N\) candidate generation and reward-model selection.

ANSWER Q15: The fairness of the held-out toxicity-reduction evaluation would be most compromised. Using evaluation prompts for direction discovery would introduce data leakage and weaken claims that toxicity steering generalizes to unseen prompts.

ANSWER Q16: Generation is autoregressive: a steered position can change the next generated token, and that token becomes context for every later position. Thus, downstream unsteered positions can inherit altered context and representations from earlier interventions.

ANSWER Q17: The conclusion that sparse steering improves the fluency–control trade-off would lose support. Flat quality metrics would provide no evidence that reducing intervention density lowers the fluency cost relative to Full Steering.

ANSWER Q18: The recovery experiments hold α fixed at the value calibrated for \(p=1\), even though the paper finds that the best-performing α rises as \(p\) falls. Retuning α at low \(p\) could therefore recover more behavioral effect while remaining within the fluency constraint.

ANSWER Q19: No. SBS \(W=32,p=0.9\) gives a fear gain of 0.070, whereas SBS \(W=64,p=0.5\) gives 0.092 at a similar realized budget.

ANSWER Q20: A 64-token window contains roughly twice as many potentially steered positions as a 32-token window. Since the whole window is activated with the same probability \(p\) and sequence lengths are comparable, its expected realized ratio is approximately doubled.

ANSWER Q21: Intervention placement matters as well as token count: SBS concentrates its budget coherently in influential early positions, whereas STS distributes gates randomly. The difference is modest and the reported uncertainty intervals overlap, so Table 1 does not establish a definitive superiority at this point.

ANSWER Q22: No. The calibration was performed for generations of at most 128 tokens, while longer generations permit more interventions and longer propagation of altered context, potentially accumulating drift or repetition. Stability at 512 tokens would require separate validation.

ANSWER Q23: It can fail when the selected decoder vectors differ greatly in discriminative strength or norm, or point in opposing directions and cancel. Because the paper uses an unweighted sum rather than weighting directions by \(\Delta_i\), normalization alone does not ensure that the final direction reflects the most discriminative features proportionally.

ANSWER Q1: Not settled. The paper discusses DExperts, PPLM, and GeDi only as related work and does not experimentally compare STS against them.

ANSWER Q2: Contradicted. At matched realized budgets, STS retains an advantage over SBS on toxicity reduction, while SBS is described as competitive on fear elicitation; this does not show position-anchored gating as especially competitive on the safety-like task.

ANSWER Q3: No, it would not necessarily disappear. The repetition penalty is shared across steering densities, while the observed advantage is attributed to sparse steering causing less residual-stream perturbation; however, removal of the penalty was not directly tested.

ANSWER Q4: Not settled. The ablation establishes large improvements in perplexity and repetition, but it does not report behavioral scores, so applying the nominal steering signal identically does not prove that the guards leave its behavioral effect unchanged.

ANSWER Q5: No. The full-steering value was calibrated at 2.5 just below the fluency-degradation inflection, so an alpha* well above 2.5 at p=1 would conflict with its fluency-preservation constraint.

ANSWER Q6: No. At p=0.9, SBS with W=32 gains only 0.070 in fear probability versus 0.251 for STS, and increasing the gate probability to 1 would still restrict steering to the leading 32-token window.

ANSWER Q7: LLaMA STS at p=0.5 recovers over 95% of full-steering toxicity reduction, whereas both emotion tasks require about p=0.7 to recover over 75% of their full-steering gains. Toxicity also crosses the prompting baseline at approximately p=0.5 or below, while some emotion settings require higher ratios or never cross it.

ANSWER Q8: No. Activation clamping caps the projection onto the steering direction at 40, so increasing alpha from 35 to 70 can be partly or entirely clipped rather than producing the full additional projection.

ANSWER Q9: Not settled. Appendix D.3 shows that lower p produces less displacement from corresponding unsteered hidden states, which is supporting proxy evidence, but it does not directly measure distance from the model’s full native activation distribution or manifold.

ANSWER Q10: Yes, it should generally be expected to remain stable. That alpha was selected to be stable under the denser p=1 condition, and the paper finds that perplexity and repetition decrease as intervention density falls.

ANSWER Q11: The interpretation that fixed-alpha experiments conservatively understate sparse steering’s best performance would lose support. That interpretation depends on low-p settings having a higher optimal alpha than the value calibrated at p=1.

ANSWER Q12: Not settled. The authors use the top 10 features but report no ablation over K or comparison showing that 10 is optimal.

ANSWER Q13: Yes. Selecting the prompting baseline on the evaluation prompts would introduce evaluation leakage and undermine the validity and generalizability of claims that STS beats prompting, even if the reported numerical wins remained.

ANSWER Q14: No. Gemma-2 2B sadness is the stated exception in which prompting remains ahead of STS across all tested ratios.

ANSWER Q15: Norm preservation fixes the activation’s length, not its direction. A larger alpha can rotate the activation farther from the original state on the same-norm sphere, increasing their Euclidean displacement.

ANSWER Q16: No. Because the best-performing alpha tends to increase as p decreases, an alpha optimized at p=0.3 may be too large under dense p=1 steering and push perplexity or repetition beyond the stable region.

ANSWER Q17: No. STS gives a fear gain of 0.012±0.010, whereas SBS W=32 gives 0.035±0.016 at the nearby realized budget.

ANSWER Q18: The assurance that sparse results received no tuning at a sparse intervention ratio would be compromised. Calibrating at p=0.5 would specifically favor that sparse operating point, even if the resulting alpha were then held fixed elsewhere.

ANSWER Q19: Not settled. The paper cites adversarial-suffix fragility as a limitation of prompting but does not test STS or prompting under adversarial suffixes.

ANSWER Q20: STS is the better of the two because it can intervene at positions throughout the generation, whereas SBS stops after its leading window. For a strict guarantee at every final token, however, stochastic STS is insufficient unless p is set to 1 or another deterministic scheme is used.

ANSWER Q21: No. STS independently samples Bernoulli gates, and temperature-based generation can add further randomness, so repeated runs require fixed random seeds or deterministic gating and decoding to produce identical outputs.

ANSWER Q22: No. STS scores 0.055±0.019 and SBS W=64 scores 0.052±0.020, so the 0.003 difference is far smaller than the reported standard deviations.

ANSWER Q23: Not settled. The experiments cover only toxicity reduction and fear/sadness steering, and the limitations explicitly identify hallucination reduction and persona enforcement as targets requiring future validation.

ANSWER Q1: Contradicted. The top 10 features are selected by their mean activation differentials, but their decoder directions are then summed without weighting by the differential magnitudes.

ANSWER Q2: It would be misleading when the methods have different realized intervention budgets at the same nominal \(p\). For example, SBS affects only a bounded leading window, whereas STS gates positions throughout generation, so comparisons should control for the empirical fraction of tokens steered.

ANSWER Q3: It would weaken the inference that sparse STS provides a meaningful improvement over a strong prompt-engineering baseline. Beating a naive instruction would say less about whether activation steering outperforms carefully optimized prompting.

ANSWER Q4: They should increase \(\alpha\), since the paper finds that stronger per-token intervention can compensate for lower intervention frequency. They must check perplexity, repetition, and other fluency indicators to ensure the larger magnitude does not push activations off-manifold.

ANSWER Q5: Contradicted. At \(p=0.7\), Gemma’s fear gain is \(0.165\), only about 66% of the \(p=0.9\) gain of \(0.251\), so it is already below 75% of even this near-full operating point; Table 1 does not list \(p=1\).

ANSWER Q6: No. SBS samples one sequence-level gate, so at \(p=0.5\) approximately half of outputs receive no intervention at all, and even gated outputs are steered only within the leading window.

ANSWER Q7: Supported. The paper reports that LLaMA STS overtakes prompting by about \(p=0.5\) or below for toxicity and fear, while the sadness crossover occurs at about \(p=0.7\).

ANSWER Q8: Probably not. Saturation at \(p=1\) means some dense interventions are behaviorally redundant, whereas an \(\alpha\) in the steep, unsaturated region would likely make the effect more sensitive to removing interventions and thus reduce recovery at lower \(p\).

ANSWER Q9: Yes, it would be expected to exceed 2.5. Figure 3’s reported trend is that the best-performing \(\alpha^*\) rises as \(p\) falls, while 2.5 was calibrated under full steering at \(p=1\).

ANSWER Q10: Yes. At \(p=0.5\), Gemma STS achieves a toxicity reduction of \(0.237\), about 90% of the \(0.263\) achieved at \(p=0.9\), while the paper finds that lower steering density generally reduces perplexity and repetition costs.

ANSWER Q11: Yes. SBS with \(W=64\) achieves \(0.092\) versus STS’s \(0.108\), which is about 85% of the STS fear gain.

ANSWER Q12: Not settled. The paper shows that sparse steering generally has lower fluency cost than denser steering, but it does not report a direct fluency comparison between STS and the prompting baseline at their behavioral crossover ratios.

ANSWER Q13: At the same nominal \(p\), SBS generally has a smaller realized intervention ratio because it can affect only a bounded leading window, while STS gates positions throughout the sequence. Once realized budgets are matched, the paper finds no universal STS-over-SBS ordering.

ANSWER Q14: Yes. The gain from \(p=0.7\) to \(0.9\) is \(0.251-0.165=0.086\), whereas the gain from \(p=0.1\) to \(0.3\) is \(0.055-0.012=0.043\).

ANSWER Q15: Contradicted. The paper reports over 95% recovery at \(p=0.5\) for LLaMA toxicity, but its emotion tasks require about \(p=0.7\) for only over 75% recovery, and Gemma fear at \(p=0.5\) is far below 90% of its near-full effect.

ANSWER Q16: Gemma used different calibrated magnitudes by task: \(\alpha=35\) for toxicity but \(\alpha=30\) for fear. Because the paper finds that increasing \(\alpha\) can substitute for increasing \(p\), fear’s need for higher ratios is partly confounded by its lower calibrated magnitude.

ANSWER Q17: No. Gemma fear gains only \(0.012\) at \(p=0.1\), compared with \(0.251\) at \(p=0.9\), or roughly 5% of the near-full effect under the fixed-\(\alpha\) protocol.

ANSWER Q18: No. Raising \(p\) from 0.7 to 0.9 adds only \(0.263-0.252=0.011\) toxicity reduction, while raising it from 0.1 to 0.3 adds \(0.193-0.122=0.071\).

ANSWER Q19: SBS sometimes obtains competitive effects despite steering a much smaller realized fraction of tokens. For example, \(W=32\) at \(p=0.9\) achieves \(0.230\) toxicity reduction with a realized ratio of 0.274, close to STS’s \(0.237\) at a realized ratio of 0.492; that efficiency would be surprising if early tokens had no disproportionate influence.

ANSWER Q20: Contradicted. Although \(p\) is the main sparsity control after setup and \(\alpha\) is held fixed across ratios, the paper separately calibrates \(\alpha\) for each model and task and also chooses the SAE layer, steering features, and SBS window size.

ANSWER Q21: \(p\approx0.7\). This is the lowest ratio the paper supports for retaining over three-quarters of LLaMA Full Steering’s sadness gain while reaching the crossover with the curated prompting baseline.

ANSWER Q22: No similar reduction should be assumed. The evaluation deliberately uses prompts with toxicity at least 0.6, leaving substantial room for reduction; low-toxicity prompts would have a lower baseline and therefore less possible absolute decrease.

ANSWER Q23: Not settled, and direct carryover should not be expected without new validation. The steering vector and SAE features are layer-specific, and the intermediate-layer placement gives subsequent layers time to integrate the signal, an advantage absent at the final layer.

ANSWER Q1: No. STS requires an SAE-derived steering direction; without a pretrained SAE, the team would have to train one, so the pipeline would no longer be training-free.

ANSWER Q2: The claim that most per-token interventions under dense steering are redundant would lose its main support. Recovering only 60% at \(p=0.5\) would no longer show that half-density steering preserves nearly all of the toxicity-reduction effect.

ANSWER Q3: No. SBS with \(W=64\) achieves \(0.108\) toxicity reduction versus STS’s \(0.237\), or about 46%, well below 80%.

ANSWER Q4: Yes. The team could reuse Gemma’s SAE and overall pipeline, but would need joy-versus-neutral discovery data, recompute the top SAE features and steering direction, and recalibrate \(\alpha\); it should also construct joy-specific prompting and evaluation conditions.

ANSWER Q5: Yes. Section 4.1 says STS overtakes prompting on LLaMA fear steering by approximately \(p=0.5\) or below.

ANSWER Q6: The claim that toxicity reduction requires a lower intervention ratio than emotion steering would lose its Gemma support. A 90% fear recovery at \(p=0.5\) would make Gemma fear behave much like Gemma toxicity in this respect.

ANSWER Q7: Yes. Whenever the SBS gate fires, it steers the fixed leading positions \(t\leq W\), so both generations would have the same positional window steered, although their generated token contents could differ.

ANSWER Q8: No. Raising \(\alpha\) increases per-token residual displacement and can sharply increase perplexity, repetition, or off-manifold behavior, so matching full steering’s behavioral effect could erase the fluency advantage observed at fixed \(\alpha\).

ANSWER Q9: No. The reported nominal-\(p\) comparison uses a shared fixed \(\alpha\), while the methods realize different budgets and may respond differently to magnitude tuning; the paper does not test whether STS’s ordering survives method-specific \(\alpha^*\) optimization.

ANSWER Q10: A high recovery ratio says little when Full Steering itself produces only a small absolute behavioral gain. STS could recover nearly all of a negligible effect without meaningfully controlling the target behavior.

ANSWER Q11: Yes. The paper reports that Gemma STS overtakes prompting on toxicity reduction by approximately \(p=0.5\) or below, substantially below full steering.

ANSWER Q12: Contradicted. Although STS is generally stronger at matched nominal \(p\), Appendix D.2 says no single ordering holds at matched realized budgets, and SBS can be competitive or stronger on fear at comparable budgets.

ANSWER Q13: No. STS independently steers the first generated position with probability only \(0.3\), leaving it unsteered 70% of the time; later interventions cannot reliably repair a behavior determined by that first token.

ANSWER Q14: Not settled. The matched-realized-budget analysis is reported only for Gemma-2 2B, so it does not establish the corresponding result for LLaMA-3.1-8B.

ANSWER Q15: Not necessarily. The toxicity classifier may assign lower scores when identity-related terms disappear because of known identity-term biases, so the reduction could reflect classifier behavior rather than genuinely less harmful text.

ANSWER Q16: Raising \(\alpha\) can fail when low \(p\) causes the gate to miss behaviorally critical positions, because magnitude only deepens displacement at positions that are actually selected. It can also fail when larger magnitudes saturate, are limited by clamping, or push activations off-manifold and damage fluency.

ANSWER Q17: They should use 300 toxicity evaluation prompts and 700 evaluation prompts for each emotion task. Toxicity reserves 300 of 600 toxic prompts for evaluation, while each emotion uses 300 of 1,000 neutral prompts for discovery and the remaining 700 for evaluation.

ANSWER Q18: SBS \(W=32,p=0.9\) has the larger point estimates: \(0.230\) versus \(0.193\) for toxicity and \(0.070\) versus \(0.055\) for fear, at realized ratios \(0.274\) and \(0.287\), respectively. The trade-off is that SBS concentrates steering in the first 32 positions and leaves 10% of sequences wholly unsteered, whereas STS distributes interventions randomly across tokens.

ANSWER Q19: The additive vector has relative size approximately \(\alpha/\lVert h\rVert\), so it produces a smaller angular change when the original activation norm is large. Norm preservation restores magnitude after addition but does not change this direction.

ANSWER Q20: SBS with \(W=64\) and \(p=0.7\). It reaches a fear gain of \(0.113\) at a realized ratio of \(0.379\), the smallest listed budget achieving at least \(0.10\).

ANSWER Q21: They should prefer STS. It uses the existing SAE direction, needs no reward or value model, and generates one completion, whereas SIA requires a separately trained value model and auxiliary guidance during decoding and is reported with more expensive selection procedures.

ANSWER Q22: Not settled. The paper says STS at \(p=0.5\) roughly doubles SBS \(W=32\)’s fear gain and that STS crosses the prompting baseline around that ratio, but it does not provide enough information to determine whether the lower SBS gain also exceeds prompting.

ANSWER Q23: SBS samples one sequence-level Bernoulli gate, so its expected mean effect is approximately \(p\) times the effect of steering the fixed 32-token block, plus \(1-p\) times the unsteered effect. This mixture structure naturally produces roughly linear growth with \(p\), subject to sampling variation.

ANSWER Q1: No. The experiments use RealToxicityPrompts, and the paper explicitly says generalization to other targets and settings remains to be validated.

ANSWER Q2: The statement that “the trend holds across SBS window sizes, indicating it is not a method-specific artifact” would lose support. The monotone relationship would then have been demonstrated only for STS.

ANSWER Q3: No. At fixed calibrated α, the behavioral effect generally increases with intervention ratio, so STS at \(p=0.5\) should produce less toxicity reduction than Full Steering at \(p=1\).

ANSWER Q4: Not settled. The experiments use one decoding configuration with temperature 0.1, and the limitations explicitly state that interactions with higher temperatures and nucleus sampling remain unexplored.

ANSWER Q5: Norm preservation fixes activation magnitude but does not prevent large changes in direction, feature projection, or downstream representations. Thus increasingly strong steering can still move representations away from their natural distribution and cause repetition or incoherence.

ANSWER Q6: Contradicted. The paper explicitly says no single ordering holds at matched budgets; for example, SBS \(W=32\) achieves \(0.230\) reduction at ratio \(0.274\), versus STS’s \(0.193\) at the comparable ratio \(0.287\), although the uncertainty intervals overlap.

ANSWER Q7: Extrapolating linearly from \(p=0.9\), SBS \(W=32\) at \(p=1\) would have a realized ratio of about \(0.274/0.9\approx0.304\) and toxicity reduction of about \(0.230/0.9\approx0.256\). This is close to STS at \(p=0.9\), which gives \(0.263\) reduction, but uses a much larger realized ratio of \(0.869\).

ANSWER Q8: Table 1 defines the realized ratio as the fraction of generated tokens actually steered, and SBS has substantial nonzero ratios that increase with \(W\). If steering were applied only to prompt tokens, its realized ratio among generated tokens would be zero.

ANSWER Q9: The probability is \((1-0.3)^5=0.7^5\approx0.168\), or about 16.8%. Thus on short outputs STS has a meaningful chance of applying no intervention, making individual-generation behavior less reliable even if average performance is good.

ANSWER Q10: No. Norm preservation keeps the post-intervention activation at the original activation’s norm, so its immediate displacement is bounded by twice that norm and should eventually saturate rather than grow without bound.

ANSWER Q11: Not settled. The paper does not experimentally compare STS with SIA and says their different intervention spaces, training requirements, inference procedures, and evaluation protocols make reported results non-comparable.

ANSWER Q12: Not settled. Toxicity required lower ratios than fear or sadness in these experiments, but toxicity is the paper’s only suppression task, so this does not establish a general suppression-versus-elicitation rule.

ANSWER Q13: If \(W\) covered the entire generation, a fired SBS gate would steer every generated token and an unfired gate would steer none, giving an expected realized ratio near \(p\). At \(p=1\) it would equal Full Steering; for \(p<1\), it would be a sequence-level mixture of fully steered and unsteered generations.

ANSWER Q14: Not settled. The top ten features are selected by their mean activation differential, but the paper provides no human interpretation or validation showing that each represents a recognizable toxicity or emotion concept.

ANSWER Q15: No. The paper says the sadness crossover on LLaMA-3.1-8B occurs only around \(p=0.7\), so \(p=0.5\) remains below the Prompting baseline.

ANSWER Q16: Contradicted if interpreted literally. The full inference pipeline also samples gates, rescales activations for norm preservation, clamps projections, and applies a decoding-time repetition penalty, although the core steering intervention itself is an activation-vector addition.

ANSWER Q17: No. Activation clamping caps the projection to the allowed range, so increasing α from 2 to 4 would not yield the full added projection whenever the unclamped result exceeds the bound.

ANSWER Q18: Supported. The paper says Prompting remains ahead of STS at every tested ratio for Gemma-2 2B sadness, and STS at \(p=1\) is equivalent to Full Steering.

ANSWER Q19: Residual displacement is only a geometric proxy, not a behavioral outcome. Changes in α deepen each intervention while changes in \(p\) alter how many and which positions are intervened on, and nonlinear downstream effects could make equal displacement produce different behavior.

ANSWER Q20: No. The calibrated value assumes the guards are enabled, and the ablation shows that disabling them sharply raises perplexity and repetition; therefore α=35 is not established as a stable unguarded operating point.

ANSWER Q21: No. The fear gain is \(0.012\pm0.010\), which is close to zero relative to its variability, whereas toxicity reduction is \(0.122\pm0.021\) and is clearly separated from zero.

ANSWER Q22: Doubling \(W\) adds interventions at positions 33–64, whose usefulness is task-dependent. The earliest positions appear nearly sufficient or saturated for toxicity, while fear elicitation benefits substantially from steering the broader early context; the paper does not establish a more specific causal mechanism.

ANSWER Q23: SBS steers only a bounded leading window when its sequence-level gate fires, so at the same nominal \(p\) it realizes a much smaller fraction of steered generated tokens than STS. Fewer perturbed positions generally mean less accumulated residual-stream displacement and therefore less fluency degradation.

ANSWER Q1: Because generations can terminate before the 128-token maximum, the 64-token window can constitute more than half of the actually generated tokens. The realized ratio uses actual generated-token counts and is also affected by finite-sample gate randomness.

ANSWER Q2: It could steer a correlated or confounded behavior when the positive and neutral corpora differ in attributes besides the intended target. Polysemantic or low-quality SAE features and unrepresentative contrastive data could make the top differential features encode those other attributes instead.

ANSWER Q3: The team should use the curated prompting baseline. Prompting remained ahead of STS at every tested ratio for sadness steering on Gemma-2 2B.

ANSWER Q4: Toxicity reduction is already near saturation by moderate STS ratios, so the additional intervention produces little gain, whereas fear elicitation continues to benefit strongly from denser, distributed steering. Moreover, at nominal \(p=0.9\), STS realizes a much larger budget than SBS—0.869 versus 0.531.

ANSWER Q5: Not settled. The paper identifies an intermediate residual stream and says the SAEs are applied at the feed-forward sublayer, but it does not unambiguously specify the exact hook location within that layer, such as before or after the feed-forward update.

ANSWER Q6: Figure 4’s preservation ablation shows that disabling the guards raises perplexity from roughly 30 to 82 and increases Rep-3 and Rep-4 by about threefold. Thus, Figure 2’s absolute fluency values depend strongly on having preservation enabled.

ANSWER Q7: Yes. For example, the hypothetical SBS \(W=64\) result at realized ratio 0.261 would have fear gain 0.050, close to STS’s 0.055 at realized ratio 0.287; SBS \(W=32\) at ratio 0.274 already gives 0.070.

ANSWER Q8: Not based on the reported evidence. The paper says Gemma fear STS eventually surpasses prompting, but it does not place that crossover at \(p=0.5\); the explicit \(p\approx0.5\) fear crossover applies to LLaMA.

ANSWER Q9: Not settled. Figure 3 directly plots \(\alpha^*\) only for GoEmotions fear, while toxicity and sadness are not separately shown despite the paper’s broader summary claim.

ANSWER Q10: Residual displacement and behavioral effectiveness need not grow linearly together. Gemma’s toxicity reduction is near saturation by \(p=0.5\), so further displacement mostly yields diminishing behavioral returns rather than a comparable classifier-score decrease.

ANSWER Q11: It is possible in principle only if completions are sufficiently short, because 128 tokens is a maximum rather than a fixed length; a 64-token window is about 70% of a 91-token completion. However, Table 1 does not report an SBS operating point near a 0.7 realized ratio.

ANSWER Q12: Yes. Figure 2 reports that perplexity rises with steering density and places Full Steering at the high end, so STS at \(p=0.5\) should have lower perplexity under the same guards and fixed \(\alpha\).

ANSWER Q13: The fluency-constrained calibration of \(\alpha\) would lose its basis. In particular, there would be no perplexity/repetition inflection below which the authors could choose the largest effective, fluency-preserving operating point.

ANSWER Q14: SBS uses one sequence-level gate, producing a mixture of sequences whose whole leading window is steered and sequences receiving no steering. STS averages many independent token-level gates within each sequence, so its realized exposure concentrates more tightly around \(p\).

ANSWER Q15: Not settled. The largest model evaluated is LLaMA-3.1-8B, so the results provide no direct evidence for models much larger than 8B parameters.

ANSWER Q16: Not settled. The paper does not clearly specify the sign convention or reversal used to turn features identified from toxic-positive examples into a detoxifying direction, so positive \(\alpha\) and the \([0,40]\) clamp alone do not explain why toxicity decreases.

ANSWER Q17: Not settled. The evaluation reports increased probability for the target emotion but does not report changes in all other emotion-class probabilities.

ANSWER Q18: Full Steering’s fear gain should be approximately at least the \(p=0.9\) STS point estimate of 0.251, given the reported tendency for effect to increase with intervention ratio. Its exact \(p=1\) value cannot be recovered from Table 1.

ANSWER Q19: Yes. SBS \(W=32\) at \(p=0.9\) achieves \(0.230\) toxicity reduction at realized ratio 0.274, versus \(0.108\) for SBS \(W=64\) at \(p=0.5\) and ratio 0.261.

ANSWER Q20: The assumption that gate-zero positions are unperturbed would fail. Clamping could modify those activations even when \(m_t=0\), so \(p\) and the reported realized ratio would no longer represent the fraction of positions receiving any intervention.

ANSWER Q21: No. The crossover is measured using the specified RoBERTa toxicity classifier, which may be biased or disagree with human judgments, and the paper provides no human evaluation.

ANSWER Q22: The prompting baseline’s mean toxicity reduction must be below approximately 0.237, the STS point estimate at \(p=0.5\), because STS is reported to overtake prompting by about that ratio. This is an approximate bound subject to the reported \(\pm0.030\) sampling variation.

ANSWER Q1: No, not directly. The emotion classifier predicts Ekman’s six basic emotions plus neutral, and gratitude is not a separate class; at best, the pipeline could use a coarse proxy such as joy.

ANSWER Q2: The caveat that matched nominal \(p\) unfairly allocates fewer actual interventions to SBS would lose its basis. That caveat arises because SBS’s bounded window produces much lower realized ratios than STS at the same \(p\).

ANSWER Q3: STS’s realized ratio would remain approximately \(p\), while SBS’s average realized ratio would fall toward \(pW/512\), roughly one quarter of its value for 128-token generations. SBS’s apparent disadvantage at matched nominal \(p\) would therefore become larger because its fixed window covers a smaller fraction of the sequence.

ANSWER Q4: No such guarantee follows from the paper. Very large \(\alpha\) can push activations off-manifold, cause perplexity and repetition spikes, encounter clamping or saturation, and violate the fluency constraint used to choose \(\alpha^*\).

ANSWER Q5: The two methods do not steer the same number of tokens at nominal \(p=0.5\). Table 1 shows realized ratios of about 0.492 for STS versus only 0.134 for SBS \(W=32\), so the comparison does not establish greater efficiency per steered token.

ANSWER Q6: Not settled. Figure 4 ablates the combined preservation bundle on a subset of the Gemma toxicity setting, but it does not report the effect separately at STS \(p=0.1\).

ANSWER Q7: Choose SBS with \(W=32\) and \(p=0.9\). It achieves approximately \(0.230\) toxicity reduction with a realized ratio of only \(0.274\), lower than the realized ratios of the other configurations reaching about 0.23.

ANSWER Q8: Not settled. STS has a slightly higher point estimate, \(0.012\) versus \(0.010\), but the reported standard deviations overlap heavily, so Table 1 does not establish a meaningful advantage.

ANSWER Q9: Generally no. STS independently resamples Bernoulli gates for each generation, so two runs can steer different positions, although some positions may coincide by chance.

ANSWER Q10: Choose SBS \(W=64\) at \(p=0.5\). Its realized ratio is slightly lower than STS at \(p=0.3\) (0.261 versus 0.287), while its fear gain is substantially higher (0.092 versus 0.055).

ANSWER Q11: No. Magnitudes were calibrated separately by model and task: Gemma-2 2B toxicity used \(\alpha=35\), whereas the LLaMA toxicity value was \(\alpha=2\), so reusing 2 would likely under-steer Gemma.

ANSWER Q12: Not settled. The ablation toggles the three guards as a bundle, so it cannot attribute the fluency improvement to norm preservation, clamping, or the repetition penalty individually.

ANSWER Q13: Gemma fear must cross prompting somewhere above \(p=0.5\) but within the tested range, likely at \(p=0.7\) or \(0.9\). Using Table 1, this implies the prompting gain is above the \(p=0.5\) STS gain of about 0.108 but below the gain reached at the eventual crossover, and thus below roughly 0.251.

ANSWER Q14: Not settled. The paper compares STS and prompting separately but does not test a combined curated-prompt-plus-STS intervention.

ANSWER Q15: No. At \(p=0.9\), toxicity reduction is \(0.230\pm0.033\) for \(W=32\) and \(0.232\pm0.033\) for \(W=64\), an insubstantial difference.

ANSWER Q16: No; anger should receive its own magnitude calibration. The paper calibrates \(\alpha\) separately for every model–task combination, and it provides no evidence that fear’s value of 30 is optimal for anger.

ANSWER Q17: The choice to enable the full fluency-preservation bundle by default would lose its perplexity-based justification. Similar perplexity with preservation on and off would no longer support the claim that the guards keep generation closer to the natural manifold, although separate repetition improvements could still provide some justification.

ANSWER Q18: No demonstrated improvement. Random STS at \(p=0.3\) steers about 28.7% of tokens and obtains \(0.193\pm0.028\) reduction, so 0.18 is slightly worse and lies within the random baseline’s variability.

ANSWER Q19: Yes. STS obtains \(0.193\pm0.028\), compared with \(0.068\pm0.024\) for SBS \(W=64\); the 0.125 gap is several times larger than either reported standard deviation.

ANSWER Q20: The statement that toxicity reduction can use a smaller intervention ratio than emotion steering would lose its strongest low-\(p\) Gemma evidence. The reported \(0.122\) reduction at \(p=0.1\) is what demonstrates meaningful detoxification at that especially sparse setting, though results at \(p=0.3\) would still offer some support.

ANSWER Q21: Figure 2 provides that inference. It shows Gemma toxicity perplexity and repetition increasing with intervention density, with Full Steering at the high-cost end, so an STS operating point near \(p=0.5\) should have lower fluency cost.

ANSWER Q22: Not settled. The directly presented monotonic fluency result is for Gemma-2 2B on toxicity reduction, not LLaMA-3.1-8B on emotion steering.

ANSWER Q23: Roughly \(0.27\) toxicity reduction. Full Steering is equivalent to \(p=1\), and STS already reaches \(0.263\) at \(p=0.9\), with the effect appearing close to saturation.

ANSWER Q2: No. At \(p=0.9\), toxicity reduction is \(0.230\pm0.033\) for \(W=32\) and \(0.232\pm0.033\) for \(W=64\), so the increase is negligible.

ANSWER Q3: No, not directly. The emotion classifier measures Ekman’s six basic emotions plus neutral, and gratitude is not one of its output classes.

ANSWER Q4: Not settled. DExperts, PPLM, and GeDi are discussed as related detoxification methods, but the paper does not experimentally compare STS against them under a common protocol.

ANSWER Q5: SBS with \(W=32,p=0.9\) gives the larger point estimates: toxicity reduction \(0.230\) versus \(0.193\), and fear gain \(0.070\) versus \(0.055\), while using a slightly smaller realized ratio (\(0.274\) versus \(0.287\)). The differences are modest relative to the reported uncertainties, and SBS concentrates intervention in the leading window rather than distributing it throughout the output.

ANSWER Q6: Extrapolating roughly linearly from \(p=0.9\), SBS \(W=32,p=1\) would have a realized ratio around \(0.30\) and toxicity reduction around \(0.25\)–\(0.26\). ANSWER Q7: No. The reported crossover information implies that Gemma fear does not overtake prompting until approximately \(p=0.9\), so STS at \(p=0.5\) should remain below the curated prompting baseline.

ANSWER Q8: Yes. At \(p=0.5\), STS achieves \(0.237\) toxicity reduction versus \(0.263\) at \(p=0.9\), recovering about 90% of that effect while steering substantially fewer tokens; fluency degradation also rises with steering density.

ANSWER Q9: Roughly \(0.27\). STS already reaches \(0.263\) at \(p=0.9\), so Full Steering at \(p=1\) should be only slightly higher under the fixed-\(\alpha\) protocol.

ANSWER Q10: The missing fifth successful setting must be Gemma fear, with its crossover around the remaining tested ratio, \(p=0.9\). Since Gemma STS fear gains are \(0.165\) at \(p=0.7\) and \(0.251\) at \(p=0.9\), the prompting baseline’s gain must lie roughly between those values.

ANSWER Q11: Toxicity saturates at lower ratios: on Gemma, STS gives \(0.237\) at \(p=0.5\) and \(0.252\) at \(p=0.7\), close to its \(p=0.9\) value of \(0.263\). Fear rises much more slowly, from \(0.108\) at \(p=0.5\) to \(0.165\) at \(p=0.7\) and \(0.251\) at \(p=0.9\), showing that emotion steering requires denser intervention.

ANSWER Q12: They should use 300 evaluation prompts for toxicity reduction and 700 neutral evaluation prompts for each emotion task. Toxicity reserves 300 of the 600 toxic prompts after discovery, while each emotion task uses 300 of 1,000 neutral samples for discovery and leaves 700 for evaluation.

ANSWER Q13: Not settled. STS has a slightly higher point estimate at \(p=0.1\)—\(0.012\) versus \(0.010\) for SBS \(W=64\) and \(0.008\) for \(W=32\)—but the uncertainty intervals overlap heavily.

ANSWER Q14: It can fail when equally weighting the selected features ignores large differences in their discriminative strength, or when their decoder vectors cancel or point in conflicting directions. ANSWER Q15: Not settled. The ablation reports large improvements in perplexity and repetition with preservation enabled, but it does not report behavioral-effect measurements for the two ablation conditions, so it does not directly establish that effectiveness was unchanged.

ANSWER Q16: STS is preferable because it can intervene throughout the generation, whereas the tested SBS windows stop after token 32 or 64 and cannot directly steer later positions. If maintaining sadness at every final token is a strict requirement, however, Full Steering would be more reliable than either stochastic method.

ANSWER Q17: Contradicted. Gemma’s fear gain at \(p=0.7\) is \(0.165\), only about 66% of even the \(p=0.9\) gain of \(0.251\), so it cannot represent over 75% of a full-steering effect that is at least approximately that large.

ANSWER Q18: SBS draws one sequence-level gate, so a fraction \(p\) of sequences receive essentially the same fixed 32-token intervention and the rest receive none. Averaging this mixture across sequences therefore makes the expected behavioral gain approximately proportional to \(p\).

ANSWER Q19: No. Extrapolating SBS \(W=32\)’s fear gain of \(0.070\) at \(p=0.9\) gives only about \(0.078\) at \(p=1\), far below STS’s \(0.251\) gain at \(p=0.9\).

ANSWER Q20: No. At \(p=0.1\), Gemma STS produces a fear gain of only \(0.012\), compared with \(0.251\) already reached at \(p=0.9\) and a similar or larger Full Steering effect; that is under 5% of the dense effect, not “most.”

ANSWER Q21: The intervention changes the current token distribution, and the sampled token then becomes part of the autoregressive context for all later tokens. Later unsteered positions can also attend to representations produced at previously steered positions, allowing the effect to propagate.

ANSWER Q22: At the same nominal \(p\), SBS steers only a bounded leading window on the fraction \(p\) of sequences whose gate fires, whereas STS steers approximately a fraction \(p\) of positions throughout every generation. SBS therefore has a much smaller realized intervention ratio, which generally produces less fluency degradation.

ANSWER Q23: Not settled. The directly presented \(\alpha^*\)-versus-\(p\) result is for GoEmotions fear on both models; the paper does not directly present corresponding \(\alpha^*\) evidence for toxicity or sadness.

ANSWER Q24: With \(W\ge128\), each gated sequence would be steered at every generated position, while each ungated sequence would receive no steering. The realized ratio across many outputs would therefore be approximately \(p\), the average behavior would be a mixture of Full Steering and No Steering, and \(p=1\) would be exactly Full Steering.

ANSWER Q1: The claim that toxicity reduction requires a smaller intervention ratio than emotion steering would lose some of its Gemma support. The substantial toxicity effect at very low \(p\) helps establish that task-dependent difference.

ANSWER Q2: Not settled. V9Q shows that residual displacement from the unsteered state increases with \(p\) and \(\alpha\), and fluency worsens with density, but the paper does not directly measure distance from the model’s native activation distribution or manifold.

ANSWER Q3: SBS uses one sequence-level gate, so a completion receives either the whole leading-window intervention or none of it. This all-or-nothing mixture creates greater between-generation variance than STS’s many independent token gates, whose realized intervention fraction concentrates around \(p\).

ANSWER Q4: Behavioral response saturates: additional residual displacement need not translate proportionally into lower classifier-rated toxicity. By \(p=0.5\), STS has already captured most of the available toxicity reduction, leaving little room for improvement.

ANSWER Q5: Not settled. The paper describes contrastive feature selection and says the model is steered toward detoxification, but it does not unambiguously identify the positive/neutral class orientation for toxicity or fully explain how positive \(\alpha\) and the \([0,40]\) projection clamp guarantee movement toward lower toxicity.

ANSWER Q6: Yes. At \(p=0.9\), increasing the SBS window from 32 to 64 raises fear gain from \(0.070\) to \(0.135\), nearly doubling it.

ANSWER Q7: Choose SBS with \(W=32\) and \(p=0.9\). It achieves about \(0.230\) toxicity reduction with H9C \(=0.274\), the smallest realized intervention ratio among configurations meeting the target.

ANSWER Q8: The claim that toxicity reduction requires a smaller intervention ratio than emotion steering would lose its Gemma support for fear. If fear were already about 90% recovered at \(p=0.5\), its density requirement would resemble toxicity’s.

ANSWER Q9: Contradicted. The matched-budget discussion says STS retains an advantage on toxicity over much of the range, whereas SBS is competitive on fear, so position-anchored gating is not shown to be especially competitive on the safety-like toxicity task.

ANSWER Q10: The claim that the majority of dense per-token interventions are redundant would lose its strongest LLaMA toxicity evidence. That interpretation is primarily supported by the reported recovery of over 95% at \(p=0.5\).

ANSWER Q11: Yes. The gain from \(p=0.7\) to \(0.9\) is \(0.251-0.165=0.086\), while the gain from \(0.1\) to \(0.3\) is \(0.055-0.012=0.043\).

ANSWER Q12: No. The calibrated stable region includes the fluency guards; turning them off raised perplexity from roughly 30 to 82 and increased repetition about threefold in the ablation, so full steering at \(\alpha=35\) should not be assumed stable without them.

ANSWER Q13: Not settled. The paper says steering occurs in the residual stream at a single intermediate layer and Appendix C places it at the feed-forward sublayer, but it does not specify an exact pre- or post-sublayer hook point unambiguously.

ANSWER Q14: Generations are capped at 128 tokens but need not reach that length. For shorter completions, a steered 64-token window constitutes more than half—and sometimes all—of the generated tokens, raising the average realized ratio above \(0.9\times64/128\).

ANSWER Q15: Not settled. Figure 4 demonstrates a large guard benefit in a subset of the Gemma toxicity setting, but it does not separately test low-density STS at \(p=0.1\), where perturbations accumulate much less.

ANSWER Q16: Figure 2 supplies that inference. On Gemma toxicity, perplexity and repetition rise monotonically with realized steering density, so STS near \(p=0.5\) has lower fluency cost than Full Steering at \(p=1\).

ANSWER Q17: Not settled. The matched-realized-budget table and its claim of SBS competitiveness on fear cover only Gemma-2 2B, not LLaMA-3.1-8B.

ANSWER Q18: Not settled. The largest evaluated model is LLaMA-3.1-8B, so the results provide no evidence for models substantially larger than 8B parameters.

ANSWER Q19: No. The increase from \(p=0.7\) to \(0.9\) is only \(0.263-0.252=0.011\), compared with \(0.193-0.122=0.071\) from \(0.1\) to \(0.3\).

ANSWER Q20: Table 1 does not determine Full Steering’s exact fear gain because it has no \(p=1\) row. It shows only that STS already reaches \(0.251\pm0.021\) at \(p=0.9\), suggesting Full Steering is around or above that level if the reported monotonic trend continues.

ANSWER Q21: No. The crossover is established using a particular automated toxicity classifier, which the paper acknowledges can be biased, and no human evaluation was conducted.

ANSWER Q22: A high recovery ratio says little when Full Steering’s absolute behavioral effect is tiny or statistically uncertain. Dividing one negligible gain by another can produce a high percentage without meaningful target control.

ANSWER Q23: At the same nominal \(p\), STS steers far more tokens than bounded-window SBS. For example, Gemma at \(p=0.5\) has H9C \(0.492\) for STS but only \(0.134\) for SBS \(W=32\), so doubling the effect does not establish greater effect per steered token.

ANSWER Q24: Figure 4’s guard ablation shows this dependence. Disabling preservation raises perplexity from roughly 30 to 82 and increases Rep-3 and Rep-4 by about a factor of three.

ANSWER Q25: No. Toxicity evaluation used prompts from RealToxicityPrompts, and the paper did not test cross-dataset generalization; a different source could have different language, toxicity patterns, and classifier behavior.

ANSWER Q1: Yes. At \(p=0.9\), increasing \(W\) from 32 to 64 raises fear probability gain from \(0.070\) to \(0.135\), nearly doubling it.

ANSWER Q2: Not settled. The paper identifies the residual stream and says the SAE is applied at the feed-forward sublayer, but it does not specify the exact hook location within that sublayer, such as before or after the MLP/residual update.

ANSWER Q3: Roughly \(0.27\) toxicity reduction. STS already achieves \(0.263\) at \(p=0.9\), so Full Steering at \(p=1\) should be only somewhat higher.

ANSWER Q4: Contradicted. At matched realized budgets, STS retains an advantage over SBS on much of the toxicity range, whereas SBS is described as competitive on fear; thus the matched-budget results do not show position-anchored gating as especially competitive on the safety-like task.

ANSWER Q5: No clear expectation can be made at \(p=0.5\). The paper says Gemma fear STS eventually overtakes prompting, but it does not report that the crossover occurs by \(p=0.5\).

ANSWER Q6: Choose SBS with \(W=32\) and \(p=0.9\). It gives about \(0.230\) toxicity reduction at a realized ratio of only \(0.274\), the smallest reported budget meeting the target.

ANSWER Q7: Not settled. DExperts, PPLM, and GeDi are discussed only as related work and are not included as experimental baselines.

ANSWER Q8: No. The calibration used the fluency-preserving setup, while the ablation without guards increased perplexity from roughly 30 to 82 and approximately tripled repetition, indicating that generation can leave the stable-fluency regime.

ANSWER Q9: Not settled. The matched-realized-budget experiment is reported only for Gemma-2 2B, not LLaMA-3.1-8B.

ANSWER Q10: Extrapolating from \(p=0.9\), SBS \(W=32\) at \(p=1\) would have a realized ratio around \(0.274/0.9\approx0.30\) and toxicity reduction around \(0.230/0.9\approx0.26\). That is approximately the same reduction as STS at \(p=0.9\) (\(0.263\)) while steering far fewer tokens than its \(0.869\) realized ratio.

ANSWER Q11: Yes. The gain rises by \(0.086\), from \(0.165\) to \(0.251\), between \(p=0.7\) and \(0.9\), versus \(0.043\), from \(0.012\) to \(0.055\), between \(p=0.1\) and \(0.3\).

ANSWER Q12: It can fail when the selected decoder directions cancel, are redundant, or differ greatly in discriminatory strength. The formula sums them without weighting by \(\Delta_i\), so a feature with a much larger activation differential receives the same aggregation weight as a weaker one, and a near-zero sum would be unstable to normalize.

ANSWER Q13: Not settled. The largest model tested is LLaMA-3.1-8B, so the paper provides no evidence for models substantially larger than 8B parameters.

ANSWER Q14: Contradicted. At \(p=0.7\), Gemma fear gain is \(0.165\), only about 66% of the already-near-full \(p=0.9\) gain of \(0.251\), and therefore less than 75% of the actual Full Steering effect.

ANSWER Q15: If the window covers every generated position, the realized ratio would be approximately \(p\). Each sequence would receive Full Steering with probability \(p\) and no steering with probability \(1-p\), so aggregate behavior would be a mixture of those two conditions rather than tokenwise sparse steering.

ANSWER Q16: Generations often terminate before the 128-token maximum. A 64-token window therefore covers more than half of the tokens in many completed outputs, making the realized ratio larger than the calculation that assumes every output contains exactly 128 tokens.

ANSWER Q17: Not settled. Figure 4 clearly shows improved perplexity and repetition, but it does not report a behavioral metric for the guard-on and guard-off conditions, so it does not directly establish that behavioral effect was unchanged.

ANSWER Q18: No. Raising \(p\) from \(0.7\) to \(0.9\) adds only \(0.011\) toxicity reduction, from \(0.252\) to \(0.263\), whereas raising it from \(0.1\) to \(0.3\) adds \(0.071\), from \(0.122\) to \(0.193\).

ANSWER Q19: Not settled. The paper shows that sparse steering is more fluent than denser steering, but it does not report a direct fluency comparison between STS and the prompting baseline at their behavioral crossover points.

ANSWER Q20: They should use 300 evaluation prompts for toxicity reduction and 700 neutral evaluation prompts for each emotion task. Toxicity reserves 300 of 600 toxic prompts for evaluation, while each emotion uses 300 of 1,000 neutral prompts for discovery and leaves 700 for evaluation.

ANSWER Q21: Not settled. The ablation is reported for a subset of the Gemma toxicity setting and does not separately test low-ratio conditions such as STS at \(p=0.1\).

ANSWER Q22: No. SBS \(W=32\) gives only \(0.070\) at \(p=0.9\), so extrapolating to \(p=1\) yields roughly \(0.078\), far below the \(0.251\) achieved by STS at \(p=0.9\).

ANSWER Q23: SBS \(W=32,p=0.9\) gives the larger effects: \(0.230\) versus \(0.193\) toxicity reduction and \(0.070\) versus \(0.055\) fear gain, at realized ratios \(0.274\) versus \(0.287\). The trade-off is greater sequence-level variability from SBS’s all-or-none gate, reflected in somewhat larger standard deviations.

ANSWER Q24: No. At \(p=0.1\), Gemma STS fear gain is only \(0.012\), compared with \(0.251\) at \(p=0.9\) and an at-least-comparable Full Steering gain, so it recovers under about 5% rather than “most” of the effect.

ANSWER Q25: SBS samples one gate for the entire sequence, producing a mixture of fully block-steered and completely unsteered completions. STS averages many independent token-level gates within each completion, so its realized intervention and effect concentrate more tightly around their expectations.

ANSWER Q1: Not settled. STS overtakes prompting on behavioral effectiveness at several ratios, and sparse steering generally improves fluency relative to denser steering, but the paper does not directly compare STS’s fluency with the prompting baseline at those crossover points.

ANSWER Q2: No. At \(p=0.9\), toxicity reduction is \(0.230\) for \(W=32\) and \(0.232\) for \(W=64\), an essentially negligible increase despite the larger realized ratio.

ANSWER Q3: No. The emotion classifier covers Ekman’s six basic emotions plus neutral, and gratitude is not one of its output classes, so the pipeline could not directly measure gratitude-steering success.

ANSWER Q4: Not settled. DExperts, PPLM, and GeDi are discussed as dense detoxification methods with fluency costs, but the paper does not directly benchmark STS against them under a common evaluation protocol.

ANSWER Q5: SBS with \(W=32,p=0.9\) has the larger point estimates: \(0.230\) toxicity reduction and \(0.070\) fear gain, versus STS at \(p=0.3\) with \(0.193\) and \(0.055\). SBS uses a slightly smaller realized budget (\(0.274\) versus \(0.287\)), but concentrates intervention in an all-or-nothing leading block, and the reported uncertainty intervals overlap.

ANSWER Q6: Extrapolating from \(p=0.9\), SBS \(W=32,p=1\) would give approximately \(0.25\)–\(0.26\) toxicity reduction at a realized ratio around \(0.30\). That is close to STS at \(p=0.9\), which gives \(0.263\), but STS uses a much larger realized ratio of \(0.869\).

ANSWER Q7: No. The results imply that Gemma fear does not overtake prompting until approximately \(p=0.9\); at \(p=0.5\), STS’s fear gain is only \(0.108\).

ANSWER Q8: Yes. STS at \(p=0.5\) achieves \(0.237\) toxicity reduction versus \(0.263\) at \(p=0.9\), recovering about 90% of that effect while steering only \(0.492\) rather than \(0.869\) of tokens; lower steering density generally causes less perplexity and repetition degradation.

ANSWER Q9: Roughly \(0.27\) mean toxicity reduction. STS already reaches \(0.263\) at \(p=0.9\), and the toxicity effect appears close to saturation there.

ANSWER Q10: It must be the remaining fifth successful setting, with the crossover apparently between \(p=0.7\) and \(p=0.9\), or at the tested \(p=0.9\) point. Thus the prompting baseline’s fear gain is plausibly above the \(0.165\) STS gain at \(p=0.7\) but below the \(0.251\) gain at \(p=0.9\).

ANSWER Q11: Toxicity approaches its maximum at relatively low ratios: on Gemma, STS gives \(0.237\) at \(p=0.5\) versus about \(0.27\) under full steering. Fear is only \(0.108\) at \(p=0.5\) and \(0.165\) at \(p=0.7\), compared with at least \(0.251\) near full steering, so emotion elicitation requires denser intervention for a comparable fraction of its maximum effect.

ANSWER Q12: They should use 300 evaluation prompts for toxicity reduction and 700 neutral evaluation prompts for each emotion task. The toxicity split leaves 300 toxic prompts after discovery, while each emotion split leaves 700 of the 1,000 neutral samples.

ANSWER Q13: Not settled. STS has a slightly higher fear point estimate at \(p=0.1\)—\(0.012\) versus \(0.010\) for SBS \(W=64\) and \(0.008\) for \(W=32\)—but the uncertainty intervals overlap substantially.

ANSWER Q14: It can fail when the selected decoder directions cancel one another, are highly redundant, or have geometries that make the unweighted sum poorly aligned with the target. Normalizing the sum also discards the individual \(\Delta_i\) strengths, so features that discriminate well individually need not form a good combined direction.

ANSWER Q15: Not settled. The ablation clearly shows that preservation lowers perplexity and repetition—perplexity fell from about 82 to 30—but it does not report a corresponding behavioral-effect comparison establishing that effectiveness was unchanged.

ANSWER Q16: They should use STS, preferably at a sufficiently high ratio, because it can intervene throughout the full generation, including late positions. SBS with the paper’s \(W=32\) or \(64\) stops intervening after the leading window, so final tokens in a 128-token output are never directly steered.

ANSWER Q17: Contradicted. Gemma STS gives a fear gain of \(0.165\) at \(p=0.7\), only about 66% of the \(0.251\) obtained at \(p=0.9\), and full steering should be at least as strong as the \(p=0.9\) result.

ANSWER Q18: SBS draws one Bernoulli gate per sequence, so with fixed \(W\) and \(\alpha\), approximately a fraction \(p\) of outputs receive the same leading-window intervention while the rest receive none. The corpus-average toxicity reduction therefore behaves approximately like a linear mixture of steered and unsteered outputs.

ANSWER Q19: No. SBS \(W=32\) gives only \(0.070\) fear gain at \(p=0.9\), and linear extrapolation to \(p=1\) suggests roughly \(0.078\), far below STS’s \(0.251\) at \(p=0.9\).

ANSWER Q20: No. At \(p=0.1\), Gemma STS produces only \(0.012\) fear gain, compared with \(0.251\) already at \(p=0.9\) and likely a still larger full-steering value, so it recovers under 5% of the near-full effect.

ANSWER Q21: An intervention at an intermediate layer changes the current token distribution, and the sampled token then becomes part of the autoregressive context for all later positions. Consequently, steering selected positions—especially early ones—can redirect the entire continuation and affect later tokens whose activations are not directly modified.

ANSWER Q22: At the same nominal \(p\), SBS only steers a bounded leading window when its sequence-level gate fires, so its realized fraction of steered tokens is generally much lower than STS’s. Fewer displaced residual states should therefore produce less perplexity and repetition degradation.

ANSWER Q23: Not settled. The paper’s direct \(\alpha^*\)-versus-ratio figure is for J2V fear, while toxicity and sadness do not receive corresponding direct \(\alpha^*\) plots in the provided results; the broader trend is asserted but not directly demonstrated for those two tasks.

ANSWER Q24: With \(W\ge128\), every generated position would lie inside the SBS window. Each sequence would therefore be either fully steered with probability \(p\) or completely unsteered with probability \(1-p\), giving an average realized ratio near \(p\); at \(p=1\), SBS would be identical to full steering.
